rows.title: Constitutional evolution - Regulating Act 1773 to the Government of India Act 1935 (act-by-act provisions)
sub: Group-II M1-B-2: Constitutional development - Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act and the Charter Acts
Group-II M1-B-3: Constitutional development - Government of India Acts of 1858, 1909, 1919 and 1935

secs.t: Company-rule Acts → year → provisions (1767–1853)

x: The Charter Act of 1833 centralised legislation, reduced the powers of Madras and Bombay and made the Company purely administrative.
The Charter Act of 1853 separated legislative and executive functions, added six legislative members and introduced open competition for civil services.

The Regulating Act, 1773 provided for the Governor-General of Bengal and the Supreme Court at Calcutta; Pitt's India Act created the Board of Control; the 1909 Act introduced Muslim separate electorates; and the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy and central bicameralism.
The
Charter Act, 1853
created a functioning central Legislative Council, often referred to as a mini-parliament, by separating legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council.
Evangelical pressure, associated particularly with Charles Grant and William Wilberforce, contributed to the changes introduced by the Charter Act of 1813.

secs.t: Company-rule Acts → year → provisions (1767–1853) — Regulating Act 1773 - why Parliament stepped in

x: The correct sequence is Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Act 1793 and Charter Act 1813.
The Bengal famine, declining revenue and the Company's financial crisis compelled the British Parliament to intervene in 1772 and take control of Bengal away from the Company.
The Charter Acts were passed in 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853.
The 1833 Act barred discrimination by religion, birth, descent or colour.

secs.t: Crown-rule Acts → year → provisions (1858–1935)

x: The Act restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras and granted ordinance-making power to the Viceroy.
The Indian Councils Act, 1861 empowered the Viceroy to promulgate ordinances, each of which could remain in force for
six months
The indirect system under the 1892 Act operated through recommendations from universities, municipalities and chambers of commerce.
The 1919 Act provided for a High Commissioner for India in London, a Public Service Commission and separated provincial budgets from the central budget.

secs.t: Indian Councils Acts 1861, 1892, 1909 → provisions compared — Indian Councils Act 1861

x: Exam angle: "Indirect election launched in?" The answer is
The Act incorporated Indian nomination, recognised the portfolio system introduced in 1859 and retained emergency ordinance-making power with the Viceroy.
The
Indian Councils Act, 1892
began the practice of indirect election through nominations made on the recommendation of bodies such as universities, municipalities and chambers of commerce.

secs.t: Indian Councils Acts 1861, 1892, 1909 → provisions compared — Indian Councils Act 1909 - Morley-Minto Reforms

x: Exam angle: "Which Act..." one-liners; the 2018 key: the Act that allowed some
elected representation
Additional members were raised to 60 (total 69).
The
Indian Councils Act, 1909
(Morley-Minto) introduced separate electorates for Muslims and formal elected representation.

secs.t: GoI Act 1919 and dyarchy → provinces vs Centre

x: Montagu's declaration of 20 August 1917 stated the aim of gradually introducing responsible government in India and provided the basis for the Government of India Act, 1919.
The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy and ministries responsible to the legislatures took office from April 1937.
Provincial dyarchy was introduced by the Act of 1919, while provincial autonomy and proposed central dyarchy belonged to the Act of 1935.

secs.t: GoI Act 1935 → features, implemented or not — Basis and federation

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2024 paired "All India Federation" (correct) with "Defence and Foreign Affairs under the federal legislature" (wrong).
The Government of India Act, 1935 was based on the
Third Round Table Conference and the White Paper
Although legislative subjects were divided into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists, residuary powers were placed with the
Governor-General

secs.t: GoI Act 1935 → features, implemented or not — Legislatures and representation

x: The Act provided for Burma's separation from India, Sindh's separation from Bombay and Orissa's separation from Bihar.
The federal scheme
, office of Governor, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details were among the features carried into the Constitution.
Section 63 concerning the Governor's address became the basis of
Article 175
of the Constitution of India.

secs.t: Persons → role under the Acts

x: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
attributed part of the crisis to the absence of Indian opinion in the council, a concern addressed through later expansion and nomination of Indian members.
The first three Indians nominated by Canning were the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.
Satyendra Sinha
became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council under the Morley-Minto reforms of 1909.

secs.t: Institutions, councils and commissions → Act

x: Exam angle: "Board of Control was set up by?" - Pitt's India Act 1784.
The Council of India created under the Government of India Act, 1858 was abolished, and the Secretary of State was provided with advisers.
The RBI was set up in 1935 under the
Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Act provided for the Federal Court at Delhi, Federal/Provincial/Joint Public Service Commissions and the Reserve Bank of India.
The
Charter Act, 1853
introduced open competition for civil-service recruitment, although the idea had been considered earlier in 1833.

secs.t: Terms → meaning

x: Police, finance and land revenue
were reserved subjects administered by the Governor with the assistance of the Executive Council.

secs.t: FIRSTs and "which Act" → revision tables

x: Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and the United Provinces had bicameral legislatures.
Nomination of Indians began in 1861, indirect election in 1892, separate electorates in 1909 and a bicameral central legislature under the Government of India Act, 1919.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: These enactments progressively transferred control from the Company to the British authorities in London, strengthened centralisation and laid foundations for codified law and India’s legal-administrative system.
Section 63 of the GoI Act 1935 let the Governor address the provincial legislature, and ministries drafted the speech from April 1937.
Under the constitutional arrangements of 1919 and 1935, elected Indians occupied ministerial positions, and British officials had to function under Indian ministers.

rows.title: Indian Independence Act 1947; the Constituent Assembly - demand, composition, functioning
sub: Group-II M1-B-4: Indian Independence Act 1947 and the transfer of power
Group-II M1-B-5: Constituent Assembly - composition, committees, working and criticisms

secs.t: Indian Independence Act 1947 → dominion status, Governor-General, princely states

x: The arrangement permitted one common Governor-General or separate Governors-General, who were to act on ministerial advice.
India's Dominion status ended on
26 January 1950
, when the Constitution came into force and India became a Republic.
Paramountcy lapsed, ending British suzerainty over the princely states.
About 565 princely states were theoretically free after paramountcy lapsed, although in practice they were expected to join India or Pakistan.

secs.t: Composition → Cabinet Mission scheme, method of election, seats

x: The Cabinet Mission consisted of
Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander
The 1946 results recorded 208 seats for the Congress, 73 for the Muslim League and 15 for independents.

Provincial seats were divided among Muslims, Sikhs and General by population, and each community's members in the Provincial Assembly elected their representatives by proportional representation with single transferable vote.

secs.t: Persons → offices and roles in the Assembly

x: C.
Rajagopalachari
served as Governor-General from June 1948 to January 1950 and was the last and only Indian to hold the office.
The Drafting Committee included Ambedkar, N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, K.M. Munshi, Saadullah, N. Madhava Rau and T.T. Krishnamachari.
The original Preamble was illuminated by
Beohar Rammanohar Sinha
Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary President, Rajendra Prasad the permanent President, B.N. Rau the Constitutional Adviser and G.V. Mavalankar the Dominion Legislature Speaker.

secs.t: Committees → chairmen

x: Exam angle: Prasad - procedural committees; Nehru - Union ones; Patel - provincial and rights/minorities.
Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2004 wrong pair: "Steering Committee - Nehru" (it was
Prasad
Exam angle: APPSC GS 2025 asked for the Linguistic Provinces Committee chairman; the answer is
S.K. Dar
Dr Rajendra Prasad
chaired the procedural committees: Steering, Rules of Procedure, Finance and Staff, and the Ad hoc Committee on the National Flag.

secs.t: Dates → events (Assembly chronology)

x: Exam angle: "adopted on?" The answer is

The Objectives Resolution was adopted on 22 January 1947, the Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947, the Draft Constitution was published on 21 February 1948, and the third reading began on 14 November 1949.

Rajendra Prasad was elected President on 11 December 1946; the Objectives Resolution was adopted on 22 January 1947; the Assembly met as Dominion Legislature on 17 November 1947; and the Draft Constitution was published on 21 February 1948.

secs.t: Numbers game → time, sittings, cost, size

x: The Constituent Assembly completed its work in
2 years, 11 months and 18 days
The Assembly held 11 sessions, sat for 165 days, discussed the draft for 114 days and consulted about 60 constitutions.
The Drafting Committee sat for
141 days
The framers consulted the constitutions of about 60 countries and the expenditure was about Rs 64 lakh.

secs.t: Functions → symbols, language, legislature

x: Rajendra Prasad declared
Vande Mataram
the national song on 24 January 1950 and stated that it would be honoured equally with the National Anthem.

The National Flag was adopted on 22 July 1947 (a-iii), Commonwealth membership was ratified in May 1949 (b-iv), the Munshi-Ayyangar formula was adopted on 14 September 1949, now Hindi Diwas (c-i), and Rajendra Prasad was elected first President on 24 January 1950, the same day as the Anthem and the National Song (d-ii).

secs.t: Interim Government → dates and portfolios

x: The Muslim League called Direct Action Day as a protest against Wavell inviting the Congress to form the Interim Government.
Sardar Patel held the portfolios of Home, Information and Broadcasting.
Jogendra Nath Mandal held Law, not Defence.
The Interim Government was formed on 2 September 1946 under Nehru, the League joined in October 1946, and Prasad held Food and Agriculture.

secs.t: Statements and criticisms → who said

x: Naziruddin Ahmed called the Drafting Committee a "Drifting Committee" (a–ii); Viscount Simon called the Assembly "a body of Hindus" (b–iv); Winston Churchill said it represented "only one major community" (c–i); Granville Austin called it "a one-party body in an essentially one-party country" (d–iii).
The Constitution was called 'borrowed' or a 'patchwork' because it drew heavily on provisions from various constitutions and sources.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee rejected linguistic States at the time, but the Andhra demand continued and resulted in the Andhra State of 1953.
The debate has been connected with the Constituent Assembly’s statement of 24 January 1950 and the Supreme Court decision in Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986).

rows.title: Sources of the Indian Constitution - borrowed features and their origin countries
sub: Group-II M1-B-6: Sources of the Indian Constitution and borrowed features

secs.t: GoI Act 1935 → the single largest source

x: The 1935 Act contributed extensive administrative provisions, making the Indian Constitution unusually detailed and bulky.

secs.t: Feature → source country (parliamentary, rights, Preamble)

x: Britain has no single written Constitution, yet India borrowed its parliamentary system and conventions from the British model.
The Directive Principles were inspired by
Ireland
; Ireland had, in turn, taken the idea from Spain.
The Emergency-related provision for suspension of Fundamental Rights was influenced by the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

secs.t: Feature → source country (federal, judicial, amendment)

x: All four features are associated with the Canadian model: a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, centrally appointed Governors and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
The framers followed the Canadian scheme of dividing subjects but added the Concurrent List, which came from Australia.
Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of the judiciary and impeachment of the President are among the features borrowed from the United States.
The method of election of the President of India was borrowed from Ireland, whereas the impeachment procedure was borrowed from the United States.

secs.t: Country → features (match list)

x: Prerogative writs were borrowed from Britain.
The office of Vice-President was borrowed from the United States of America.
The Directive Principles and nomination of Rajya Sabha members came from Ireland.
The ideals of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble were borrowed from the USSR.
Fundamental Duties were borrowed from the USSR, not France.
Residuary powers with the Centre were borrowed from Canada.

secs.t: Articles → borrowed feature (number game)

x: Most Fundamental Rights can be suspended during a National Emergency, an idea borrowed from Weimar Germany, but Articles 20 (protection in respect of conviction for offences) and 21 (life and personal liberty) cannot.

secs.t: Traps, disputes and PYQ keys

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2023 matching key -
Emergency provisions → GoI Act 1935
Suspension of FRs → Weimar Germany
Concurrent List → Australia
Single citizenship → Britain
Exam angle: APPSC asked "bicameralism from?", "single citizenship from?" and "which borrowed feature is from Britain?" (cabinet system, GS 2019). The answer each time is
Britain
. Distractors are USA and Canada.
Exam angle: the traps are residuary powers (Canada, not USA; in the US they rest with the states) and the Concurrent List (Australia, not Canada).
Exam angle: List I (feature) - List II (country) matching, and "which of these is from Britain?" (APPSC-GS 2019 key:
Cabinet system

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form important elements of the Constitution’s philosophical part, while the parliamentary system belongs to its political part.
The description refers to the large number of provisions and institutional ideas drawn from foreign constitutions and earlier governing laws.

The framers adapted borrowed provisions to Indian conditions and incorporated distinctive features, including the Directive Principles as a novel feature and the federal-unitary flexibility suited to India.

rows.title: Salient features of the Indian Constitution - lengthiest, blend of rigidity and flexibility, quasi-federal etc.
sub: Group-II M1-B-7: Salient features of the Indian Constitution

secs.t: Lengthiest Constitution — counts, Parts and FIRSTs — Written, single document — who said

x: Exam angle: "How many Articles in the original Constitution?" → 395.
The original Constitution had 395 Articles in 22 Parts.
New provisions are frequently inserted through lettered Articles, such as Article 21A and Article 51A, while the original numbering continues to end at Article 395.
H.V. Kamath
used the expression 'elephantine size' for the Constitution (APPSC 2018 key).

secs.t: Lengthiest Constitution — counts, Parts and FIRSTs — Parts added and repealed → amendment

x: Part VII was repealed by the Seventh Amendment in 1956; Part IVA was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976; Part IXA by the 74th Amendment in 1992; and Part IXB by the 97th Amendment in 2011.

All four factors contributed to the Constitution's length: India's diversity, the 1935 Act's influence, the prominence of lawyers in the Assembly and the inclusion of detailed administrative provisions.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: constitutionalism, supremacy, democracy, republic

x: Constitutionalism means that governmental power is limited by a supreme Constitution and exercised according to established rules rather than the personal will of the ruler.
The Preamble begins with '
We, the People of India
', signifying that the people are the ultimate source of constitutional authority.
India is a sovereign democratic republic because its head of state, the President, is elected rather than hereditary; ultimate authority rests with the people.

secs.t: Parliamentary form — features and comparisons with the USA and Britain

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2019 keyed "India's head of state is elected; Britain rests on parliamentary sovereignty; Indian Parliament is not sovereign" as correct, and "Britain's head is elected" as wrong.
India adopted the parliamentary form of government from the British model rather than the American presidential model.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the
Lok Sabha
under the parliamentary system.

secs.t: Other salient features → provisions, Articles and amendments

x: India blends parliamentary sovereignty (Britain) with judicial supremacy (USA), and courts can strike down laws.
The Right to Property ceased to be a Fundamental Right and is now protected by Article 300A as a constitutional legal right.
The 73rd (Panchayats) and 74th (Municipalities) Amendments of 1992 created the third tier.
The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age under universal adult franchise from 21 to 18.

secs.t: Which is NOT a feature — odd-one-out sets

x: India is a secular state and has no state religion.
India has a parliamentary form of government, not a presidential form.
India is described as
a Union of States with a parliamentary system of government

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The quasi-federal character is explained by the combination of federal features with a strong Centre and a parliamentary system.
The associations are: written Constitution—United States; parliamentary government—Britain; strong Centre—Canada; Concurrent List—Australia; amendment procedure—South Africa.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950; the commencement of the Republic under the Constitution corresponds to the latter date.

rows.title: Preamble - text, keywords, 42nd Amendment; is the Preamble part of the Constitution (Berubari, Kesavananda)
sub: Group-II M1-B-8: Preamble - text, keywords, the 42nd Amendment and its amendability

secs.t: Making of the Preamble — Objectives Resolution and sources → country

x: The ideal of social, economic and political justice is associated with the
Russian Revolution
The Preamble is a modified version of the
Objectives Resolution
moved by Jawaharlal Nehru and adopted by the Constituent Assembly.
The language of the Preamble is credited to the
Australia
n Constitution, while the idea of having a Preamble is associated with the United States Constitution.

secs.t: Preamble text — order of words, dates, original vs absent words

x: The Preamble does not contain the expression “
adult franchise
.” It does refer to unity and integrity of the Nation, dignity of the individual and economic justice.

The Preamble now reads 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'. 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were inserted by the 42nd Amendment between 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic' of the original 'Sovereign Democratic Republic'.

secs.t: Keywords and objectives → meaning — Keywords

x: ‘Sovereign’ means that India is internally and externally free, is not subject to external control and can determine its own foreign policy.
Before 1976, the word ‘secular’ appeared in Article 25(2)(a), which refers to secular activities associated with religious practice.
Indian socialism is democratic socialism with a mixed economy, a blend of Marxism and Gandhism leaning towards Gandhian socialism.

secs.t: Keywords and objectives → meaning — Objectives → kinds named in the text

x: The Preamble specifically mentions liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, and equality of status and opportunity.
Social justice concerns equality without social distinctions, economic justice seeks to remove glaring inequalities and political justice provides equal political rights and access to office.
Liberty means the absence of unreasonable restraints on individual activity along with opportunities for the development of one’s personality; it does not mean absolute freedom from all restraints.

secs.t: Cases on the Preamble → year and holding; legal effect — Is the Preamble part of the Constitution

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2025 asked "Preamble is an integral part - which case?" The answer is
Kesavananda Bharati
. Golaknath, Minerva Mills and Gopalan are the distractors.

In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Preamble was held not to be a part of the Constitution, although it was regarded as a key to the minds of the framers and an aid to interpretation in cases of ambiguity.

secs.t: Cases on the Preamble → year and holding; legal effect — Amendability and secularism as basic structure

x: Waman Rao (1981) held that basic-structure review applies to amendments made after
24 April 1973
On 25 November 2024, the Supreme Court upheld ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble and rejected challenges to the 42nd Amendment insertions.
The constitutional position is that secularism was part of the basic structure even before the word was inserted in 1976.

secs.t: Cases on the Preamble → year and holding; legal effect — Legal effect

x: The Preamble is neither a source of nor a limit on power, and it is non-justiciable.

secs.t: 42nd Amendment, 1976 → words added and other changes

x: Exam angle: APPSC asked "Secular added by?" in G2 2023 and G2 2025, and "Socialist and Secular added by?" in GS 2025. The answer is always the
42nd
. Distractors are the 44th, 43rd, 45th, 52nd and 86th.
The 42nd Amendment, the only amendment of the Preamble so far, added three words: Socialist, Secular and Integrity ('unity and integrity of the Nation').

secs.t: Persons → descriptions of the Preamble (who said)

x: Palkhivala called it the 'identity card' and Ernest Barker the 'key-note'.
K. M. Munshi is associated with the description ‘Political horoscope’ of the Constitution.
In the Berubari case, the Supreme Court referred to the Preamble as the ‘key to the minds of the makers’ of the Constitution.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The counter-view is that secularism was inherent in the Constitution even before the insertion of the word, with Articles 25 to 28 cited in support.
The Supreme Court upheld the words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble and rejected challenges to their insertion through the 42nd Amendment.
The Preamble has been amended only once, by the 42nd Amendment of 1976, which inserted 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'.

rows.title: Parts, Schedules and Articles of the Constitution - structural map and the twelve schedules

secs.t: Parts → subject matter and Article range

x: Exam angle: "Part dealing with the Union Executive?" The answer is
Part V
Part XV (Elections) covers Articles 324 to 329A, not 352 to 360; Articles 352-360 form Part XVIII (Emergency).
Part XII deals with Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits and covers Articles 264 to 300A (Article 300A now protects the right to property as a legal right).

secs.t: Deleted Parts and Articles → amendment
Twelve Schedules → subject matter and Articles

x: Exam angle: "First Schedule contains?" The answer is the
states and UTs
. "Official languages schedule?" The answer is the
Eighth
The
First Schedule
contains the names of the States and Union Territories and specifies their respective territories.
The Seventh Schedule has the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Art. 246); oaths and affirmations are in the Third Schedule.

secs.t: Schedules number game — Seventh and Ninth lists, Third Schedule oaths

x: The Ninth Schedule originally contained 13 Acts, presently contains 282 Acts, is connected with Article 31B, and laws added after 24 April 1973 may be examined by the Supreme Court.
The Third Schedule prescribes the oath or affirmation for the
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
The Union List grew from 97 to 98 subjects and the State List shrank from 66 to 59.

secs.t: Articles number game → subject; special provisions for states

x: Article 371A is for Nagaland; Assam is Article 371B (371C is Manipur).
Articles 371D and 371E were inserted by the 32nd Amendment Act, 1973, in the context of the Six-Point Formula following the Jai Andhra and Telangana agitations.
Article 371J provides special provisions for
the Hyderabad-Karnataka region of Karnataka
and was introduced by the 98th Amendment Act, 2012.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gor Boli, also known as Lambadi, is the Banjara language of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana for which continuing demands for Eighth Schedule inclusion have been reported.
The First Amendment Act, 1951, followed Champakam and land-reform cases and inserted Article 15(4), Articles 31A and 31B, and the Ninth Schedule.
Articles 371D and 371E were inserted by the
32nd Amendment, 1973
, as Andhra Pradesh-specific provisions.

rows.title: Union and its territory - Articles 1-4; formation of new states, cession of territory

secs.t: Reorganisation Acts → states formed, year and amendment — Linguistic reorganisation

x: Exam angle: chronological ordering (Andhra State → Nagaland → Haryana → Sikkim → Goa → Telangana) and amendment-to-state matching.
The correct sequence is Andhra State (1953), Nagaland (1963), Haryana (1966), Sikkim (1975), Goa (1987) and Telangana (2014).
The SR Act 1956 created 14 States and 6 UTs, formed Andhra Pradesh from Andhra State plus the Telangana region of Hyderabad, and set up Zonal Councils (Kerala was also formed).

secs.t: Reorganisation Acts → states formed, year and amendment — J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 — first state downgraded to Union Territories

x: The Article 370 order was issued on
5 August 2019
; the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act took effect later, on 31 October 2019.
After Jammu and Kashmir became two Union Territories in 2019 - the first State so downgraded - India has 28 States; the count of 29 applied only before August 2019.

secs.t: Cession of territory → cases, agreements and amendments

x: The 1969 position distinguished boundary settlement from cession of territory and held that executive action could suffice without a constitutional amendment.
The arrangement involved 111 Indian enclaves going to Bangladesh and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves going to India.
The Land Boundary Agreement was implemented through the 100th Constitutional Amendment, 2015, which amended the First Schedule entries relating to Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura.

secs.t: Union Territories — number game and administration

x: The Act created Jammu and Kashmir as a Union Territory with a legislature and Ladakh without one, abolished the Legislative Council and took effect on 31 October 2019.
Article 239(2) permits
the Governor of an adjoining State
to be appointed as the administrator of a Union Territory; the Governor of Punjab administers Chandigarh as an example.
The merged UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu came into effect on
26 January 2020

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The sequence is Andhra State in 1953, Andhra Pradesh in 1956, bifurcation in 2014, and the 2026 amendment making Amaravati the sole capital of Andhra Pradesh.
The proposed Chapter K under Article 371 is for Ladakh, not Jammu and Kashmir.
Jammu and Kashmir became the first State to be downgraded to Union Territories in 2019.

rows.title: Citizenship - Articles 5-11; Citizenship Act 1955, acquisition and loss, OCI, CAA 2019
sub: Group-II M1-B-9: Union and its territory (Articles 1-4) and citizenship (Articles 5-11)

secs.t: Articles 5–11 → provision; citizen-only rights and authority

x: Article 5 recognised citizenship at commencement for a person domiciled in India who fulfilled conditions such as birth in India, birth of either parent in India, or ordinary residence in India for five years.

Articles 6, 7 and 8 respectively concern migrants from Pakistan, certain returnees from Pakistan, and persons of Indian origin residing abroad who are registered by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
The Union Home Ministry frames citizenship rules, whereas the Election Commission checks citizenship in relation to electoral rolls under Article 324.

secs.t: Single vs dual citizenship — features and other countries

x: The United States and Switzerland recognise national as well as state or cantonal citizenship.
The Indian Constitution adopted the idea of single citizenship from
Britain
India has single citizenship and Article 9 deals with voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.

secs.t: Citizenship Act 1955 → Sections: acquisition and loss — Acquisition - five modes (Sections 3-7)

x: Citizenship by descent applies to a person born outside India when either parent was an Indian citizen at the time of birth, subject to registration of the birth at an Indian consulate.
Birth relates to birth in India, descent to birth abroad with consular registration, naturalisation to residence and oath, and incorporation to a territory joining India.
The three modes of loss are renunciation, automatic termination on voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship, and deprivation by the Central Government in specified cases.
The Centre may deprive only citizens by naturalisation, registration or Art. 5(c), on grounds such as fraud, disloyalty or aiding an enemy.

secs.t: Citizenship Act 1955 → Sections: acquisition and loss — Loss - three modes (Sections 8-10)

x: Renunciation is effected by declaration.

secs.t: Citizenship (Amendment) Acts → year and change

x: For the specified categories covered by the CAA, 2019, the naturalisation residence requirement was reduced to
five years

D is the 1986 amendment (one Indian-citizen parent for births from 1 July 1987), B the 2003 amendment (OCI registration and Sec. 14A), C the 2005 amendment (OCI widened) and A the 2015 amendment (PIO-OCI merger).

secs.t: CAA 2019 — provisions, Rules, orders and challenge

x: The CAA route covers Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014.
The 19 August 2026 MHA order transferred processing in the specified eight States and Union Territories to
District Collectors
instead of Empowered Committees.
The Act gives citizenship effect from the date of entry, reduces the naturalisation residence requirement to five years and amends the Third Schedule.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: NRI, PIO, OCI, Commonwealth citizen; OCI rights

x: Exam angle: NRI = citizen abroad; PIO and OCI = foreign citizens.
A PIO is a foreign citizen whose ancestors were Indian nationals, whereas an NRI remains an Indian citizen ordinarily residing outside India.
OCI cardholders are foreign nationals of Indian origin and enjoy a lifelong visa facility.
OCI cardholders are not Indian citizens and do not have voting rights, the right to contest elections, eligibility for constitutional offices or public employment as a general rule.

secs.t: States and UTs → date and instrument

x: The 35th Amendment introduced Sikkim as an associate State, while the 36th Amendment made it a full State in 1975.
The Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh came into existence on
31 October 2019
under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
Potti Sriramulu died in
December 1952
during his fast, after which Andhra State was created in 1953.

secs.t: Territory of India, cession and UT administration

x: The Berubari reference held that territory could not be ceded under Article 3 and required an Article 368 amendment, resulting in the 9th Amendment Act, 1960.
Article 239 provides that Union Territories are administered by the President through
an Administrator
The administrator is designated as a Lieutenant Governor in Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A passport is a travel document and is not conclusive proof of citizenship.
India has shifted from jus soli, citizenship based primarily on place of birth, towards jus sanguinis, citizenship based primarily on descent or blood relationship.
The Election Commission may check citizenship during revision of electoral rolls, while doubtful cases may go to the Central Government.

rows.title: Fundamental Rights - Article 12 (State), Article 13 and doctrines of eclipse, severability, waiver
sub: Group-II M1-B-10: Fundamental Rights - Article 12, Article 13 and related doctrines

secs.t: Fundamental Rights — definitions, six groups and number game

x: Exam angle: "How many FRs do citizens have?" →
Six
The sequence is right to equality (Articles 14–18), right against exploitation (23–24), right to freedom of religion (25–28), and cultural and educational rights (29–30).
Fundamental Rights are in
Part III, Articles 12 to 35
(Art. 12 defines State, Art. 13 voids inconsistent laws, Arts.

secs.t: Features of Part III → justiciable, qualified, negative vs positive

x: FRs are justiciable and Art. 32 lets an aggrieved person go to the SC directly.
Fundamental Rights are qualified rather than absolute, and courts review restrictions for constitutional validity and reasonableness.
Articles 21A, 29 and 30
confer educational or cultural privileges and are treated as examples of positive rights.
Although most Fundamental Rights operate against State action,
Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24
also impose obligations relevant to private persons.

secs.t: Articles → rights for citizens only vs all persons

x: Articles 23 and 24 are not denied to aliens.
Article 15 is among the Fundamental Rights available only to citizens.
Article 21
is available to all persons.

secs.t: Articles 12 and 13 → meaning of State and law

x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely on the basis of their public activity.
Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
Article 13 is the constitutional basis of judicial review of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights and establishes the supremacy of Fundamental Rights over ordinary law.

secs.t: Cases and amendments on Articles 12 and 13 → holdings

x: Rajasthan SEB (1967) held statutory bodies are 'other authorities'; R.D. Shetty (1979) laid down the instrumentality/agency tests; Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) used the financial, functional and administrative domination test.
Golaknath (1967)
gave FRs a transcendental position and held Parliament could not abridge them; the 24th Amendment (1971) responded by adding Art. 13(4).

secs.t: Doctrines → meaning and case

x: Exam angle: doctrine-to-case matching; pith and substance is the doctrine for Union-State List encroachment.
The
doctrine of severability
invalidates only the inconsistent portion of a law, provided that portion can be separated from the valid remainder.
In
Basheshar Nath v. CIT
(1959), it was held that a person cannot waive a Fundamental Right.
Eclipse means dormancy and possible revival; Severability preserves the separable valid part; Waiver cannot operate against Fundamental Rights; Prospective overruling operates only in the future.
Progressive Interpretation reads the Constitution as a living document capable of responding to present social and constitutional needs.
Pith and substance
is the relevant doctrine for examining Union-State List encroachment by looking at the true nature and character of the law.

secs.t: Articles 33-35 and 359 → limiting and suspending FRs

x: Article 35 assigns legislative power exclusively to Parliament for matters including Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34, and for prescribing punishments for offences under Part III.

Article 33 concerns specified forces and security services, Article 34 concerns martial law, Article 35 gives Parliament exclusive legislative power on specified matters, and Article 359 concerns the President’s order suspending enforcement of named rights.

secs.t: Claimed rights → FR or not

x: Equal pay for equal work is a constitutional goal under Article 39(d), voting is a statutory right connected with Article 326 and election laws, and property is protected under Article 300A.
Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, making education for children aged six to fourteen a Fundamental Right.

secs.t: Scenarios → Article violated

x: Less than minimum wage is forced labour under Art. 23 (PUDR/Asiad, 1982); a child below 14 in a factory or mine violates Art. 24; denial of admission to a State-aided institution on religion, race, caste or language violates Art. 29(2).
Where the alleged violation is by a private individual and does not involve enforceable public-law action, the ordinary legal remedy is generally available rather than a writ.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The right to vote is presently treated as statutory under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and is constitutionally connected with Article 326.
Fundamental Rights check governmental power, protect minorities, support liberty and the rule of law, and limit Parliament through Article 13.
Britain does not have codified Fundamental Rights in the Indian constitutional sense; protection rests largely on conventions and the rule of law.

rows.title: Right to Equality - Articles 14-18; reasonable classification, reservation jurisprudence
sub: Group-II M1-B-11: Right to Equality - Articles 14-18 and reservation jurisprudence

secs.t: Articles 14-18 → content and type of equality — Articles 14-18 → content

x: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice and treats enforcement of any disability arising from it as an offence.
Article 16(2) includes place of birth and residence among the prohibited grounds, along with religion; language is not included in the specified list here.
Article 18 advances social equality by abolishing artificial distinctions arising from State-conferred titles, subject to the stated exceptions.

secs.t: Articles 14-18 → content and type of equality — Types of equality → Article

x: Ambedkar described liberty, equality and fraternity as
an inseparable trinity

secs.t: Article 14 terms → meaning (rule of law, equal protection, classification)

x: The recognised exceptions include constitutional immunity of the President and Governors during their term, diplomatic immunity and immunities of UN agencies.

The twin test of reasonable classification is an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons or things and a rational nexus between the differentia and the object sought to be achieved.
The ruling held that the State cannot arbitrarily treat pensioners differently from serving employees in relation to dearness allowance.

secs.t: Cases on equality and reservation → ruling — Article 14 - arbitrariness

x: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
(1974) established the close constitutional relationship between equality and non-arbitrariness.
Maneka Gandhi reinforced the principle that arbitrary State action is inconsistent with Article 14.

secs.t: Cases on equality and reservation → ruling — Reservation cases → issue decided

x: Champakam Dorairajan was decided in 1951, M.R. Balaji in 1962, Indra Sawhney in 1992 and M. Nagaraj in 2006, giving
B, A, C, D
Jarnail Singh (2018) held that separate data establishing backwardness of SCs and STs was not necessary, while applying the creamy-layer principle to SC/ST promotions.

Champakam Dorairajan concerned the Communal Government Order; M.R. Balaji concerned caste and the 50 per cent principle; M. Nagaraj concerned promotional reservation conditions; Jarnail Singh concerned creamy layer in SC/ST promotions.

secs.t: Clauses of Articles 15-16 and reservation Articles → beneficiaries and amendments

x: Article 16(4A)
concerns reservation in promotion for SCs and STs, along with consequential seniority as reflected in the relevant amendments.
Extraordinary situations, carry-forward vacancies under the 81st Amendment and the EWS reservation recognised in Janhit Abhiyan are stated qualifications or exceptions.

Article 15(4) concerns special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs; Article 16(4A) concerns promotion for SCs and STs; Article 16(4B) concerns backlog vacancies; and Article 340 concerns a commission on SEBC conditions.

secs.t: Creamy layer and the 50% ceiling — issues and debates

x: The OBC creamy-layer income limit mentioned in the 2017 notification is ₹8 lakh a year.

secs.t: Article 18 → titles, foreign titles, consent, national awards

x: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring titles, except military and academic distinctions.
Under Art. 18(2) a citizen shall not accept a foreign title at all; there is no consent route.
The Supreme Court held that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles under Article 18.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The case in which the Supreme Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the UGC equity regulations was
Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India
Andhra Pradesh aligned its OBC creamy-layer definition and thresholds with the central income limits in April 2026.
The debate includes the relationship between the 50 per cent reservation ceiling and the EWS quota, along with the creamy layer for Scheduled Castes and sub-classification.

rows.title: Right to Freedom - Article 19 (six freedoms) and reasonable restrictions
sub: Group-II M1-B-12: Right to Freedom - Article 19 and reasonable restrictions

secs.t: Article 19(1) → six freedoms (number game) and who gets them — Clauses → freedom

x: 19(1)(b) = assemble peaceably and without arms; 19(1)(c) = associations, unions or co-operative societies; 19(1)(e) = reside and settle; 19(1)(g) = profession, occupation, trade or business.
The
freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property
was Article 19(1)(f), but it was deleted by the 44th Amendment in 1978.
The right to strike is not a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(b), although peaceful protest is protected within constitutional limits.

secs.t: Article 19(1) → six freedoms (number game) and who gets them — Availability

x: Article 19 rights are available only to citizens; foreigners cannot claim them, and a company as a legal person cannot itself claim them, though citizen shareholders may bring a challenge in appropriate circumstances.
Article 19 primarily protects citizens against State action.
Imprisonment or detention curtails movement but does not by itself extinguish freedom of expression.

secs.t: Reasonable restrictions → clause, grounds and amendments — Clause → grounds

x: Article 19(4) permits restrictions on freedom of association in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, public order and morality.
Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
is a ground under Article 19(5), relating to movement and residence.

secs.t: Reasonable restrictions → clause, grounds and amendments — Amendments → grounds added

x: The reasonableness test, involving factors such as the nature of the right, the purpose and urgency of the restriction, and proportionality, is associated with V.G. Row (1952).
The court decides whether a restriction is reasonable by examining factors including purpose, extent, urgency and proportionality.
Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public and for protecting the interests of Scheduled Tribes.

secs.t: Reasonable restrictions → clause, grounds and amendments — Profession, trade - 19(6) State monopoly and qualification limits

x: Article 19(6) permits the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications and to carry on a trade to the exclusion of citizens, thereby permitting State monopolies.
The
First Amendment
, 1951 rewrote Art. 19(6) and inserted the clause letting the State carry on any trade to the exclusion of citizens (State monopoly), shielding nationalisation.

secs.t: Implied rights under 19(1)(a) → case

x: Romesh Thappar was decided in 1950, Sakal Papers in 1962, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain in 1975, and Naveen Jindal in 2004.
Bijoe Emmanuel = right to silence (not singing the anthem); Tata Press = commercial speech; Anuradha Bhasin = speech over the internet; Naveen Jindal = hoisting the national flag.

secs.t: Cases on speech and press → ruling

x: Exam angle: case-to-ruling matching; Romesh Thappar → 1st Amendment.
In
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
(1950), the ban on *Cross Roads* was struck down because public order was not then a ground under Article 19(2).
Kaushal Kishor held that the grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive and that no extra restriction can be imposed on ministers' speech.

secs.t: Assembly, association and strikes → scope and status

x: The right to protest is read from freedom of speech and expression, peaceful assembly, and the right to life and personal liberty under
Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 21
The Centre has invoked
Article 19(4)
, which concerns reasonable restrictions on the freedom to form associations or unions, in defending FCRA curbs.

secs.t: Acts and sections → IPC/CrPC to BNS/BNSS

x: Criminal defamation is now s.356 BNS; hate speech is s.196 BNS; acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity are punished by s.152 BNS, while sedition (s.124A IPC) is gone.
Unlawful assembly (five or more) moved from IPC s.141 to BNS s.189.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court's decision in Maneka Gandhi linked
Articles 14, 19 and 21
as the constitutional golden triangle.
The criticism characterised the prohibition of the NCERT chapter as censorship implicating freedom under
Article 19
The Supreme Court recognised peaceful and lawful protest as everybody's right while emphasising that dissent must not occupy public space or trouble citizens.

rows.title: Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22 - protection in conviction, life and liberty, education, preventive detention
sub: Group-II M1-B-13: Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22 - life, liberty, education and preventive detention

secs.t: Articles 20 and 22(1)-(3) — clauses → protections and who gets them — Article 20 - three protections

x: Physical evidence such as fingerprints is not treated as testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3), as recognised in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961).
Selvi (2010) held that narco-analysis, polygraph examination and brain-mapping without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
Article 21 protects citizens and non-citizens and has been expansively interpreted to include dignity, health, mental health, protection against solitary confinement and compensation for violations.

secs.t: Articles 20 and 22(1)-(3) — clauses → protections and who gets them — Article 22(1)-(2) - rights of arrested persons

x: Art. 22(2) requires production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time.
Art. 22(1) gives the right to be told the grounds of arrest and to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice (now Secs.
Sections 47 and 58 of the BNSS correspond broadly to the earlier CrPC Sections 50 and 57 concerning the relevant arrest safeguards.

secs.t: Article 21 — doctrines: procedure established by law vs due process

x: ‘Procedure established by law’ requires compliance with a law enacted by the legislature. ‘Due process of law’ additionally requires the law and procedure to satisfy standards of fairness and reasonableness.
A.K. Gopalan treated Article 21 narrowly and did not subject legislation to the later fairness review.
“Procedure established by law” is associated with Japan, while “due process” is associated with the United States.

secs.t: Cases → rights read into Article 21

x: Shafin Jahan (Hadiya case) = marry a person of choice; Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity = emergency medical care; M.H. Hoskot = free legal aid; Puttaswamy = privacy.
Maniyar Iliyaz v. P. Ayyappan
(2026) connected safe walking on footpaths with Articles 19(1)(d) and 21 and referred to restitutionary remedies.

Maneka Gandhi recognised fair, just and reasonable procedure; Francis Coralie Mullin recognised the right to live with human dignity; Hussainara Khatoon concerned speedy trial; and M.H. Hoskot concerned free legal aid.

secs.t: Right to die and euthanasia — cases → ruling

x: P. Rathinam was decided in 1994, Gian Kaur in 1996, Aruna Shanbaug in 2011 and Common Cause in 2018.

P. Rathinam struck down s.309 IPC; Gian Kaur overruled it (no right to die, but a right to die with dignity; s.309 valid); Aruna Shanbaug allowed passive euthanasia under High Court supervision; Common Cause upheld the living will.

secs.t: Article 21A — 86th Amendment, RTE Act and education cases — Article 21A and the 86th Amendment

x: Article 21A covers only free and compulsory elementary education for children aged 6 to 14 years.
The Right to Education is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and is treated as an extension of the right to life under Article 21.
The 86th Amendment changed all three: Art. 21A (FR, 6-14 years), Art. 45 (DPSP, early childhood care below 6 years) and Art. 51A(k) (the 11th Fundamental Duty, for parents of children 6-14).

secs.t: Article 21A — 86th Amendment, RTE Act and education cases — RTE Act 2009 - provisions

x: Exam angle: amendment number (86th) and year (2002); Art. 21A vs Art. 45 vs Art. 51A(k) age groups.
Section 3 gives every child aged 6 to 14 years the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until elementary education is completed.
Mohini Jain was decided in 1992, Unnikrishnan in 1993, the 86th Amendment was enacted in 2002, and the RTE Act was enacted in 2009.

secs.t: Preventive detention — Article 22(4)-(7) safeguards, law-making power, laws → year

x: Article 22(4) requires an Advisory Board, consisting of High Court judges or persons qualified to be High Court judges, to report sufficient cause before preventive detention continues beyond three months.
COFEPOSA targets smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators; NSA allows detention up to 12 months without charges; UAPA is the anti-terror and unlawful-associations law.
Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act
are identified as important historical roots of preventive detention legislation in India.

secs.t: Old codes → new sections (IPC / CrPC → BNS / BNSS)

x: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect.
Section 226 BNS applies only to an attempt to compel or restrain a public servant from exercising lawful powers or discharging official duties; it is not a general offence of attempted suicide.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on
1 July 2024

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana emphasised that
the grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee
The Supreme Court observed on 6 January 2026 that delay alone is not a “trump card” for bail in UAPA cases.
In the Harish Rana matter, his parents sought
withdrawal of life support before the Supreme Court
after he had remained in a persistent vegetative state for 13 years.

rows.title: Right against Exploitation - Articles 23-24; Right to Freedom of Religion - Articles 25-28
sub: Group-II M1-B-14: Right against Exploitation and Right to Freedom of Religion - Articles 23-28
Group-II S3-10: Religion in India - religious pluralism, secularism and the Indian model

secs.t: Articles 23-28 — classification, number game and who gets them

x: Exam angle: clause-text matching; distractors are Arts 19(1), 26(1), 29(1).
Article 24 is directed at employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment; harmless or innocent work is not covered by the constitutional prohibition.
Article 27 embodies the neutrality principle that no person can be compelled to pay a tax specifically appropriated for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion.

secs.t: Articles 23-24 — provisions on trafficking, begar and child labour

x: Article 24 protects children below 14 from employment in factories, mines or hazardous work, while Article 21’s life-with-dignity principle supports mandatory victim rehabilitation.
Articles 39(e) and 39(f) direct the State to ensure that the tender age of children is not abused and that children develop in a healthy manner with protection against exploitation.

secs.t: Acts → year → scope (trafficking, bonded labour, child labour)

x: The
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956
penalises brothels, pimping and living off another person’s earnings from prostitution.
The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 abolishes bonded labour, including
debt bondage
found in sectors such as brick kilns, agriculture and domestic work.
Section 143 addresses trafficking, the BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024, and victim consent does not validate trafficking.

secs.t: Article 25 — text, terms → meaning, State powers and Explanations — Article 25(1) - text

x: Exam angle: quoted text of 25(1) → identify the Article (asked 2018, 2023).
Conscience is the inner freedom (iii), profess is open declaration through words or symbols (iv), practise is worship and rituals (i) and propagate is spreading beliefs (ii), so A is correct.
Propagation means spreading one's beliefs, but it does not include a right to convert another person because that would impinge on the other person's freedom of conscience.

secs.t: Article 25 — text, terms → meaning, State powers and Explanations — Article 25(2) - State powers

x: 25(2)(a) covers economic, financial, political or other secular activity.
Wearing and carrying kirpans is specifically deemed part of the profession of the Sikh religion.
Freedom of religion is not absolute.

secs.t: Articles 26-28 — clauses → rights and limits

x: Article 26 concerns denominational religious affairs; Article 27 concerns taxes; Article 28(1) concerns State-funded religious instruction; and Article 28(3) protects freedom from compulsory attendance.
Article 28(2) exempts State-administered trust institutions where the trust requires instruction.
The issue left to the Ministry of Education concerns whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under Article 26(a), rather than under Articles 19(1)(g) or 30(1).

secs.t: Religion cases → issue / holding (ERP test) — ERP test

x: Essential Religious Practice (ERP):
court-made test (formulated by the SC in
) to decide which practices are integral to a religion and therefore protected.

secs.t: Religion cases → issue / holding (ERP test) — Cases

x: The Sabarimala judgment allowed women of all ages, rejected gender discrimination in devotion and reaffirmed secularism as part of the Basic Structure.
The Sabarimala ruling stated that the State cannot endorse a practice and that a claim of essential practice cannot be used to bar others' participation.
Section 295A IPC is now
Section 299
of the BNS, and Ramji Lal Modi v. State of UP had upheld it on public-order grounds.

secs.t: Religion cases → issue / holding (ERP test) — Sabarimala

x: Exam angle: case → religion/issue matching; ERP test origin.
Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga
were reported as the first women of the barred age group to enter Sabarimala in January 2019.
A 9-judge Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant heard it.
The Karnataka High Court held in 2022 that hijab was not an Essential Religious Practice.

secs.t: Conversion and sacrilege laws → State → year

x: The Orissa Freedom of Religion Act was enacted in 1967, while the Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam was enacted in 1968.
The early laws came from concern over missionary activity.
Assent came in April 2026.

secs.t: Secularism — meaning, Articles, Indian vs Western model, basic structure — Meaning and Indian model

x: Indian secularism requires equal respect for all religions and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion.
The Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal to add the word “
God
” to the Preamble in 1949.
Ashoka's Dhamma, the Nehru Report of 1928 and the Karachi Resolution of 1931 are all identified as roots associated with Indian secular thought.

secs.t: Secularism — meaning, Articles, Indian vs Western model, basic structure — Indian vs Western model; theocratic state

x: India has no state religion and follows a model allowing positive state intervention for reform.
The Western model is generally based on strict separation and mutual exclusion.
Kesavananda Bharati set out the basic structure doctrine, and S.R. Bommai recognised secularism as part of the basic structure.
S.R. Bommai recognised that a State government acting against secularism may be dismissed under
Article 356

secs.t: Terms → meaning: pluralism, fundamentalism, revivalism

x: Communalism, separatism and fanaticism are identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India, particularly in the context of religion becoming fused with politics since the 1970s.
The cited examples are the 1984 anti-Sikh violence, the 1992 Babri Masjid episode, the 2002 Gujarat riots and the 2023 Haryana violence.
Hate speech on social media and illegal conversions
have been identified as threats that erode the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb.

secs.t: Sociologists → statements on religion; religious terms

x: Max Weber
examined the relationship of karma, dharma and caste to economic life in *The Religion of India*.
Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of good, and Angra Mainyu, the destructive or evil spirit, belong to
Zoroastrianism
, followed by Parsis in India.
Tirthankara means ‘Ford-maker’, and Jain tradition identifies 24 Tirthankaras, beginning with Rishabhanatha and ending with Mahavira.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sabarimala nine-judge reference is examining the scope of the Essential Religious Practices test and the extent to which courts may determine what constitutes an essential religious practice.
A major criticism is that the Essential Religious Practices test permits courts to decide theological questions and thereby makes them arbiters of religion.

rows.title: Cultural and Educational Rights - Articles 29-30; the right to property and the 44th Amendment

secs.t: Minorities — meaning, types, Articles and notified minorities

x: The six notified religious minorities are Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains.
Article 350A
deals with facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups.
National notification brings a community within the National Commission for Minorities and makes it eligible under central minority schemes such as scholarships, PMJVK and PM VIKAS.

secs.t: Article 30 — minority educational institutions and the compensation clause

x: Article 30(1A) concerns compulsory acquisition of the property of a minority educational institution.
In Pramati, decided in 2014, the Supreme Court held that the RTE Act's 25 per cent quota does not apply to minority schools.
Article 30(1) covers all minorities, religious or linguistic.

secs.t: Right to property — Amendments → year → change

x: Exam angle: A-R pairs "legal right under 300A in Part XII" + "44th Amendment, 1978".

In 1950, the Right to Property was a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f), relating to acquiring, holding and disposing of property, and Article 31, relating to deprivation and acquisition of property.
The 44th Amendment deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from Part III and made property a constitutional legal right under Article 300A in Part XII, Chapter IV.

secs.t: Article 300A and LARR Act 2013 — provisions

x: Article 300A states that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
Article 300A
protects against deprivation of property without authority of law and operates against executive action.
The figures are reversed; consent is 70% for PPP and 80% for private projects.

secs.t: Fundamental vs constitutional/legal right — classification

x: The right to vote rests on adult suffrage under Article 326 and on statutory provisions (Section 62 of the RPA, 1951; registration under Section 19 of the RPA, 1950).
All three - the right to know candidate details, NOTA and ballot secrecy - have been recognised under Article 19(1)(a), even though voting itself is a statutory right.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kerala Malayalam Bhasha Bill received assent in March 2026 and was contested on the ground that it could harm the Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod.
A criticism in the debate is that minority status may sometimes be misused to escape obligations under the Right to Education framework.
The Andhra Pradesh High Court insisted on
strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A

rows.title: Right to Constitutional Remedies - Article 32; the five writs and their scope
sub: Group-II M1-B-15: Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30) and the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32)

secs.t: Article 32 — clauses, scope, status and FIRSTs

x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
Dr. Ambedkar described
Article 32
as the heart and soul of the Constitution because it provides the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
The writs were borrowed from English law, where they were known as prerogative writs of the King, regarded as the fountain of justice.

secs.t: Writs → literal meaning, purpose and scope

x: Prohibition is issued by a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal with judicial or quasi-judicial functions from exceeding its jurisdiction.
Mandamus may lie against public officials, public corporations, inferior courts, tribunals and government authorities, but not against the President or Governor for their official acts.
Article 32(2) refers to
five
writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
Habeas Corpus
is regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty because it provides a prompt judicial remedy against unlawful detention.
Quo warranto means 'by what authority' (iv), mandamus 'we command' (i), habeas corpus 'to have the body of' (ii) and certiorari 'to be certified' (iii), so the first code is right.

secs.t: Writ limits — Mandamus; Prohibition vs Certiorari

x: Prohibition is primarily preventive and stops a judicial or quasi-judicial body from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction.
The scope of certiorari has extended, since 1991, to certain administrative bodies in addition to judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.
Both prohibition and certiorari are traditionally issued against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies and both check excess of jurisdiction.

secs.t: Article 32 vs Article 226 — SC and HC writ jurisdiction

x: When a High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits, the same plea cannot ordinarily be raised before the Supreme Court under Article 32; the appropriate course is an appeal.
The Judiciary
is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, and the Supreme Court has the constitutional role of protecting and guaranteeing those rights.

secs.t: Persons, cases and amendments on writ jurisdiction

x: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure.
PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi by permitting a public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so themselves or for a larger public interest.
Letters and postcards are treated as writ petitions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: D is the answer: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose', so their subject-matter scope is wider, while Article 32 is confined to Fundamental Rights.
The Supreme Court was examining an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings in matters involving threats to life and liberty, strengthening practical access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
On 20 January 2026, a Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma agreed to examine
whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction

rows.title: Directive Principles of State Policy - Articles 36-51, classification, implementation
sub: Group-II M1-B-16: Directive Principles of State Policy - classification, content and implementation

secs.t: DPSP — definitions, source and antecedents

x: India borrowed the idea through the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had itself copied it from the Spanish Constitution; it was not borrowed directly from Spain.
The Sapru Committee suggested dividing rights into justiciable and non-justiciable categories, an idea reflected later in the distinction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

secs.t: Article 37 — non-justiciability and the FR–DPSP balance

x: Fundamental Rights mostly restrain the State from certain actions, while Directive Principles generally require the State to undertake measures for social and economic welfare.
However, non-enforceability arises from the express provision in Article 37; their role as a legislative guide does not explain the legal bar on enforcement.
Although DPSPs are not independently enforceable, courts use them as interpretive aids and have read several welfare-oriented principles into the scope of Article 21.

secs.t: Articles → directive (Part IV and Art. 39 clauses) — Part IV - Article → directive

x: Exam angle: match directive → Article; "which is NOT a DPSP" statements (APPSC GS 2024 tested Art. 39A).
Agriculture and cow slaughter = Art. 48 (iii), monuments = Art. 49 (i), separation of judiciary = Art. 50 (iv), international peace = Art. 51 (ii), so A is correct.

Article 41 concerns work, education and public assistance; Article 43 concerns living wage and decent living standards; Article 45 concerns early childhood care up to six years; and Article 47 concerns nutrition, public health and prohibition.

secs.t: Articles → directive (Part IV and Art. 39 clauses) — Article 39 - clauses (a) to (f)

x: Article 39(f)
directs that children should develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, and be protected against exploitation and abandonment.
Article 39(b) concerns distribution of material resources of the community to subserve the common good, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production.

secs.t: Classification — socialist, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual

x: Articles 38, 39A and 47 are generally grouped under the Socialist principles.
Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46
are generally included among Gandhian principles.
Article 43B concerns the promotion of co-operative societies and is generally classified as a Gandhian principle.
The relevant order is Article 40 (village panchayats), Article 46 (weaker sections), Article 47 (prohibition) and Article 48 (cattle protection).

secs.t: Amendments → DPSP changes, 1976 to 2011

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2024 asked two chronology questions on exactly these four changes.
The 42nd Amendment made the changes in C in 1976, the 44th Amendment made the change in D in 1978, the 86th Amendment changed Article 45 in 2002, and the 97th Amendment added Article 43B in 2011.

secs.t: Directives outside Part IV; ideals shared with Fundamental Duties and Preamble

x: Article 45 directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years of age.
Article 42
directs the State to make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.

Several themes, including environmental protection, heritage, education and women’s dignity, appear in both the Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties, though the corresponding provisions are not always identical.

secs.t: Acts, programmes and cases implementing DPSPs

x: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) are implemented through land reforms and related laws; Article 40 through the 73rd Amendment; Article 39A through the Legal Services Authorities Act; and Article 41 through MGNREGA.
Section 3 of the Right to Education Act, 2009, provides free education for children from
six to fourteen years
of age in a neighbourhood school.
Goa follows
the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867
, making it a distinctive example in discussions concerning a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44.

secs.t: Persons → statements on DPSP

x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Directive Principles as a “novel feature” of the Indian Constitution.
K.C. Wheare
described the Directive Principles as a “manifesto of aims and aspirations.”.
Ivor Jennings
referred to the Directive Principles as “pious aspirations.”.
K.T. Shah called the DPSPs a cheque payable at the bank's convenience (iii).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pavini Shukla suggested a UCC to end gender discrimination.
The Directive Principles set the goal of a welfare state and provide a framework for social and economic democracy.
The Constituent Assembly debate on whether the right to work should be a Fundamental Right or remain a Directive Principle involved
K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar

rows.title: Conflict and harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP - Champakam, Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills
sub: Group-II M1-B-17: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and DPSP - Champakam, Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills

secs.t: FR vs DPSP — differences, legal status and doctrine

x: Courts have used Directive Principles to interpret and enrich Fundamental Rights; non-justiciability does not exclude them from constitutional interpretation.
The validity of such a law is examined against the basic structure doctrine and, in particular, the constitutional guarantees represented by Articles 14, 19 and 21, known as the golden triangle.

secs.t: Landmark cases → position: Gopalan (1950) to Sanjeev Coke (1983)

x: In re Kerala Education Bill adopted harmonious construction, requiring both Parts III and IV to be given effect as far as possible, while Fundamental Rights continued to prevail in case of direct conflict.
Minerva Mills held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights in Part III and DPSPs in Part IV are part of the basic structure; absolute primacy to either would destroy that balance.
The correct sequence is A.K. Gopalan (1950), Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), and Sanjeev Coke (1983).

secs.t: Cases on material resources and the Ninth Schedule — Ranganatha Reddy (1977) to Property Owners Association (2024) — Material resources of the community - Art. 39(b)

x: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that private ownership alone does not automatically bring a resource within Article 39(b).

The broad interpretation associated with Justice Krishna Iyer in Ranganatha Reddy was followed in Sanjeev Coke, while the 2024 Property Owners Association decision rejected its automatic application to every privately owned resource.

secs.t: Cases on material resources and the Ninth Schedule — Ranganatha Reddy (1977) to Property Owners Association (2024) — Ninth Schedule and Art. 31B

x: Waman Rao was decided in 1981, not 2007.
Waman Rao used 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda judgment, as the cut-off.

secs.t: Amendments responding to courts — 1st (1951) to 42nd (1976)

x: The Seventeenth Amendment widened ‘estate’ in Article 31A and dealt with land under personal cultivation.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment responded to Golaknath by affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment responded to the Privy Purses case associated with Madhav Rao Scindia and abolished privy purses and the privileges of former rulers.

secs.t: Article 31C — 25th Amendment (1971) to Minerva Mills (1980)

x: The original Article 31C contained both protections: specified laws were protected from Articles 14, 19 and 31 challenges, and the declaration that they implemented the policy was placed beyond judicial questioning.
Minerva Mills struck down the Forty-second Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs.
The
Property Owners Association
decision of 2024 affirmed that the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, continues in force.
Minerva Mills recognised that an Emergency proclamation is not wholly immune from judicial review.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Champakam Dorairajan and the First Amendment belong to 1951, followed later by Minerva Mills and then I.R. Coelho in 2007.
The conflict also generated debates over judicial supremacy and parliamentary supremacy.
Fundamental Rights were drawn from the United States, while the Directive Principles were inspired by Ireland.

rows.title: Fundamental Duties - Article 51A, Swaran Singh Committee, enforceability
sub: Group-II M1-B-18: Fundamental Duties - Article 51A, Swaran Singh Committee and enforceability

secs.t: Swaran Singh Committee and amendments — numbers and FIRSTs — Swaran Singh Committee, 1976

x: The Congress party set it up in 1976 under Sardar Swaran Singh; it suggested 8 duties and the 42nd Amendment (1976) added 10.
The proposal that Parliament could prescribe penalties for non-compliance was not accepted.
The committee suggested that
payment of taxes
should be a Fundamental Duty, but this proposal was not accepted.

secs.t: Swaran Singh Committee and amendments — numbers and FIRSTs — Part IVA - amendments

x: Exam angle: options mix 86th/96th and 2001/2002 - the answer is
The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added Article 51A(k), relating to educational opportunities for children or wards aged six to fourteen.
The Eighty-Sixth Amendment inserted Article 21A, substituted Article 45 and added the eleventh Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k).

secs.t: Article 51A (a) to (k) — the list, types and distractors

x: Exam angle: "which is not a Fundamental Duty" - check the list word for word.
Article 51A(a)
requires citizens to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
Article 51A(c)
requires every citizen to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
Article 51A(k)
places this duty on a parent or guardian in respect of a child or ward aged six to fourteen years.
Article 51A(e) expressly refers to harmony and common brotherhood, whereas the Preamble uses the term fraternity.
Article 51A(k) specifically addresses
parents or guardians
, requiring them to provide opportunities for education to children or wards within the constitutionally prescribed age group.
Protecting the elderly, the differently abled and children is not in Article 51A; APPSC Group 2, 2025 used it twice as the distractor.

secs.t: Applicability, source and comparison

x: Fundamental Duties are addressed to every citizen of India and do not extend to foreigners.
The Fundamental Duties were inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR.
Japan
's Constitution is identified as the only major democratic Constitution with a comparable list of citizens' duties.

secs.t: Environmental duty — Articles, Acts and cases

x: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted the environmental duty in Article 51A(g), added DPSP Article 48A and moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List through Entries 17A and 17B.
Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing international agreements, and this power forms the constitutional basis for the
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

secs.t: Enforceability — cases, laws and Verma Committee — Non-justiciable nature

x: Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable: the Constitution provides no direct court enforcement or penalty, although legislation may enforce them and courts may refer to them in interpretation.
In Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Duties cannot override Part III rights and that respectful conduct towards national symbols does not require compelled participation.

secs.t: Enforceability — cases, laws and Verma Committee — Enforcing laws and Verma Committee

x: The
Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
gives statutory effect to aspects of Article 51A(a), concerning respect for the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
Imputations prejudicial to national integration are now dealt with under
Section 197
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the corresponding earlier reference was Section 153B of the Indian Penal Code.

secs.t: Criticism — vague, not exhaustive, placement

x: A is the odd one out: direct court enforcement without legislation is not a criticism, and it is not even true, because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable.
Because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and do not carry direct constitutional sanctions, they have been described as a code of moral precepts and, by critics, as superfluous.
The list is criticised as non-exhaustive because it does not expressly include duties such as
voting
, paying taxes and family planning.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Fundamental Duties cannot be used to curtail the freedom of religion guaranteed under Articles 25 and 26; a Fundamental Duty does not automatically override a Fundamental Right.
Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their obligations, assist courts in judging the reasonableness of laws and support action against anti-national activities.
The prescribed corporate social responsibility expenditure is at least
2% of the average net profit
, as referred to under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013.
