rows.title: Amendment of the Constitution - Article 368, types of majorities, procedure, limitations
sub: Group-II M1-B-19: Amendment of the Constitution - Article 368, procedure and types of majority

secs.t: Article 368 — location, source, nature and persons

x: Article 368 states that Parliament may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
The Indian Constitution combines different methods of amendment and is therefore neither purely rigid nor purely flexible; it is a synthesis of both.
Granville Austin
described the process as appearing complicated but being merely diverse.

secs.t: Amendment procedure → step-by-step rules

x: Exam angle: "prior permission", "joint sitting" and "President may return" are all false for amendment bills.
Exam angle: statement sets on "private member needs prior permission" (false) and "joint sitting possible" (false).
Article 108 does not apply to constitutional amendment bills and no joint sitting can resolve a disagreement between the Houses.

secs.t: Types of majority → requirement → used for

x: Article 32 may be amended by special majority without ratification by the States, although the Supreme Court's power under it cannot be destroyed because it is part of the basic structure.
Article 368 type relates to constitutional amendment; Article 61 type to presidential impeachment; Article 249 to legislation on a State List subject; and Article 312 to new All-India Services.

The Article 368 type of majority is used for removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges, the CAG, the CEC and State Election Commissioners, constitutional amendment, and approval of a National Emergency.

secs.t: Simple-majority provisions → Articles (not amendments)

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT amended by special majority?" - official language, citizenship, Fifth/Sixth Schedule are simple-majority items.
Formation and alteration of States, Legislative Councils and official language provisions are among matters amendable by simple majority outside Article 368.
Parliamentary quorum, salaries of MPs and parliamentary privileges are among provisions amendable by simple majority outside Article 368.

secs.t: Federal provisions → State ratification (Art. 368(2))

x: Articles 54 and 55 concern the election of the President; Article 279A establishes the GST Council; the Fourth Schedule concerns representation of States in Parliament; Article 11 concerns citizenship.
The election of the President, judicial powers, distribution of legislative powers and related federal provisions require State ratification.
The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 added Article 279A relating to the GST Council to the federal provisions requiring State ratification.

secs.t: Cases and amendments → limits on amending power

x: The 24th Amendment amended Articles 13 and 368, empowered Parliament to abridge or take away Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), under which an amendment made under Article 368 is not ‘law’ for Article 13.
Golaknath was the first limitation of the amending power over Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda Bharati first propounded the basic-structure doctrine; and Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain first applied it.

secs.t: Amendment Bills → year → fate

x: The Bill sought to raise Lok Sabha strength from 550 to 850 and failed on 17 April 2026 with 298 for and 230 against out of 528 present and voting, short of the 352 needed.
The Delimitation Bill, 2026 was withdrawn on 20 April 2026, three days after the 131st Amendment Bill was negatived in the Lok Sabha on 17 April.

secs.t: Criticism of the amendment procedure

x: The Constitution provides no joint sitting mechanism for resolving a deadlock between the Houses on an amendment Bill.
Parliament alone amends most provisions, no special body or referendum is required, and States cannot initiate amendments.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The vote was viewed as demonstrating the protective role of a special majority against a slim majority.
The bill required 352 affirmative votes, representing two-thirds of 528 members present and voting, but received only 298.
Only certain provisions can be altered through the simple-majority route, while other provisions require special procedures and are subject to the basic-structure limitation.

rows.title: Important amendments - 1st, 7th, 24th, 25th, 42nd, 44th, 52nd, 61st, 69th, 73rd, 74th, 86th
sub: Group-II M1-B-20: Important amendments - 1st, 24th, 42nd, 44th, 73rd, 74th, 101st, 103rd, 106th

secs.t: Amendments → year → subject (number game)

x: The Seventh Amendment, 1956 accompanied the reorganisation of States, abolished the Part A, B, C and D classification, repealed Part VII and dealt with Union Territories.

The 44th Amendment removed the right to property from Part III while retaining it as a legal right; the 52nd introduced the Tenth Schedule; the 69th provided Delhi's special constitutional framework; and the 86th inserted Article 21A.
The 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A concerning education for children aged 6–14 years, modified Article 45 and added Article 51A(k) as a Fundamental Duty.
The 103rd, 105th and 106th Amendments correspond to EWS reservation, restoration of States' SEBC-identification power and women's reservation respectively.
Pair 3 is a trap: the 62nd Amendment extended SC/ST seat reservation to 2000; anti-defection came with the 52nd (1985) and was modified by the 91st (2003).

secs.t: Statehood amendments → State → Article

x: The Fifty-sixth Amendment of 1987 dealt with Goa’s statehood and inserted Article 371I.
The Fifty-third Amendment of 1986 dealt with Mizoram statehood.
The 13th Amendment (1962) dealt with Nagaland (Art. 371A); the 36th (1975) made Sikkim a full State and omitted Art. 2A; the 55th (1986) gave Arunachal Pradesh statehood (Art. 371H).

secs.t: 1st Amendment, 1951 → enacting body, provisions, rulings overcome

x: Reservation of one-third seats for women in State Assemblies
is associated with the 106th Amendment, not the First Amendment.

Kameshwar Singh concerned zamindari abolition/land reform (a-ii); Champakam Dorairajan struck down the communal admissions order and led to Art. 15(4) (b-iii); Romesh Thappar (1950) concerned speech (c-i).
The First Amendment was upheld by the Supreme Court in
Shankari Prasad

secs.t: 42nd Amendment, 1976 → Mini-Constitution changes and what was undone

x: The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in
September 1976
during the Emergency period.
The Forty-second Amendment added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble. 'Justice' was already present in the original Preamble.
The
Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978
restored the normal five-year term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies and restored judicial review in important respects.

secs.t: 44th Amendment, 1978 → Emergency safeguards and property

x: The Forty-fourth Amendment strengthened the power of the
Lok Sabha
to disapprove or revoke a Proclamation of Emergency.
It reversed the bar created by the Thirty-ninth Amendment and restored judicial consideration of election disputes concerning the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Speaker.
The 44th required a written Cabinet recommendation (PYQ 2025) and substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance'.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 2026 debate was linked to
the 75th anniversary of the First Amendment and the 50th anniversary of the Emergency
, reviving discussion on the 42nd and 44th Amendments.
The AP-specific reference identifies the 32nd Amendment Act of 1973 as having inserted Articles 371D and 371E relating to the Six-Point Formula and the Central University.

rows.title: Recent amendments - 97th, 100th, 101st (GST), 102nd, 103rd (EWS), 104th, 105th, 106th (women's reservation)

secs.t: Recent amendments → year → subject (number game)

x: The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014, provided for the National Judicial Appointments Commission, which was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.
The 104th Constitutional Amendment, 2019, extended the reservation of seats for SCs and STs up to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination.
All four pairs are correct as per the amendment table: 97th co-operatives, 101st GST, 103rd EWS reservation and 106th women's reservation.

secs.t: 97th Amendment, 2011 → Articles, Part IXB provisions, case

x: In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB insofar as it applied to State cooperative societies because the required State ratification was absent.
Article 43B
was inserted to promote the voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.

secs.t: Pending amendment Bills → subject → status

x: The 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, concerns simultaneous elections under the
One Nation, One Election
proposal.
The 129th Amendment Bill proposes insertion of
Article 82A
and amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327 in connection with simultaneous elections.
The 130th Amendment Bill proposes provisions concerning the removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days on serious charges.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A revised delimitation Bill is expected
in the context of implementing the women's reservation law.
The women's quota remains unimplemented.
Both the assertion and the reason are true.
Local bodies have had one-third reservation for women since 1992.

rows.title: Basic Structure doctrine - evolution and content; Kesavananda Bharati and after (Indira Gandhi, Minerva Mills, Waman Rao, I.R. Coelho)
sub: Group-II M1-B-21: Basic Structure of the Constitution - evolution, elements and later application

secs.t: Basic structure — meaning, origin, persons and FIRSTs — Meaning

x: The doctrine permits amendment of any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but prohibits alteration, damage or destruction of features that give the Constitution its identity.
Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368, but the amendment remains subject to the basic structure limitation.
The Preamble is part of the Constitution and is amendable subject to the basic structure doctrine.

secs.t: Basic structure — meaning, origin, persons and FIRSTs — Origin & nature

x: Exam angle: statement sets testing "judge-made vs inserted by amendment" and "can Parliament amend FRs today" (yes, subject to basic structure).
German jurist
Dietrich Conrad
argued in India in 1965 that constitutional amending power is subject to implied limitations, drawing on the experience of Germany's Basic Law.
Justice Mudholkar’s dissent in
Sajjan Singh
(1965) is noted as the first judicial reference to the idea of basic features.

secs.t: Cases → year → contribution (evolution, 1951 to 2015)

x: Exam angle: "In which case was basic structure first propounded?" - Kesavananda Bharati, not Golaknath or Shankari Prasad.
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain
(1975) marked the first application of the basic structure doctrine, and the relevant clause of the 39th Amendment was struck down; free and fair elections were recognised as a basic feature.
Minerva Mills (1980) affirmed judicial review, the limited nature of the amending power, and the balance or harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

secs.t: Ninth Schedule and Arts. 31A, 31B, 31C → origin, cut-off, Coelho test — Origin & purpose

x: The Ninth Schedule was created by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, along with Article 31B.
The Ninth Schedule covers Central and State laws, inclusion requires a constitutional amendment by Parliament, and its original focus was land-reform legislation.
The Tamil Nadu 69 per cent reservation law was placed in the Ninth Schedule through the 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994.

secs.t: Ninth Schedule and Arts. 31A, 31B, 31C → origin, cut-off, Coelho test — Judicial review of entries

x: The Ninth Schedule has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not provide blanket immunity from judicial review, particularly after the decisions in Waman Rao and I.R. Coelho.
I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity and held that post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws can be examined to determine whether they damage the basic structure.

secs.t: Elements declared basic structure → case

x: Kesavananda Bharati associated
secularism, federalism and separation of powers
, among other constitutional principles, with the basic structure.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
(1994), decided by a nine-judge Bench, reaffirmed secularism and federalism as basic-structure principles.
Free and fair elections go with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (and Kuldip Nayar), not Minerva Mills; HC powers under Arts.

secs.t: Doctrines → origin (Supreme Court vs Parliament)

x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines.
Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle.
Prospective overruling is a judge-made doctrine that the Supreme Court first applied in
Golaknath (1967)

secs.t: Scope, supremacy debate and criticism

x: The doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of courts to review constitutional amendments against its basic features.
The doctrine is defended as a major contribution of the judiciary to constitutionalism because it checks the misuse of the amending power by a temporary majority.
The 42nd Amendment attempted to bar High Courts from reviewing central laws, and the
43rd Amendment Act, 1977
removed that restriction.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The argument is based on the view that democracy and free and fair elections are basic features of the Constitution, and therefore voting deserves stronger constitutional protection.

B.R. Gavai told the Joint Parliamentary Committee that the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, did not violate the basic structure, whereas former Chief Justices U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised basic-structure doubts.

rows.title: Landmark judgments - Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy (privacy), Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano
sub: Group-II M1-B-22: Landmark judgments shaping constitutional interpretation

secs.t: Fundamental-rights judgments → year → principle

x: Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 protects more than mere existence, includes dignity and travel abroad, and requires a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable.
The nine-judge S.R. Bommai judgment made President's Rule reviewable, emphasised the floor test and recognised secularism as part of the basic structure.
S.R. Bommai concerned Article 356, judicial review, floor tests and secularism as a basic feature; it did not concern abolition of untouchability.

secs.t: Personal law, marriage and sexuality → case

x: The five-judge Bench in Navtej Singh Johar read down Section 377 and decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults.
Shayara Bano declared instant triple talaq invalid and held that it was not an essential religious practice under Articles 25 and 26.
Sarla Mudgal (1995) and Lily Thomas (2000) addressed conversion and bigamy, while Lily Thomas (2013) concerned disqualification of convicted legislators.

secs.t: Guidelines and directions → case

x: D.K. Basu dealt with safeguards relating to arrest and custody, including an arrest memo, informing kin and medical checks.
Lalita Kumari made FIR registration mandatory for cognizable offences under Sec. 154 CrPC, now Sec. 173 BNSS.
Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
(1980) held that handcuffing should be confined to exceptional cases.

secs.t: Aadhaar (Puttaswamy II, 2018) → rulings

x: The Supreme Court struck down Section 57, preventing private entities from demanding or using Aadhaar on that statutory basis.
Aadhaar was held mandatory for specified subsidies and benefits funded from the Consolidated Fund, and for PAN and income-tax return requirements.
Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act provides that Aadhaar does not by itself prove
citizenship, domicile or date of birth

secs.t: Electoral and governance judgments → holding

x: The ADR judgment required candidates to disclose their criminal record, assets and educational qualifications.
The Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) of the RPA, resulting in immediate disqualification of convicted MPs and MLAs, subject to the applicable legal position.
The Court's committee was PM, LoP and CJI, and the 2023 Act replaced the CJI with a Union Minister.

secs.t: Recent Constitution Bench cases → bench → held

x: The seven-judge Bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, by a 6:1 majority, held that States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes and overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
The December 2023 Article 370 judgment treated Article 370 as temporary, upheld the power of the President to make it inoperative and directed elections.
In February 2024, the Court unanimously struck down the electoral bonds scheme in the context of
voters’ right to information

secs.t: Case → bench size and Chief Justice

x: Vishaka was decided by a three-judge Bench headed by CJI J.S. Verma.
Bommai and Puttaswamy were nine-judge cases; Puttaswamy was associated with CJI J.S. Khehar.
Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar
were five-judge Bench cases associated with CJI Dipak Misra.

secs.t: Judgments on AP matters → reservation, capital

x: E.V. Chinnaiah struck down AP's 2000 sub-categorisation Act and was overruled by Davinder Singh (2024).
After the Andhra Pradesh High Court’s 2022 ruling against three capitals, Amaravati became the sole capital from 2 June 2024.
E.V. Chinnaiah was decided in 2004, Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao in 2020, Davinder Singh in 2024 and the amendment Bill in 2026.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The SC issued notice (Aug 2026) on a PIL to ban polygamy among Muslims; Javed (2003) held that polygamy is not an essential religious practice; and bigamy is an offence under Sec. 82 BNS.
Articles 32, 141 and 142 provide the constitutional basis through which judicial decisions can fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts, as illustrated by Vishaka and Seema.

rows.title: Doctrines of constitutional interpretation - harmonious construction, colourable legislation, pith and substance, territorial nexus

secs.t: Doctrines → meaning and field

x: The
doctrine of territorial nexus
permits a State law to operate beyond the State when a sufficient nexus exists between the State and the subject matter of the law.
The doctrine of
pith and substance
is used to reconcile Central and Provincial, or Union and State, legislative powers by examining the true nature of the law.
Transformative constitutionalism treats the Constitution as an instrument for transforming an unequal society and advancing substantive constitutional values.

secs.t: Judicial and executive doctrines → constitutional anchor

x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court in
Golaknath (1967)
Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India, reflecting the principle of stare decisis.
Article 310 embodies the pleasure doctrine, while Article 311 provides safeguards for civil servants against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.

secs.t: Cases → doctrine applied

x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure even though it incidentally touched imports.
State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957)
concerned taxation of prize competitions run from outside the State and is associated with territorial nexus.
R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and the Calcutta Gas case are associated with the principle that an entry includes matters incidental and ancillary to it.

secs.t: Doctrines borrowed from foreign law → country of origin

x: The doctrine of pith and substance was borrowed from Canada.
The doctrine of public trust has its origin in
Roman law
The basic structure doctrine is identified with
Germany
as its foreign origin in the given constitutional comparison.
'procedure established by law' comes from Japan and separation of powers from Montesquieu (France).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Critics argue that constitutional morality may be subjective and may provide a route to judicial overreach.
These doctrines make federal lawmaking workable and establish the manner in which Fundamental Rights operate in relation to legislation.

rows.title: Structure of the Indian government - separation of powers and checks and balances
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-24

secs.t: Separation of powers — definitions, thinkers and degree in India

x: Constitutionalism includes constitutional limits on power, rule of law, checks and balances, judicial review and protection of Fundamental Rights.
Montesquieu discussed the separation of powers in The Spirit of Laws, published in 1748.
Articles 50, 121, 211 and 235 collectively reflect safeguards relating to judicial separation, discussion of judges and control of subordinate courts.

secs.t: Legislative and executive checks → devices and Articles

x: The Council of Ministers is subordinate to the legislature and remains in office only while it enjoys the confidence of the
Lok Sabha
Question Hour/Zero Hour give day-to-day watch, and a no-confidence motion removes the government and lies only in the Lok Sabha.

Articles 86 and 87 concern presidential addresses and messages, Article 175 concerns the Governor's addresses and messages, Article 123 concerns Union ordinances, and Article 213 concerns State ordinances.

secs.t: Judicial checks → Articles

x: Judicial review covers laws and executive action; Articles 13, 32 and 226 provide important constitutional bases, and an ultra vires law is void.
122 and 212 are the reverse bar - courts cannot inquire into the validity of legislative proceedings on the ground of irregular procedure.
Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice and may allow it to fill legal gaps.

secs.t: Cases on separation of powers

x: In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution does not provide for a rigid separation of powers.
The Court held that the legislature cannot decide an election dispute because it is a judicial function; the case also struck down the relevant provision of the 39th Amendment.

secs.t: Options against a judgment → method and limit

x: Exam angle: "Parliament can overrule a judgment by a simple resolution" - false; it must change the law or the Constitution.
After I.R. Coelho, Ninth Schedule entries inserted after 24 April 1973 may be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.
Parliament can override a judgment only by changing the law or the constitutional basis of the ruling, and every such override is tested against the basic structure.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A legislative or political majority cannot override constitutionalism.
The One Nation One Election Bill is associated with amendments to
Articles 83, 172 and 327
Judicial overreach, frequent use of Article 142 and the ordinance route have been criticised as capable of eroding separation of powers.
The Collector’s judicial powers were separated in the Madras Presidency in 1816.

rows.title: President of India - election, qualifications, term, impeachment; executive, legislative, financial, judicial powers
sub: Group-II M1-B-24: President of India - election, powers, veto and ordinance-making power

secs.t: Election of the President — electoral college, value of vote, disputes — Composition (Art 54)

x: Nominated MPs and all Legislative Council members do not vote, while elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry do (70th Amendment, 1992).
The
70th Amendment Act, 1992
added an Explanation to Article 54 so that 'State' includes the NCT of Delhi and Puducherry, bringing their elected MLAs into the Presidential electoral college.

secs.t: Election of the President — electoral college, value of vote, disputes — Voting system & value of vote

x: Article 55(3) prescribes proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and voting by secret ballot.
The Presidential election method of proportional representation by single transferable vote was borrowed from
Ireland
Article 55(1) achieves these principles by assigning vote values to MLAs based on State population and distributing the aggregate MLA vote value among elected MPs.

secs.t: Qualifications, term, oath, resignation and emoluments

x: A presidential candidate must be an Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, qualified for election to the Lok Sabha and must not hold an office of profit.
Article 58
prescribes the qualifications for election as President, including the condition that the person must not hold an office of profit under the Union, a State or a local or other authority.

secs.t: Impeachment and vacancy — Articles 61, 62, 65 — Impeachment (Art. 61)

x: Exam angle: "Removal of the President is under Article ___" - answer
Article 61 provides impeachment only for
violation of the Constitution
In the constitutional terminology stated here, impeachment is used only for the President.
The charge may be initiated in either House.
Elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament participate in impeachment.

secs.t: Impeachment and vacancy — Articles 61, 62, 65 — Causes & election time limit (Art 62)

x: Declaration of the result alone does not terminate the outgoing President’s office.
When both offices are vacant,
the Chief Justice of India
acts as President; in the absence of the CJI, the senior-most Supreme Court judge performs the function.
While acting as President, the Vice-President stops functioning as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Powers of the President — executive, financial, judicial, legislative; appointments

x: Articles 72, 143 and 352 correspond respectively to the pardoning power, consultation with the Supreme Court and National Emergency.
Articles 148, 155, 76 and 324 respectively concern the CAG, Governors, Attorney General, and the Election Commission.
The President can summon and prorogue Parliament, dissolve the Lok Sabha, summon a joint sitting, and send messages to either House.
The President addresses both Houses assembled together at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year under Articles 86 and 87.

secs.t: Position of the President — Article 74 and amendments

x: Article 74
(1) provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President.
The President is the nominal or de jure executive, while the Prime Minister, heading the Council of Ministers, functions as the real or de facto executive.
Article 74(2) provides that the question, if any, and what advice was tendered by Ministers to the President cannot be inquired into by any court.

secs.t: Pardoning power — terms, Article 72 vs 161 and cases — Article 72 scope

x: A
pardon
removes the sentence as well as the conviction.
Remission reduces the period of punishment while retaining its character.

secs.t: Pardoning power — terms, Article 72 vs 161 and cases — Article 72 vs Article 161 (Governor)

x: Maru Ram (1980)
established that the President exercises the pardoning power on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
Kehar Singh and Epuru Sudhakar recognised limited judicial review where the exercise is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant grounds.
In Kehar Singh (1989), the Supreme Court held that the President may examine the evidence afresh, but there is no right to an oral hearing.

secs.t: Veto types → meaning and the President's veto (Article 111)

x: A suspensive veto permits the President to return an Ordinary Bill once for reconsideration.
Pocket veto means keeping a Bill pending without taking a decision.
Absolute veto may apply to a private member's Bill and to a Government Bill when the Cabinet resigns before assent.
The President may assent to or withhold assent to a Money Bill but cannot return it for reconsideration.

secs.t: Presidents of India → order and FIRSTs

x: V.V. Giri won the 1969 Presidential election on
second-preference votes
Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India and the only President elected twice; Pratibha Patil was the first woman President.
N. Sanjiva Reddy assumed office in 1977, K.R. Narayanan in 1997, Pratibha Patil in 2007 and Droupadi Murmu in 2022.

secs.t: Articles 52-78 → content (number game)

x: Article 52 provides for the office of the President, Article 54 concerns the electoral college, Article 60 concerns the oath or affirmation, and Article 71 concerns election disputes.
Article 60 concerns the oath or affirmation, while eligibility for re-election is dealt with by Article 57.
Articles 52 to 78 fall under Part V, Chapter I, which deals with the Union Executive.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Articles 65 and 68
deal respectively with the Vice-President acting as President and the filling of a vacancy in the office of Vice-President.

Impeachment of the President is modelled on the USA, while election by proportional representation through the single transferable vote is taken from Ireland. 'Ireland and USA' reverses them; the UK has no elected President to impeach; Canada is the source of a strong Centre and residuary powers, not impeachment.

rows.title: Veto powers and the ordinance-making power (Article 123); pardoning power (Article 72)

secs.t: Veto by type of bill and pocket veto

x: Pocket veto means keeping the Bill pending without assent, rejection or return.
President Zail Singh used the pocket veto in 1986 in relation to the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.
The Supreme Court held in 2025 that indefinite inaction by the Governor under Article 200 is justiciable; therefore, the Governor does not possess a presidential-style pocket veto.

secs.t: Ordinance (Article 123) — conditions, force, origin and life

x: An Ordinance can cover matters within Parliament’s legislative competence, but it cannot be used to amend the Constitution.
The President's ordinance-making power under Article 123 is a relic of the
Government of India Act, 1935
, which gave the Governor-General power to issue ordinances.
The maximum possible life of an Ordinance is six months plus six weeks, linked to the interval between parliamentary sessions and the post-reassembly period.

secs.t: Amendments and cases on ordinance satisfaction and re-promulgation

x: The 38th Amendment of 1975 made the President’s satisfaction final, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.
D.C. Wadhwa held that routine re-promulgation without placing the Ordinance before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution.
Krishna Kumar Singh held that re-promulgation can be a fraud on the Constitution and that laying before the legislature is mandatory.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.
Frequent ordinances are criticised because
they bypass parliamentary deliberation
The US President has only a qualified veto, which can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
A Governor's ordinance-making power for a State is exercised under
Article 213
; the Andhra Pradesh ordinance concerned organ-transplant committees.

rows.title: Vice-President; Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers - Articles 74, 75, 77, 78
sub: Group-II M1-B-25: Vice-President, Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers

secs.t: Vice-President — office, qualifications and election (Arts 63, 64, 66)

x: Exam angle: "Who elects the VP" (both Houses only) and "Where can the removal resolution first be moved" (Rajya Sabha).
The Vice-President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha.
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote when the votes are equally divided.

secs.t: Vice-President vs President — oath, term, removal, acting, disputes (Arts 65, 67-71) — Oath and term

x: A five-year term, continuing till the successor takes charge (Art. 67(c)).
Removal is initiated in the Rajya Sabha, requires a majority of all the then members of that House, and must be agreed to by the Lok Sabha by simple majority.
Under Article 67(a) the Vice-President resigns by writing to the President, and the resignation takes effect immediately.

secs.t: Vice-President vs President — oath, term, removal, acting, disputes (Arts 65, 67-71) — Acting President (Art. 65)

x: Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with exclusive authority to decide doubts and disputes concerning Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections.
The 39th Amendment of 1975 took away the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over these disputes, while the 44th Amendment of 1978 restored it.
Article 68 requires an election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President as soon as possible.

secs.t: Vice-Presidents → FIRSTs, records and mid-term vacancies

x: Hamid Ansari
served two full terms as Vice-President from 2007 to 2017.
S. Radhakrishnan became President in 1962, Zakir Husain in 1967, V.V. Giri in 1969 and K.R. Narayanan in 1997.
C.P. Radhakrishnan
was elected Vice-President after the mid-term vacancy caused by Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation in July 2025.
Dr.
S. Radhakrishnan
was the first Vice-President (two terms, 1952-62) and later became President in 1962.

secs.t: Prime Minister and ministers — appointment, membership, tenure (Art 75)

x: The Prime Minister has no fixed tenure and ordinarily continues while enjoying the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
Article 75(5) requires a non-member Minister to become a member of either House of Parliament within six consecutive months; otherwise, the person ceases to be a Minister.
The Supreme Court held that the constitutional provision for a non-member Minister cannot be used for repeated reappointments without the person securing election to the legislature.

secs.t: Articles 74, 77, 78 → content

x: Exam angle: "All work of the GoI is done in the name of the President" - Art 77.
A National Emergency does not confer discretionary power on the President to disregard the binding advice of the Council of Ministers.
The provisions occur in the order Article 74(1), Article 75(3), Article 77(1) and Article 78: advice, collective responsibility, executive expression and Prime Ministerial duties.

secs.t: Council of Ministers — size, categories and non-constitutional posts — Union - 91st Amendment

x: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A), limiting the Union Council of Ministers including the Prime Minister to
15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
Article 75(1B), inserted by the 91st Amendment, prevents a member disqualified for defection from being appointed a minister until re-elected to Parliament.

secs.t: Council of Ministers — size, categories and non-constitutional posts — Categories of ministers

x: A Cabinet Minister heads an important ministry and attends Cabinet meetings; a Minister of State with independent charge heads a ministry independently; a Minister of State is attached to a Cabinet Minister; and a Deputy Minister assists a senior Minister.

The Constitution itself does not classify ministers into ranks; by convention the Council comprises Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (Independent Charge), Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers.

secs.t: Council of Ministers — size, categories and non-constitutional posts — Non-constitutional posts

x: The office of Deputy Prime Minister is not mentioned in the Constitution; the Deputy Prime Minister takes oath as an ordinary Minister, Sardar Patel was the first, and the office has rank 5A in the Table of Precedence.
The Leader of the House is not a constitutional office; under Manmohan Singh, a Rajya Sabha member, Pranab Mukherjee was named Leader of the House in the Lok Sabha.

secs.t: Prime Ministers → FIRSTs, records and unique facts

x: Gulzarilal Nanda was the first acting PM (1964, 1966); Indira Gandhi was the first PM from the Rajya Sabha (1966); A.B. Vajpayee had the shortest regular tenure (13 days, 1996); Charan Singh (1979) never faced the Lok Sabha.
The Prime Ministers from the Rajya Sabha were Indira Gandhi (the first, 1966), H.D. Deve Gowda, I.K. Gujral and Manmohan Singh.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: 30 consecutive days of detention for an offence punishable with 5+ years leads to removal on the 31st day.
The UK Prime Minister must belong to the House of Commons, while the Indian Prime Minister may be a member of either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.
The 1956 Gentlemen’s Agreement fixed the united Andhra Pradesh cabinet proportion at
60% Andhra and 40% Telangana

rows.title: Cabinet system, Cabinet committees, collective and individual responsibility; Attorney General of India
sub: Group-II M1-B-26: Cabinet system in India - functioning, committees and collective responsibility

secs.t: Parliamentary form — features and defining principle

x: Majority party rule, collective responsibility and the Prime Minister as the centre of power are necessary features of India’s parliamentary form.
Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers
to the elected House is the characteristic feature distinguishing the parliamentary system.
UPSC 2017 key: the Cabinet form is
a mechanism of parliamentary democracy for ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people

secs.t: Terms → meaning: Cabinet, Council of Ministers, kitchen cabinet, GoMs

x: The Cabinet is the smaller nucleus consisting of Cabinet Ministers; it takes policy decisions and directs and supervises the wider Council of Ministers.
The wider Council of Ministers rarely meets as a body; the Cabinet is the body that meets regularly and takes policy decisions.
A kitchen cabinet is an informal inner circle consisting of trusted colleagues and friends of the Prime Minister, including some senior ministers and non-ministers.

secs.t: Articles → collective and individual responsibility

x: The word ‘Cabinet’ appears only in
Article 352
, which deals with a Proclamation of Emergency and the written advice of the Union Cabinet.
The
President
administers the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers in accordance with the Third Schedule.
Article 164(2)
provides that the Council of Ministers in a State is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.

secs.t: Articles → collective and individual responsibility — Collective responsibility

x: Art. 75(3) makes the Council collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
The Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers; therefore, the death or resignation of the Prime Minister results in the Council of Ministers going out of office.
The
oath of secrecy
ensures confidentiality of Cabinet deliberations and supports the public presentation of a united government.

secs.t: Articles → collective and individual responsibility — Individual responsibility

x: Basis:
Personal statement:
A resigned minister may explain his resignation in the House, with the Speaker's consent.
= collective.

secs.t: Reports, Business Rules and Cabinet committees — Reports and Rules on organisation of government

x: The Department of Personnel came in 1970, originated from the ARC of 1966 and was placed under the Prime Minister.
The 1949 report concerned reorganisation of the machinery of government, including grouping ministries and Cabinet Committees.
Cabinet Committees are
extra-constitutional bodies formed under the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961
, framed under Article 77(3).

secs.t: Reports, Business Rules and Cabinet committees — Cabinet committees — chair and function

x: There are
eight
Cabinet Committees (Apr 2025): Appointments, Security, Political Affairs, Economic Affairs, Parliamentary Affairs, Accommodation, Investment and Growth, and Employment and Skill Development.

The Appointments Committee deals with senior appointments; the Security Committee with defence and national security; the Economic Affairs Committee with economic and infrastructure projects; and the Parliamentary Affairs Committee with parliamentary business.

secs.t: Cabinet Secretariat and Cabinet Secretary — functions and status

x: The Cabinet Secretariat has Civil, Military and Intelligence Wings and is associated with the Directorate of Public Grievances and the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser.
The Cabinet Secretary is first among equals among Secretaries, is placed eleventh in the Table of Precedence and heads the National Crisis Management Committee.

secs.t: Attorney General — Article 76: FIRSTs, rights, limitations

x: Article 88 permits the Attorney General to speak and participate in either House, joint sittings and parliamentary committees, but does not confer a right to vote.
Article 88
confers the Attorney General's right to speak and take part in parliamentary proceedings without the right to vote.
Article 177
gives the Advocate General the right to speak and participate in the proceedings of the State Legislature, without a right to vote.

secs.t: AG vs Solicitor General vs Advocate General

x: The Advocate General is the counterpart of the Attorney General at the State level.

secs.t: Cabinet in practice — changes, issues and debates

x: The kitchen cabinet is criticised as an extra-constitutional power centre because it may shape decisions while bypassing the formal Cabinet.
During single-party majority eras, the Prime Minister and Cabinet generally dominate Parliament, leading to the criticism that the system may resemble a ‘cabinet dictatorship’.
Coalition governments had to accommodate coordination committees and the demands of alliance partners.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Excessive concentration of power in the PMO and Cabinet committees is criticised for diluting collective Cabinet decision-making.
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved the third and fourth railway lines on the
Ballari–Guntakal section
at a cost of Rs 1,264 crore.
G. Sai Prasad
took charge as the Chief Secretary of Andhra Pradesh in February 2026.

rows.title: Types of legislatures - unicameral and bicameral; arguments for a second chamber
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-28

secs.t: Legislature types — definitions and country examples

x: The United Kingdom has the House of Lords as its upper house and the House of Commons as its lower house.
China, Israel, New Zealand, Sweden and Denmark are examples of countries with unicameral national legislatures.
Bicameralism is often preferred in large and diverse countries because two Houses can represent different sections, interests and regions.

secs.t: Persons → statements and arguments on a second chamber

x: A second chamber is argued to provide a double check, regional representation and expert participation.
The criticism of a second chamber expressed in these words is attributed to
Abbé Sieyès
Ayyangar regarded the Rajya Sabha as a forum for dignified debate that could delay legislation passed in the passion of the moment.

secs.t: Rajya Sabha as federal chamber — compared with the US Senate

x: A no-confidence motion is a device of the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha.
Article 312 (creation of new All-India Services) is a special federal role of the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Articles → second chambers in States and UT legislatures

x: Rajya Sabha seats are allocated broadly according to population under the Fourth Schedule, while every US State has two Senators, making 100 Senators in all.
Delhi has 70 Assembly seats, Puducherry has 30 elected members and up to 3 nominated members, and Jammu and Kashmir has 90 elected seats.
Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir
are the three Union Territories having elected members in the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Bangladesh voted in the February 2026 referendum for a bicameral Parliament with a 100-member upper House elected according to party vote share.
Since a joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker and voting strength depends on the combined membership, a larger Lok Sabha would dilute the Rajya Sabha's relative weight.

rows.title: Parliament - composition of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, qualifications, terms, special powers of Rajya Sabha
sub: Group-II M1-B-27: Parliament - composition of the two Houses, qualifications and terms
Group-II M1-B-29: Functions and powers of Parliament; special powers of the Rajya Sabha

secs.t: Parliament — components, President's place and strength of Houses — Article 79 - components

x: Exam angle: Assertion-Reason - "Parliament consists of the President and two Houses" with the opening-address reason (both true, R explains A).
Article 86 enables the President to
address either House of Parliament or both Houses assembled together
and to send messages to them.
Article 331 permitted the President to nominate up to
two
Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented.

secs.t: Parliament — components, President's place and strength of Houses — Strength of the two Houses

x: Article 80 fixes the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha at 250, comprising 238 representatives of States and Union Territories and 12 nominated members.
The present strength is 245:
225 representatives of States, 8 representatives of Union Territories and 12 nominated members
The present strength is 543, comprising 524 members from the States and 19 from the Union Territories.

secs.t: Nominated members — Rajya Sabha and Anglo-Indians

x: The
104th Amendment Act, 2019
ended the provision for nomination of up to two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha, with effect from 25 January 2020.
Article 80(3) mentions literature, science, art and social service.
Nominated members vote in the Vice-Presidential election.
Sachin Tendulkar was nominated in 2012 and Mary Kom in 2016.

secs.t: Seats → States: Fourth Schedule, extremes and AP

x: Andhra Pradesh has 11 seats, Telangana 7, Uttarakhand 3 and Tripura 1 in the Rajya Sabha.
Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura each have one Rajya Sabha seat.
The 87th Amendment enabled readjustment of constituencies on the basis of the 2001 Census.
Andhra Pradesh has 25, Telangana 17, Uttarakhand 5 and the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir 5 Lok Sabha seats.
C is wrong: the smallest Lok Sabha constituency by area is Chandni Chowk (Delhi), not Mumbai South.

secs.t: Amendments and cases on Parliament

x: The 84th Amendment Act, 2001 froze the allocation of Lok Sabha seats based on the 1971 Census until
the first Census after 2026

secs.t: Term of each House — dissolution, extension, permanence

x: The
Fifth Lok Sabha
, constituted for the period 1971–1977, was extended during the 1975–1977 Emergency.
The
Thirteenth Lok Sabha
was dissolved in 2004 before completing its full term.
The six-year term of a Rajya Sabha member is fixed by the
Representation of the People Act, 1951
, and not directly by the Constitution.
To initiate the one-third retirement cycle, the terms of the initial members were curtailed and the members retiring first were decided by
lottery

secs.t: Qualifications and disqualifications — Articles 84, 102, 103, Tenth Schedule

x: A prospective Member of Parliament makes the prescribed oath or affirmation before
the Election Commission or a person authorised by it
, in the form given in the Third Schedule.
Article 102 includes office of profit, unsoundness of mind declared by a court, undischarged insolvency, loss or absence of Indian citizenship and disqualification under a parliamentary law.
A vote or abstention contrary to the party whip may attract disqualification unless the action is permitted or condoned by the party within
15 days

secs.t: Vacation of seats — Article 101

x: Resignation is addressed to the Speaker or Chairman, may be rejected when it is not voluntary or genuine, and absence without permission for 60 days can lead the House to declare the seat vacant.
The
33rd Amendment Act, 1974
amended Article 101(3)(b) so that a resignation takes effect only on acceptance, and the presiding officer may reject it if it is not voluntary or genuine.

secs.t: Women representation — data

x: The 17th Lok Sabha, constituted after the 2019 elections, had 78 women members, approximately 14.4 per cent of the House, the highest number at that time.
Women members crossed 10 per cent of the total strength of the House for the first time in the
15th Lok Sabha
, elected in 2009.
The
106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023
, known as the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, provides for reservation of one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.

secs.t: Sessions — terms → meaning and procedural Articles

x: An adjournment sine die is ordered by the Speaker in the Lok Sabha or the Chairman in the Rajya Sabha, without fixing a date for the next sitting.
Normally, the Speaker or Chairman first adjourns the House sine die; the President then prorogues it, followed by a recess and later reassembly in a new session.
Article 120 recognises Hindi and English for parliamentary business and permits the use of a member's mother tongue with the presiding officer's permission.

secs.t: Functions of Parliament — legislative to electoral

x: Parliament legislates on the Union and Concurrent Lists (and the State List in special cases).

A is the answer: Parliament's electoral functions are electing the Vice-President, taking part in the President's election and electing its presiding officers (the Lok Sabha elects the Speaker and Deputy Speaker).
The Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951 and the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 relate to election law.

secs.t: Parliamentary privileges — Art. 105, collective and individual, Art. 122 — Basis - Art. 105

x: Article 105 protects speech and votes in Parliament and its committees.
The seven-judge Bench in Sita Soren (2024) held that privilege does not protect bribery for voting or speaking and overruled the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao.

secs.t: Parliamentary privileges — Art. 105, collective and individual, Art. 122 — Collective and individual privileges

x: Exam angle: "only members enjoy privileges, not the House" is the
incorrect
statement.
Article 122 bars courts from questioning parliamentary proceedings on the ground of alleged
procedural irregularity
Freedom from arrest applies to civil cases during the prescribed period; it does not extend to criminal or preventive detention cases.
The House may exclude strangers, hold secret sittings, make its own rules and punish for contempt.

secs.t: Rajya Sabha vs Lok Sabha — equal and unequal status

x: The Rajya Sabha may discuss the Budget but cannot vote on demands for grants.
Under Article 67(b), a resolution for initiating the removal of the Vice-President can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha, though the Lok Sabha must agree to it.
The Houses have equal powers in the removal of higher judicial officers, approval of Ordinances and approval of Emergency proclamations.

secs.t: Special powers of Rajya Sabha — Articles 249, 312, 67(b)

x: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Rajya Sabha may approve the Emergency proclamation for the time being.
Article 312
enables Parliament to create new All-India Services on the basis of a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by the required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
Articles 249, 312 and 67(b) respectively deal with State List legislation in the national interest, creation of All-India Services and initiation of the Vice-President’s removal.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The proposed expansion has generated concern in southern States because the relative representation of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan may increase after the 1971-based freeze is lifted.
A constitutional amendment Bill must satisfy the special-majority requirement under
Article 368
; the 2026 Bill fell short of it.
The Tamil Nadu Assembly resolved to retain the Lok Sabha at 543 seats and preserve the approximate 2.2:1 Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio.
The resolution seeking removal of Speaker Om Birla was moved under
Article 94(c)
and was rejected by voice vote on 11 March 2026.
The proposals discussed were to limit party whips to confidence votes and money bills.
Both the creation of Andhra State in 1953 and the reorganisation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014 were carried out under
Article 3
, which concerns the formation and alteration of States.

rows.title: Presiding officers - Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman; Secretariat; sessions, adjournment, prorogation, dissolution

secs.t: Presiding officers → election, resignation and removal

x: Article 93
provides that the House of the People shall choose two members to be Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are charged on the
Consolidated Fund of India
under Article 97.
Under Article 100(1), the Speaker normally does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote when the votes are equally divided.
C.P. Radhakrishnan, as Vice-President, is the present ex officio Chairman, and Harivansh's term as Deputy Chairman ended on 9 April 2026.

secs.t: Speaker → powers and Articles

x: Article 110(3) gives
the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill.
Recognition of the Leader of the Opposition requires the party to have at least one-tenth of the strength of the House, according to the Speaker’s direction.
Under Article 118(4), the
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
presides over a joint sitting (the Deputy Speaker in his absence).

secs.t: Deputy Speaker, Chairman and panels → roles and status

x: The Speaker nominates a Panel of Chairpersons consisting of up to ten members.
A panel member may preside in the absence of both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.

secs.t: Office holders, removal motions, cases and vacancies

x: Removal motions against G. V. Mavalankar in 1954, Hukum Singh in 1966 and Balram Jakhar in 1987 failed.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2019.
In January 2026, the Supreme Court upheld, in the
Justice Varma case
, the Deputy Chairman’s power under Article 91 to decide on a judge-removal motion when the Chairman’s office was vacant.

secs.t: Secretariat and sessions → Articles

x: Article 98 establishes separate secretarial staff for each House while permitting the creation of posts common to both Houses.
Article 86 empowers the President to address either House or both Houses together, require members' attendance and send messages to either House regarding pending Bills.
The President need not summon both Houses together, and the maximum interval between sessions is six months.

secs.t: Secretariat and sessions → Articles — Sessions and the six-month rule

x: Under Article 100(3), the quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, including the presiding officer.
The President’s address outlining Government policy is debated through a
Motion of Thanks
in Parliament.
The usual sessions are the Budget Session from February to May, the Monsoon Session from July to August/September, and the Winter Session from November to December.

secs.t: Secretariat and sessions → Articles — Secretariat - Art 98

x: In the absence of a law by Parliament, the President may make rules after consulting the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The secretariat of each House is headed by its Secretary-General, appointed by the concerned presiding officer.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: session, recess, adjournment, prorogation, dissolution

x: The period from prorogation to the next session is called a
recess
Adjournment sine die terminates a sitting without fixing a date for the next sitting.
The President prorogues Parliament and prorogation terminates the session.
Dissolution terminates the life of the Lok Sabha.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was the Speaker, Kalluri Subbarao was the Deputy Speaker, and Madapati Hanumantha Rao was the first Council Chairman in the first Andhra Pradesh Assembly of 1956.
Only
two
oral answers were recorded in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon Session of 2026, a point cited in criticism concerning low scrutiny.

rows.title: Parliamentary devices - Question Hour, Zero Hour, motions (adjournment, no-confidence, censure, calling attention)
sub: Group-II M1-B-31: Parliamentary committees and parliamentary devices

secs.t: Devices of parliamentary control — list and FIRSTs

x: State Legislatures use the same parliamentary devices for executive control and also use estimates and public accounts committees.
Short-duration discussion is an Indian innovation of 1953, Calling Attention dates from 1954, and Zero Hour is associated with 1962.

secs.t: Question Hour and Zero Hour → timing, types, notice

x: Exam angle: "time after Question Hour when members raise matters without prior notice" = Zero Hour.
Question Hour
is regarded as the most effective method of day-to-day vigilance over the executive because Ministers are required to answer questions.
Zero Hour has no fixed duration in the Rules and in the Lok Sabha lasts until the day's regular agenda is taken up.
Zero Hour
begins immediately after Question Hour in the Lok Sabha; members raise matters with only same-day intimation to the Presiding Officer, not the notice a question needs.

secs.t: Rules of Procedure → devices

x: Rule 377 and Special Mentions serve corresponding purposes in the two Houses, while Rules 193 and 184 distinguish discussions without and with voting respectively.
A half-an-hour discussion is held on a matter that has been sufficiently debated but requires further factual elucidation.
A privilege motion is governed by Rule 222 of the Lok Sabha rules and Rule 187 of the Rajya Sabha rules.

secs.t: Motions → House and key requirement

x: An Adjournment Motion sets aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
An Adjournment Motion is a Lok Sabha device, requires 50 members' support, carries an element of censure and involves debate of at least two hours and thirty minutes.
A policy cut reduces the demand to Re 1, an economy cut reduces it by a specified amount, and a token cut reduces it by Rs 100 to raise a specific grievance.

secs.t: No-confidence vs censure → basis, Speaker's role, instances — Basis and procedure

x: A no-confidence motion is moved under
Rule 198
of the Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha.
The Speaker exercises discretion in admitting or rejecting a no-confidence motion.
The motion tests the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha.
The no-confidence motion is the most powerful weapon of executive accountability, while Question Hour is the most effective day-to-day vigil.

secs.t: No-confidence vs censure → basis, Speaker's role, instances — Censure vs no-confidence

x: "reasons must be stated" = censure motion.
The first no-confidence motion against Jawaharlal Nehru was moved in 1963 by
J.B. Kripalani
Gouthu Latchanna's motion in November 1954 was carried by 69 votes to 68.
Passing a Censure Motion does not compel resignation, whereas passing a No-confidence Motion does.

secs.t: Resolutions and the Whip → features

x: The office of Whip is not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or any parliamentary statute.
A party Whip enforces party discipline regarding attendance and voting, and defiance in relevant circumstances may attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
The
Minister of Parliamentary Affairs
keeps close contact with the Chief Whips of parties in both Houses.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: closures, guillotine, point of order, whip lines

x: Yielding the floor
occurs when the member speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair.
The guillotine refers to curtailing discussion and putting demands to vote without completing detailed debate, and is cited as an issue affecting parliamentary debate quality.
A one-line Whip is informative, a two-line Whip directs members to attend, and a three-line Whip gives a strict voting direction.

secs.t: Committees → types and composition

x: The Lok Sabha Committee of Privileges has 15 members nominated by the Speaker, while the Rajya Sabha Committee has 10 members nominated by the Chairman.
The Speaker is ex-officio Chairperson of the Business Advisory Committee, the Rules Committee and the General Purposes Committee.
The Speaker appoints the Chairpersons of Lok Sabha DRSCs, while the Chairman appoints the Chairpersons of Rajya Sabha DRSCs.
Inquiry committees may be created by a motion or by the Speaker or Chairman; the Committee on MPLADS is an example.

secs.t: Financial committees → members, chair, function, year

x: Exam angle: "which committee has no Rajya Sabha member" = Estimates; "examines CAG reports" = PAC (and CPU for PSUs).
The Public Accounts Committee has 15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha members, elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
The present form of the Estimates Committee originated in 1950 on the recommendation of
John Mathai
The Estimates Committee suggests economies, efficiency, administrative reforms, alternative policies and improvements in the form of estimates.
The
Estimates Committee
has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, elected annually by proportional representation.

secs.t: Committees → nicknames and roles

x: The Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings, Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Committee on Government Assurances and Department-related Standing Committees are described as watchdogs over the executive.
The
Committee on Government Assurances
tracks assurances and promises made by ministers until implementation.
The
Committee on Petitions
examines petitions on bills and matters of public interest and is called Parliament's 'Ombudsman'.

secs.t: Committees → reform areas (CDI)

x: Kasturirangan is linked with education and the 5+3+3+4 structure, Urjit Patel with inflation targeting at 4% plus or minus 2%, and Shanta Kumar with FCI/PDS reform including decentralised procurement and DBT for food.
The
Second Administrative Reforms Commission
(2nd ARC) is linked with a code of ethics, the Right to Public Services and e-governance.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Article 94(c), the fourteen-day notice requirement, support of fifty members and Lok Sabha Rules 200–203 govern the removal procedure.
Only
of Bills in the 17th Lok Sabha were referred to committees; the corresponding figure for the 15th Lok Sabha was 71%.
Question Hour ran for only
of its scheduled time in the cited assessment.

rows.title: Legislative procedure - ordinary, money, financial and constitutional amendment bills; joint sitting
sub: Group-II M1-B-30: Legislative procedure - ordinary, money and financial bills; joint sitting

secs.t: Bills → types: government vs private member's

x: A Government Bill requires seven days' notice, while a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice before introduction.
The Lok Sabha committee examines constitutional amendment Bills introduced by Private Members before their introduction, besides classifying Bills and allotting time.
The Rajya Sabha has no separate Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions for this purpose; its Business Advisory Committee allots the time.

secs.t: Ordinary bill → stages and President's assent (Art. 111)

x: The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.
Since no fixed time limit is prescribed for presidential action, the President may keep an ordinary Bill pending indefinitely, a situation known as a
pocket veto
A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent.

secs.t: Money Bill → Article 110 provisions, procedure and cases

x: A Money Bill may deal with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax.
All three statements describe matters covered by Article 110(1), including Public Account custody, receipt or audit of Consolidated Fund money, and incidental matters.
The Speaker's decision is final under Article 110(3), and the certificate is endorsed on the Bill sent to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.
(Art. 109: return within 14 days; otherwise deemed passed).

secs.t: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

x: The Rajya Sabha may amend or reject a Financial Bill-I; its powers are not restricted to making recommendations.
A Financial Bill-II may be introduced in either House, by a Minister or a private member, but the President's recommendation is required when it is taken into consideration.
A Money Bill deals exclusively with Article 110 matters; a Financial Bill-I contains such matters partly along with other matters; a Financial Bill-II contains none of the Article 110 matters.

secs.t: Articles → House of introduction and President's prior recommendation

x: For a Financial Bill-II involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, the President's recommendation is required
before the Bill is taken into consideration
A State Bill restricting inter-State trade cannot be introduced without the President's previous sanction.
A Bill affecting taxation in which States are interested requires the President's prior recommendation before introduction.

secs.t: Joint sitting → Article 108 provisions and instances

x: Article 108
provides for a joint sitting to resolve specified deadlocks between the two Houses over an ordinary Bill.
If the President does not summon the joint sitting, the Bill
comes to an end
The Bill is decided by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting together at the joint sitting.
The order is: Speaker, then Deputy Speaker, then
the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
, and failing all three, a member chosen by those present.

secs.t: Lapsing of bills — dissolution, prorogation, adjournment

x: Exam angle: "passed by LS but not yet taken up in RS does not lapse" is
false
(APPSC-G1 2024 statement).

Adjournment or adjournment sine die does not cause Bills to lapse; prorogation causes pending notices to lapse except notices for introducing Bills; dissolution causes all pending business before the Lok Sabha to lapse.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Bill relates to simultaneous elections and proposes Article 82A.
The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill within fourteen days.
The alteration of the name of a State is dealt with under
Article 3
Options under Article 200.
The April 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor judgment introduced fixed timelines and deemed assent.

rows.title: Budget in Parliament - stages, cut motions, appropriation and finance bills, Consolidated/Contingency/Public Account

secs.t: Budget → Article 112, terms and FIRSTs

x: The Constitution uses the expression ‘Annual Financial Statement’, not the word ‘Budget’.
The process begins with the Budget Circular, generally issued in September, and printing is traditionally marked by the Halwa ceremony.
The Budget is prepared by the Budget Division in the
Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
R. K. Shanmukham Chetty presented the first Union Budget of independent India on
26 November 1947

secs.t: Funds → Articles 266-267

x: The Consolidated Fund comprises Union revenues, loans raised through specified sources and loan repayments received by the Union.
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account of both the Union and the States.
The Consolidated Fund is covered by Article 266(1), the Public Account by Article 266(2), and the Contingency Fund by Article 267.

secs.t: Cut motions → terms

x: A policy cut proposes to reduce the demand to Re 1, thereby expressing disapproval of the policy underlying the demand.
An economy cut seeks a reduction by a specified amount to suggest economy in expenditure.
Cut motions are moved only in the Lok Sabha during voting on Demands for Grants.

secs.t: Articles → Appropriation Bill and grants (114-116)

x: The Appropriation Bill covers grants voted by the Lok Sabha as well as charged expenditure, and the amount cannot exceed that authorised in the Annual Financial Statement.

A supplementary grant meets an insufficiency; an additional grant covers a new service; an excess grant relates to expenditure beyond the amount granted; and a vote of credit meets an unexpected indefinite demand.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Supplementary, additional or excess grants are provided for under
Article 115
The Andhra Pradesh Budget 2026-27 was presented on 14 February 2026 by Finance Minister
Payyavula Keshav
K. Atchannaidu presented the separate Agriculture Budget, Governor S. Abdul Nazeer addressed both Houses at the opening, and the State Budget was presented on 14 February 2026.

rows.title: Parliamentary committees - PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings, Departmentally Related Standing Committees, ad hoc

secs.t: Parliamentary committees — types, origin and FIRSTs

x: The Estimates Committee traces to the Standing Financial Committee of 1921 but took its present form in 1950 on
John Mathai
's recommendation.
COPU was created in 1964 on the
Krishna Menon Committee
's recommendation.
The two broad kinds are inquiry committees set up for a particular subject and Select or Joint Committees constituted to examine Bills.

secs.t: Financial committees → strength, chairman and role

x: Members are elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and hold office for one year.
The Speaker appoints the chairperson of the Estimates Committee, who is invariably a member of
the ruling party
The PAC has
22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
(as associate members).

secs.t: PAC → scrutiny, reporting, limits and chairman

x: The Public Accounts Committee examines the Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts and audit reports submitted by the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
The PAC checks whether expenditure remained
within the scope of the demand for grant
approved by Parliament.
K.C. Venugopal
, an Opposition member, chairs the PAC for 2026-27, in line with the convention of an Opposition chairman.

secs.t: DRSCs and other standing committees → strength and functions — Departmentally Related Standing Committees

x: DRSCs began in 1993 with 17 committees, expanded to 24 from 2004, and were introduced on the recommendation of the Rules Committee.
DRSCs scrutinise demands for grants, referred Bills, annual reports and the long-term policy of the ministries under their jurisdiction.
The Speaker chairs the Lok Sabha
Business Advisory Committee
, which allots time for government and other business.

secs.t: DRSCs and other standing committees → strength and functions — Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs

x: The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs has 30 members, comprising 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
The committee examines welfare programmes and the reports of the National Commissions.

secs.t: Ad hoc committees → inquiries, Bills and JPCs

x: Referral of a Bill to a Select Committee or Joint Committee takes place through
a motion in the House
The investigations occurred in the order Bofors (1987), Harshad Mehta securities scam (1992), Ketan Parekh (2001), soft-drink pesticides (2003) and 2G spectrum (2011).
The 129th Amendment (ONOE) Bill and the FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 are before JPCs.

secs.t: Committee → nickname / role

x: The
Committee on Petitions
is popularly described as the Ombudsman of Parliament because it considers petitions on bills and matters of public interest.
The PAC is described as a watchdog on departmental expenditure and irregularities, and the Estimates Committee suggests economies and alternative policies.
The watchdog group comprises the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Committee on Government Assurances, Estimates Committee, PAC, COPU and Departmentally Related Standing Committees.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Jairam Ramesh issued a privilege notice against Education Minister
Dharmendra Pradhan
over remarks concerning a standing committee.
The PAC is criticised as a post-mortem mechanism because it examines expenditure after it occurs; frequent guillotine of demands can further weaken financial control.
Average attendance at the 16 DRSCs and the PAC was only 53% since the September reconstitution, and five meetings were postponed for lack of quorum.

rows.title: Parliamentary privileges; anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) and the role of the Speaker
sub: Group-II M1-B-80: Anti-Defection Law - Tenth Schedule, grounds, exemptions and the Speaker's role
Group-II M1-B-81: Anti-Defection Law - judicial interpretation, working and suggested reforms

secs.t: Parliamentary privileges → Articles, rules and punishments

x: Article 105 concerns Parliament's privileges, Article 122 concerns parliamentary proceedings, Article 194 concerns State Legislature privileges and Article 212 concerns State Legislature proceedings.
Privilege notices are raised under Rule 222 in the Lok Sabha and Rule 187 in the Rajya Sabha, usually after Question Hour.
The
Maharashtra Legislative Council
's Privileges Committee summoned Kunal Kamra on a breach notice.

secs.t: Anti-defection law — background, Amendments and FIRSTs — Background

x: The law was intended to curb horse-trading and defections for office, thereby promoting party discipline and stable governments.
The expression became associated with rampant defections in
Haryana in 1967
, a phenomenon that contributed to the enactment of the anti-defection law.
The
Y.B. Chavan Committee on Defections
studied the problem during 1967–1969.

secs.t: Anti-defection law — background, Amendments and FIRSTs — Amendment → provision

x: The 52nd Amendment amended
Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191
concerning vacation of seats and disqualification.
The 35th Amendment introduced a different Tenth Schedule concerning Sikkim, and the 36th Amendment omitted it.
The
52nd Amendment Act, 1985
inserted the Tenth Schedule and mentioned political parties in the Constitution for the first time, thereby giving them constitutional recognition.

secs.t: Anti-defection law — background, Amendments and FIRSTs — 91st Amendment Act, 2003 → changes

x: The State Council of Ministers is capped at 15 per cent of the Assembly strength, but it cannot consist of fewer than
12 ministers
Articles 75(1B), 164(1B) and 361B
impose these restrictions on a disqualified defector until re-election.

secs.t: Tenth Schedule → coverage, grounds and exceptions (Paras) — Coverage

x: Members of both Houses of Parliament and both Houses of State Legislatures, including MLCs, are covered.
An independent member is disqualified if he or she joins any political party after election.
Voting or abstaining against the party direction without permission attracts disqualification unless the party condones the conduct within
15 days

secs.t: Tenth Schedule → coverage, grounds and exceptions (Paras) — Exceptions

x: A valid merger requires two conditions: the original political party must merge with another party, and at least two-thirds of the legislature party must agree to the merger.
Both groups are protected when the Para 4 merger conditions are met.

secs.t: Speaker as deciding authority → Para 6, Para 7 and time limit

x: The Election Commission does not give an opinion in Tenth Schedule proceedings; that arrangement applies to certain other disqualifications under Articles 103 and 192.
Kihoto Hollohan preserved judicial review after the decision, but limited it to grounds such as mala fides, perversity, violation of natural justice and constitutional mandate.

secs.t: Cases → holdings on privileges and defection — Privilege cases

x: The seven-judge Bench held that privilege does not protect bribery to speak or vote, thereby overruling the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
Ravi S. Naik held that voluntarily giving up membership is not the same as resigning; it may be inferred from conduct, including publicly backing a rival party.

secs.t: Cases → holdings on privileges and defection — Kihoto Hollohan v Zachillhu (1992)

x: The Constitution Bench held that the law did not violate legislators' freedom of speech or the basic structure.
The Supreme Court indicated that the Speaker should decide disqualification petitions within
three months
, except in extraordinary circumstances.
The Court recognised extraordinary exceptions to the three-month period and suggested consideration of a permanent independent tribunal.

secs.t: Cases → holdings on privileges and defection — Subhash Desai v Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (May 2023)

x: Ravi S. Naik concerned inference from conduct; G. Viswanathan concerned the status of an expelled member; Subhash Desai concerned the party’s authority over the whip and House leader.
The Palaniswami camp cited the ruling to claim control of the
whip under Paragraph 2(1)(b)
The proceedings concerned the claim of a ‘deemed merger’ under
Paragraph 4
of the Tenth Schedule.

secs.t: Cases → holdings on privileges and defection — Later rulings

x: The Supreme Court issued a time-bound direction in the Telangana matter and later gave three weeks for the last two of ten BRS petitions, warning of contempt.
The concern arises from the absence of a fixed time limit and the partisan context in which Speakers, who do not resign from their parties, decide petitions.

secs.t: Working of the law → ways around it and Speaker delay

x: Resort politics involves keeping legislators together or sequestered before a floor test to prevent rival parties from poaching them.
In the resignation route, MLAs resign instead of defecting, thereby reducing the majority mark without being disqualified, and may later re-contest on the new party’s ticket.
The examples cited were seven AAP Rajya Sabha MPs joining the BJP in April 2026 and twenty TMC MPs joining the NPCI in June 2026.

secs.t: Anti-defection in Andhra Pradesh → events

x: The petitions were never decided, making the episode a standard example of delay by the Speaker in anti-defection proceedings.
In June 2019, four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs were treated as having merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao's defection toppled N.T. Rama Rao's government in 1984.

secs.t: Committees and bodies → reform recommendations

x: Exam angle: match a case to its holding, or a committee to its remedy.
A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

: Goswami (1990) would disqualify only for voluntarily giving up membership or defying the whip on confidence/no-confidence motions; the Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) would delete the split and merger exceptions and treat pre-poll alliances as parties; NCRWC (2002) would bar defectors from public or remunerative political office for the rest of the term and treat their votes as invalid; the EC wanted the President/Governor to decide on its binding advice.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Critics argue that the law suppresses intra-party dissent and free expression, while failing to prevent mass defections effectively.
All three statements reflect criticisms of the working of the anti-defection law, especially its effect on internal dissent and its perceived inability to prevent mass defections.
The reform proposal is to limit the operation of whips mainly to
confidence votes and Money Bills
, thereby allowing greater legislative dissent on other matters.
