rows.title: Productivity and decline of Parliament - issues of debate quality, disruptions and reforms

secs.t: Data — sittings, productivity and committee scrutiny

x: PRS data placed Lok Sabha productivity at 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha productivity at 39 per cent during the Monsoon Session of 2026.
During the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for only
60 per cent
of its scheduled time.
The
15th Lok Sabha
referred 71% of Bills to committees, against 60% in the 14th, 25% in the 16th and only 16% in the 17th.

secs.t: Articles, rules and Acts → provisions

x: The Lok Sabha sits around 60–70 days annually, whereas the UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings.
Article 85(1) bars a gap of more than six months between sessions but prescribes no minimum number of sitting days.
Rule 373 concerns withdrawal for the day, Rule 374 concerns suspension by House motion up to the remainder of the session, and Rule 374A provides automatic suspension for grave disorder.

secs.t: Issues → weak scrutiny and bypass routes

x: The increased use of ordinances under Article 123 and delegated legislation has grown as legislative engagement has fallen.
The proposals were to define immediate necessity, permit courts to test urgency, and publish reasons for ordinances.
The Money Bill route may bypass the Rajya Sabha for laws whose provisions may not strictly fit within Article 110.

secs.t: Opposition and Leader of Opposition → recognition and tools

x: The Speaker recognises the Leader of the Opposition when the party has at least
one-tenth
of the House’s strength, equivalent to 55 members in the Lok Sabha.
The Leader of the Opposition has statutory status under the
Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977
Question Hour, motions and committees are important opposition tools.

secs.t: Reform proposals and data sources → bodies

x: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended 120 sitting days for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha.
The proposals include a fixed calendar, stronger Question Hour, mandatory committee scrutiny, and protection of opposition debate time.
The official attendance and sitting data is available on the Lok Sabha website through
Digital Sansad

secs.t: State legislatures — data and AP sittings

x: The Business Advisory Committee fixing the agenda was chaired by
Speaker Chintakayala Ayyanna Patrudu
Odisha Assembly met for 43 days, while Nagaland Assembly met for only 7 days.
About 33 per cent, or nearly one-third, of the more than 600 Bills were passed in a single sitting.
The Andhra Pradesh Budget Session 2026 ran from
11 February to 7 March 2026

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Joint sittings of Parliament have been used only
three
times so far.
The 86th AIPOC was at Lucknow with the theme 'Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation'.
Lack of time and expertise, executive dominance and the guillotine are identified criticisms.
The Farm Laws of 2020 are cited as an instance of
hasty law-making
in the criticism of parliamentary debate and legislative scrutiny.

rows.title: Parliamentary form of government - features, merits, demerits; comparison with the presidential system
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-36

secs.t: Parliamentary government — meaning and features

x: Exam angle: Assertion-Reason: "India is parliamentary because the executive is responsible to the legislature" - both true, R explains A.
A non-member may become a minister, but must become a member of either House of Parliament within
six months
Both are true and R explains A: responsibility of the executive (the Council of Ministers) to the legislature is the defining test of the parliamentary system.

secs.t: Countries → system of government

x: The parliamentary system originated in
Britain
and is commonly called the Westminster model.
France, Russia and Sri Lanka
are identified as examples of countries where a President and a Prime Minister coexist under a semi-presidential arrangement.

secs.t: Presidential and semi-presidential systems → features

x: The parliamentary system is based on a fusion of executive and legislative powers, while the presidential system rests on separation of powers.
Executive responsibility and possible early dissolution are parliamentary features, while fixed tenure and removal only by impeachment are presidential features.
France's Fifth Republic dates from 1958, and Sri Lanka's 1978 Constitution provides for a directly elected President with real powers alongside a legislature-responsible Prime Minister.

secs.t: India vs Britain and USA → feature comparison

x: Britain requires ministers to be members of Parliament and has legal ministerial responsibility and an institutionalised shadow cabinet.
India and the United States share a written Constitution, a federal structure, an independent judiciary with judicial review, and constitutional rights protections.
The United States Supreme Court's
wide power of judicial review
has led to its description as a “third chamber.”.

secs.t: Merits, demerits and the Constituent Assembly's choice

x: Harmony between the executive and legislature can help resolve deadlock through fresh elections, and continuous accountability is a merit.
Executive-legislature deadlock and the danger of a personality cult around a single executive are demerits of the presidential system.
The Constituent Assembly preferred the parliamentary system partly to avoid executive-legislature conflict and to ensure accountability.

secs.t: Persons, commissions and Articles → the presidential-system debate

x: Dr B.R. Ambedkar observed that a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility.
The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution, chaired by Venkatachaliah and functioning during 2000–02, reviewed the issue and advised
retaining the parliamentary system
Critics argue that fixed tenures may introduce presidential features into the parliamentary system and weaken accountability; therefore; .

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The ruling party in the United Kingdom can replace its Prime Minister.
India has no term limit for its Prime Minister.
Public criticism of Cabinet policy by the Governor was held to run counter to the parliamentary system.
With 8,931 days, Modi passed
Pawan Kumar Chamling
's 8,930 days.

sub: Group-II M1-B-33: State executive - Governor, Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers
Group-II M1-B-63: Role of the Governor as a source of Centre-State tension; Article 356 and S.R. Bommai

secs.t: Governor — appointment, term, removal and immunities (Articles 153-159, 202, 361) — Appointment and qualifications → Article

x: Exam angle: minimum age of 35; "pleasure of the President" makes the office structurally dependent on the Centre.
Article 155 deals with appointment, Article 156 with tenure and the President's pleasure, Article 157 with qualifications, and Article 158 with conditions of office.
Under Article 159, the Chief Justice of the High Court (or, in his absence, the senior-most judge available) administers the Governor's oath.

secs.t: Governor — appointment, term, removal and immunities (Articles 153-159, 202, 361) — Term and removal

x: The normal term is five years, but the Governor continues in office until the successor enters office.
The Governor is not answerable to either House of Parliament, to the State Legislature, or to the State Council of Ministers.
Article 156 incorporates the President's pleasure, but B.P. Singhal v. Union of India held that the power cannot be exercised arbitrarily.

secs.t: Governor — appointment, term, removal and immunities (Articles 153-159, 202, 361) — Emoluments and immunities

x: Article 361 protects the Governor from being answerable to any court for official acts and bars criminal proceedings during the term of office.

secs.t: Governor's powers → Articles (legislative, executive, ordinance) — Quick-revision table (Group-II)

x: Under Article 171, the Governor nominates
one-sixth
of the members of a State Legislative Council from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in specified fields.

Article 166 concerns executive action in the Governor's name; Article 164 concerns the Chief Minister and ministers; Article 165 concerns the Advocate-General; and Article 316 concerns the State Public Service Commission.

secs.t: Governor's powers → Articles (legislative, executive, ordinance) — Legislative powers

x: The address is delivered on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers; therefore; .

secs.t: Governor's powers → Articles (legislative, executive, ordinance) — Ordinance — Governor vs President
Governor and the Council of Ministers — Articles 164, 167 and the hung House — Article 164 provisions

x: Article 164(1) provides that the Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor; other ministers are appointed by the Governor on the Chief Minister's advice.
Article 164(4) requires a non-member minister to become a member of the State Legislature within
six months
A Minister for Tribal Welfare is mandatory in
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha

secs.t: Governor and the Council of Ministers — Articles 164, 167 and the hung House — CM's role

x: The Chief Minister must communicate the decisions of the Council of Ministers to the Governor and furnish information sought by the Governor.
The stated practice is that
an early floor test
should follow the Governor’s invitation, so that majority support is demonstrated in the House.
The Governor invited C. Joseph Vijay on the basis of 120 letters of support, following the Sarkaria-Punchhi order and requiring an early floor test.

secs.t: Discretionary powers — constitutional vs situational (Article 163) — Article 163

x: Article 163(1) provides for aid and advice by the Council of Ministers except where the Governor is required to exercise discretion.
Under Art. 163(2) the Governor's decision on whether a matter is discretionary is final, and Art. 163(3) bars courts from inquiring into ministers' advice.
Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision final on whether a matter is discretionary, but it does not create complete immunity from judicial review.

secs.t: Discretionary powers — constitutional vs situational (Article 163) — Types of discretion

x: Reserving a Bill for the President under Article 200 is an express constitutional discretion.

Article 200 concerns reservation of Bills, Article 356 concerns the President's Rule report, Article 167 concerns information from the Chief Minister and Article 239 concerns administration of Union Territories.
All three are identified as special constitutional responsibilities or express areas of the Governor's discretion.

secs.t: Discretionary powers — constitutional vs situational (Article 163) — Scope of discretion

x: The constitutional position described is that the Governor's discretion is wider than the President's; the Constitution does not confer a comparable general discretion on the President.
Under Article 239(2), the Governor administering an adjoining UT acts independently of his State's Council of Ministers; it is an express discretion.

secs.t: Bills → Governor's and President's options (Articles 200/201) — Article 200 - Governor's options

x: If the Legislature re-passes a Bill that was returned for reconsideration, the Governor must assent to it and cannot withhold assent again.
A Bill may be reserved only once.
Reservation is mandatory where a Bill derogates from the powers of the High Court.
Every Bill affecting State finances need not be mandatorily reserved.

secs.t: Bills → Governor's and President's options (Articles 200/201) — Bills reserved to get protection → Article

x: Taxes on water/electricity in inter-State river projects fall under Article 288; Article 304(b) concerns restrictions on inter-State trade, which need prior Presidential sanction.

Article 200 deals with the Governor's choices on a State Bill; Article 201 deals with Bills reserved for the President; Article 254(2) concerns Concurrent List repugnancy; and Article 360 concerns Financial Emergency.

secs.t: Bills → Governor's and President's options (Articles 200/201) — Article 201 - President's options

x: Only a non-Money Bill can be returned for reconsideration.
Article 201 prescribes no fixed time limit for the President's decision on a reserved Bill.

secs.t: Cases and References on the Governor → holdings — Landmark cases

x: Nabam Rebia held that the powers under Article 174 and the address under Articles 175–176 are exercised on aid and advice.
The Perarivalan judgment of 2022 held that the Governor is bound by Cabinet advice on pardon or remission under Article 161; this position was reaffirmed subsequently.
The nine-judge Bench in S.R. Bommai held that an Article 356 proclamation is subject to judicial review and that the Centre must show relevant material supporting it.

secs.t: Cases and References on the Governor → holdings — Removal — B.P. Singhal

x: The pleasure doctrine is not unfettered: removal cannot be arbitrary or based merely on a change in the Government at the Centre.

secs.t: Cases and References on the Governor → holdings — Assent time limits — Punjab 2023, TN April 2025, Reference Nov 2025

x: Exam angle: statements on the four options, the one mandatory reservation, and whether courts can fix timelines (current position: they cannot).
Exam angle: the April 2025 timelines and deemed assent do not survive the Nov 2025 Reference opinion.
The 2023 Punjab case held that the Governor
must act as soon as possible and cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely
The Presidential Reference rejected court-imposed timelines, while permitting limited intervention in cases of prolonged unexplained inaction.
The 8 April 2025 ruling prescribed timelines and recognised deemed assent, while the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejected rigid deadlines and deemed assent.
Shamsher Singh (1974), decided by a seven-judge Bench, affirmed that the Governor ordinarily acts on
the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers

secs.t: Article 356 — provisions, FIRSTs and practice — Provisions

x: Article 356 applies when the President is satisfied that the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
Beyond one year, a National Emergency must be in force and the Election Commission must certify that elections cannot be conducted.
Article 357
provides for the exercise of legislative powers under a proclamation issued under Article 356.

secs.t: Article 356 — provisions, FIRSTs and practice — FIRSTs and frequency

x: Kerala in 1959
witnessed the first dismissal of an elected State Government under President's Rule.
In the former Jammu and Kashmir constitutional arrangement, Governor’s Rule was imposed under Section 92 of the J&K Constitution for six months, after which Article 356 could apply.
Bommai upheld the dismissals of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh on the ground of secularism, a basic feature.

secs.t: Judicial review of Article 356 — Bommai guidelines, proper vs improper use

x: S.R. Bommai established that majority must ordinarily be tested on the floor of the House, not in Raj Bhavan.
Bommai protected the Assembly pending parliamentary approval, permitted restoration of a displaced ministry, and treated secularism as a basic feature.
Intra-party disputes and maladministration alone are improper grounds.

secs.t: Commissions → recommendations on the Governor and Article 356

x: The First ARC stressed public experience and non-partisanship; Rajamannar dealt with Centre-State relations; Sarkaria recommended a neutral outsider and consultation; Punchhi recommended fixed tenure.
Rameshwar Prasad cited Sarkaria regarding misuse of Article 356 reports and urged a cooling-off period before politicians are appointed as Governors.
The Punchhi Commission recommended a localised emergency for a district for up to three months, codification of Bommai guidelines in Article 356 and fixed tenure for Governors.
The study team recommended an Inter-State Council under Article 263, suitable non-partisan Governors, maximum delegation of powers to States and greater financial resources for States.

secs.t: Persons — Governors and CMs of AP, FIRST women — Governors

x: Biswabhusan Harichandan
became the separate Governor of Andhra Pradesh in 2019 after the common-governorship arrangement under E.S.L. Narasimhan.
S. Abdul Nazeer
was the Governor of Andhra Pradesh in August 2026 and notified the Monsoon Session from 17 August 2026 under Article 174(1).
Chandrababu Naidu was CM 2014-19, Jagan Mohan Reddy 2019-24, Chandrababu Naidu again from June 2024, and S. Abdul Nazeer has been Governor since February 2023.

secs.t: Persons — Governors and CMs of AP, FIRST women — Deputy CMs

x: The office of Deputy Chief Minister is not a constitutional post; it is a political arrangement within the Council of Ministers.
Sarojini Naidu
became the first woman Governor of an Indian State, serving as Governor of Uttar Pradesh in 1947.
Pawan Kalyan (Jana Sena) is Deputy CM, and the 2019-24 government had five Deputy CMs.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The controversy concerned Governors walking out of or skipping the mandatory Article 176 address in Opposition-ruled States.
The 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill proposes automatic removal after detention for 30 consecutive days on charges carrying a possible sentence of five or more years.
The Andhra Pradesh references are President’s Rule in 1973 during the Jai Andhra movement and the 2020 Andhra Pradesh High Court episode concerning constitutional breakdown.
Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure under Article 164, which allows dismissal of a CM who has lost majority.

rows.title: Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers; Advocate General of the State

secs.t: Chief Minister — Article 164: appointment, tenure and responsibility

x: Under Article 164(3), the Governor administers the oath of office and secrecy to the Chief Minister and other ministers.
The recommended order is pre-poll alliance, then the single largest party with support of others, then a post-poll coalition, and finally a post-poll alliance with outside support, i.e.
Article 164(2) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the
Legislative Assembly
alone.

secs.t: CM's duties towards the Governor — Article 167

x: All three statements correctly describe the Chief Minister's duties and intermediary role under Article 167.
Under Article 167, the
Governor
can call on the Chief Minister for information about administration and legislative proposals, and this is a constitutional discretion of the Governor.

secs.t: Chief Ministers and Deputy CMs — FIRSTs and status

x: A Deputy Chief Minister ranks with Union Ministers of State and occupies position No. 10 in the order of precedence.
Nallapati Venkata Ramaiah
was the first Speaker of the united Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly.
Sucheta Kripalani
became CM of Uttar Pradesh in 1963, the first woman CM.
Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy
was the first CM of united Andhra Pradesh (1956-60).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Bill proposes amendments to Articles 75, 164 and 239AA.
The proposed provision applies when the offence is punishable with imprisonment of
five years or more
and the person remains in custody for 30 consecutive days.
The 11th NITI Aayog Governing Council saw the presence of all 28 Chief Ministers for the first time.

rows.title: State legislature - Assembly and Legislative Council; creation and abolition of the Council (Article 169)
sub: Group-II M1-B-34: State legislature - Assembly and Legislative Council; creation and abolition of the Council

secs.t: Legislative Assembly — strength, term and quorum (number game)

x: Parliament may extend the Assembly's term by one year at a time during a National Emergency, but the extension cannot continue beyond six months after the Emergency has ceased.
Quorum is
10 members
or one-tenth of the total membership, whichever is greater.
The
104th Constitutional Amendment Act
, 2020 discontinued the provision for nomination of Anglo-Indian members to the Legislative Assemblies of States.

secs.t: Legislative Council — composition, size and tenure (number game)

x: Registered graduates elect one-twelfth; the one-sixth share is nominated by the Governor.
The Governor nominates one-sixth of the Council from the specified fields, and the nominations are made on Cabinet advice.
Members of a State Legislative Council are elected indirectly through
proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote
A Legislative Council must have at least 40 members and cannot exceed one-third of the Assembly's strength.

secs.t: Article 169 and States with Legislative Councils

x: The constitutional process is initiated by a special-majority resolution of the Legislative Assembly and completed through a law of Parliament; the Governor has no role in initiating or approving that resolution.
Article 169 needs a special majority: a majority of the total membership of the Assembly plus not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.

Andhra Pradesh abolished its Legislative Council in 1985 (NTR government) and revived it in 2007; in January 2020 the Assembly resolved to abolish it again, but withdrew that resolution in November 2021.

secs.t: Presiding officers → powers (Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman) — Election, tenure and vacating office

x: All three statements correctly state the grounds and procedure for vacating the Speaker's office under Article 179.
Under Article 181, the Speaker does not preside while a resolution for removal is under consideration, but may speak and vote in the first instance.
The Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker (Art. 179).

secs.t: Presiding officers → powers (Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman) — Powers

x: Under Article 199(3), the
Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
Under Article 189, the Speaker does not vote in the first instance but exercises a casting vote in the event of an equality of votes.
The Assembly has a Speaker and Deputy Speaker, while the Council has a Chairman and Deputy Chairman.

secs.t: Disqualification of state legislators — Articles 190-192

x: Under Articles 191 and 192, the Governor decides such questions, but must act according to the opinion of the Election Commission.
Absence for 60 days without permission results in vacation of the seat under Article 190(4), not disqualification under Article 191.
The resignation of an MLA takes effect only upon acceptance by the Speaker.

secs.t: Assembly vs Council — bills, powers and MLAs in indirect elections — Assembly vs Council

x: An ordinary Bill may be delayed by the Council for up to three months on the first occasion and one month on the second occasion.
A Bill originating in the Council ends when rejected by the Assembly, and there is no second chance for the Council.
The State Legislative Council can delay legislation but cannot permanently veto an Assembly Bill.

secs.t: Assembly vs Council — bills, powers and MLAs in indirect elections — Order of proceedings

x: The indicated order is the Governor's address, followed by general discussion and then voting on demands in the Assembly.
The Governor addresses the Legislature on the first day of the first session of each year, and the address is followed by discussion in the House.
Elected MLAs participate in the Presidential election, elect Rajya Sabha members by PR-STV, and elect one-third of the members of the State Legislative Council.

secs.t: Articles 168-212 → content (number game)

x: Article 169 concerns Legislative Councils, Article 173 qualifications, Article 194 privileges, and Article 202 the Annual Financial Statement.
Articles 174, 175 and 176 respectively concern sessions and dissolution, the Governor's address and messages, and the special address.
Article 174 requires that not more than
six months
intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next.
Article 212 concerns the exclusion of judicial inquiry into legislative proceedings.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Deputy Speaker’s post was vacant in eight States, and Jharkhand had no Deputy Speaker for 21 years.
Muthulakshmi Reddy
was India’s first woman legislator and served in the Madras Legislative Council.
Gaddam Prasad Kumar is the Speaker, whereas Gutha Sukender Reddy is the Chairman of the Telangana Legislative Council.

rows.title: Legislature of Andhra Pradesh - structure and functioning
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-39

secs.t: AP Legislature — seat, presiding officers and FIRSTs

x: Kodela Siva Prasada Rao was the first Speaker of the residual Andhra Pradesh Assembly during 2014–2019.
Madapati Hanumantha Rao was the first Chairman of the Legislative Council, while Puchalapalli Sundarayya was the first Leader of Opposition.
K. Raghu Ramakrishna Raju
is the Deputy Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly as stated for 2026.

secs.t: AP Legislative Assembly — number game: strength, reserved seats, Assemblies

x: The Anglo-Indian nomination provision under Article 333 ended with the
104th Constitutional Amendment
In the 2024 election, the NDA won 164 of 175 seats and the YSRCP won 11 seats.
The NDA total consisted of 135 TDP seats, 21 JSP seats and 8 BJP seats.
The YSRCP won 11 of the 175 seats, which was below the one-tenth threshold required for official Opposition status.

secs.t: AP Legislative Council — year → event, strength and composition

x: The Council was created in 1958, abolished in 1985, revived in 2007, and the Assembly passed an abolition resolution in January 2020.
The Council comprises 20 members elected by local authorities, 20 elected by MLAs, 5 by graduates, 5 by teachers and 8 nominated by the Governor.
The 2015 amendment raised the maximum permissible strength of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council from the reorganisation limit of 50 to 58 members.

secs.t: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 — Section → legislature provision

x: All four provisions are correctly matched.
Sec. 18 gave one Anglo-Indian nominee each under Art. 333 (now lapsed after the 104th Amendment).
Section 26 contemplated 225 seats for Andhra Pradesh and 153 for Telangana, subject to Article 170, but the increase has not yet been implemented.

secs.t: Delimitation in AP — Order 2008 and district → seats

x: The Delimitation Order, 2008 was based on the 2001 Census and the Delimitation Commission constituted in 2002.
The present Andhra Pradesh has 175 Assembly constituencies and 25 Lok Sabha constituencies under the Delimitation Order, 2008 after the 2014 reorganisation.
Article 170(3) freezes Assembly numbers until
the first Census after 2026

secs.t: Committees and Bills of the AP Legislature

x: Both statements are true, but appointment of committee chairpersons by the Speaker does not explain the separate convention that the Public Accounts Committee chairperson belongs to the Opposition.
The November 2021 Repeal Act withdrew the three-capitals law and the CRDA repeal, thereby restoring Amaravati.
The united Assembly rejected the Draft Reorganisation Bill by a resolution through voice vote; nevertheless, the law enacted by Parliament prevailed.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Governor S. Abdul Nazeer summoned the Monsoon Session from 17 August 2026 under
Article 174(1)
17 August 2026 was the starting date of the Monsoon Session, whereas the Budget Session began on 11 February 2026.
The Bill proposed fresh delimitation and an increase of Lok Sabha seats to 850, with consequential effects on State Assemblies, but it was negatived in the Lok Sabha.

rows.title: Supreme Court - composition, appointment, collegium and NJAC, jurisdictions (original, appellate, advisory, writ)
sub: Group-II M1-B-36: Supreme Court - composition, appointment, jurisdiction and powers
Group-II M1-B-38: Independence of the judiciary - constitutional safeguards; collegium and the NJAC judgment

secs.t: Supreme Court — establishment, constitutional basis, seat and FIRSTs

x: The Federal Court was established in 1937, Privy Council appeals were abolished in 1949, the Supreme Court was inaugurated in 1950, and it shifted to Tilak Marg in 1958.
The Supreme Court is dealt with in Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124–147, and performs the role of final constitutional interpreter and guardian of Fundamental Rights.

secs.t: Chief Justices and judges → FIRSTs and roles

x: Justice M. Fathima Beevi
became the first woman Judge of the Supreme Court of India in 1989.
Justice
Y.V. Chandrachud
served as Chief Justice of India from 1978 to 1985 and was the longest-serving CJI.
K. Subba Rao served as CJI in 1966–67 and N.V. Ramana served in 2021–22; both were from Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Number of judges — Art. 124(1), year → strength

x: Article 124(1)
provides the constitutional basis for determining the number of judges of the Supreme Court.
The strength was 8 in 1950, 18 in 1977, 26 in 1986 and 31 from 2009.
The sanctioned judge strength was raised to 38 through an ordinance in May 2026, when the case backlog was nearing six figures.

secs.t: Appointment, qualifications and tenure — Articles 124 to 128 — Appointment (Art. 124(2))

x: The convention was broken in 1973 in the appointment of A.N. Ray and again in 1977 in the appointment of M.H. Beg.
Article 124(3) requires Indian citizenship and either five years as a High Court Judge, ten years as a High Court advocate, or being a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion.
Under Article 124(2) the President appoints the CJI (and other judges); by convention the senior-most judge is appointed.

secs.t: Appointment, qualifications and tenure — Articles 124 to 128 — Acting, ad hoc and retired judges

x: Article 124(2) requires consultation with the
Chief Justice of India
for appointment of a Supreme Court Judge.
Article 127 applies when there is no quorum of permanent judges available to hold or continue a sitting of the Supreme Court.
Article 126
lets the President appoint an acting CJI when the office is vacant or the CJI is unable to act.
Article 124(4) deals with removal of a Supreme Court judge, while Article 218 applies the relevant provisions to High Court judges.

secs.t: Judges cases → holding, and the collegium — Case → year → holding

x: The Second Judges Case held that consultation means concurrence, established judicial primacy and gave rise to the collegium consisting initially of the CJI and two senior-most judges.

The First Judges Case recognised executive primacy; the Second created the two-senior-judge collegium; the Third enlarged it to four senior-most Judges; and the Fourth struck down the NJAC and the 99th Amendment.

secs.t: Judges cases → holding, and the collegium — Collegium

x: The Supreme Court collegium in June 2026 comprised CJI Surya Kant and Justices Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh and P.S. Narasimha.
The Government conducts background checks, may return a recommendation once, but is bound to appoint the candidate if the collegium reiterates it.
The
Third Judges Case
, arising from the Presidential Reference under Article 143 in 1998, expanded the Supreme Court collegium to the CJI and four senior-most judges.

secs.t: Judges cases → holding, and the collegium — Transfers and Memorandum of Procedure

x: Appointment is linked with Article 217(1), transfer with Article 222, and the Memorandum of Procedure provides for recommendation by the CJI and two senior-most judges, generally from outside the candidate's parent High Court.

The sequence is recommendation by the CJI and two senior-most judges, consideration by the Union Law Minister, consultation with the concerned State, and appointment by the President after consultation with the CJI and Governor.

secs.t: NJAC and the 99th Amendment, 2014 — struck down in 2015

x: Exam angle: "Which amendment was declared void in 2015?" - 99th; "who upheld NJAC?" - Chelameswar.
The 99th Constitutional Amendment inserted
Article 124A
, among related provisions, to provide for the National Judicial Appointments Commission.
In the Fourth Judges Case (2015), the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act by 4:1 because they violated judicial independence, which is part of the Basic Structure.

secs.t: Removal of judges — Art. 124(4), Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968, attempts

x: Removal of a Supreme Court or High Court judge is permitted only for
proved misbehaviour or incapacity
, through the constitutionally prescribed procedure.
Under Articles 148 and 324(5), the CAG and the CEC have removal protection comparable to that of
a Supreme Court judge
The presiding officer may admit or refuse the motion, and an inquiry committee is formed after admission.
The statutory committee comprises a Supreme Court Judge or the Chief Justice of India, a Chief Justice of a High Court and a distinguished jurist.
The 1999 In-House Procedure handles lesser misconduct outside the removal process.

secs.t: Independence of the Supreme Court — safeguard → Article

x: Under Article 121, the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court Judge cannot be discussed in Parliament except upon a motion for the Judge’s removal.
Article 124(7) bars a retired Supreme Court Judge from practice in India, while Article 220 permits a retired High Court Judge to practise only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts.
Judges' salaries are fixed by Parliament by law and cannot be reduced to their disadvantage after appointment, except
during a Financial Emergency under Article 360

secs.t: Jurisdictions → Articles — original, writ, appellate, advisory — Jurisdiction map

x: Article 131 deals with the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction over federal disputes.
Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with original, exclusive and final jurisdiction over disputes concerning the election of the President and Vice-President.
Election disputes concerning Parliament and State Legislatures are outside the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction and ordinarily go to the High Courts.
Inter-State river water disputes are taken out of the courts' jurisdiction by Article 262.

secs.t: Jurisdictions → Articles — original, writ, appellate, advisory — Appellate, advisory and other powers (Arts 129 to 145)

x: Article 136 gives the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from judgments or orders of any court or tribunal in India, except those relating to the armed forces.
Article 142 empowers the Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice, not to complete the legislative process as such.
Article 145 requires at least
five
Judges for hearing a case involving a substantial question of interpretation of the Constitution.

secs.t: Jurisdictions → Articles — original, writ, appellate, advisory — Terms → meaning

x: The Supreme Court evolved the curative petition in
Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra
(2002), permitting a limited remedy after dismissal of a review petition in exceptional circumstances.
The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil and criminal contempt.
e-SCR means electronic Supreme Court Reports.

secs.t: Commissions and reform proposals on appointment

x: “Imperium in imperio” literally conveys the criticism that the Collegium functions like an authority within an authority, reflecting concerns about opacity and judges selecting judges.
The private member's Bill proposed social diversity in appointments, a 90-day period for the Centre to notify Collegium names and regional benches of the Supreme Court.
The debate includes criticism of Collegium opacity, concerns regarding executive delays in notifying names, and demands for diversity and regional benches.

secs.t: Supreme Court of India vs US Supreme Court

x: The Indian formulation is associated with a narrower review standard, while due process in the United States permits substantive as well as procedural review.
Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right in India and enables the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
The Indian system combines the American principle of judicial supremacy with the British principle of parliamentary sovereignty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In SCAORA v. Union of India, decided in 2015, the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act and restored the collegium system.
P. Wilson's private member's Bill (19 February 2026) pressed for regional benches of the Supreme Court and greater social diversity among judges.
The collegium is criticised for opacity, while the executive is criticised for delaying notification of the names the collegium recommends.

rows.title: High Courts and subordinate judiciary; judicial review, judicial activism, PIL and judicial overreach debate
sub: Group-II M1-B-37: High Courts and subordinate courts; the High Court of Andhra Pradesh
Group-II M1-B-39: Judicial review - meaning, scope, constitutional basis and limits
Group-II M1-B-40: Judicial activism - meaning, causes, instruments (PIL) and the judicial overreach debate

secs.t: High Courts — Articles, number, FIRSTs and common High Courts — Articles on High Courts

x: Article 214 provides a High Court for each State (ii); Article 217 covers appointment by the President (iv); Article 230, from the 7th Amendment 1956, lets Parliament extend or exclude HC jurisdiction over a UT (iii); Article 231 provides a common High Court (i).
Article 241 authorises Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a Union Territory or declare a court there to be a High Court.

secs.t: High Courts — Articles, number, FIRSTs and common High Courts — Number and FIRSTs

x: The Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over Maharashtra, Goa and the Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
The common High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has its seat at Jammu in winter and Srinagar in summer.
There are 25 High Courts, and Guwahati covers Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura got their own High Courts on 23 March 2013).

secs.t: High Court judges — Articles → appointment, tenure, transfer and removal — Strength and Articles

x: Under Article 222, the President transfers a High Court judge after consulting the Chief Justice of India; the CJI consults the collegium and the Chief Justices of both High Courts concerned.
Article 223 concerns an acting Chief Justice, Article 224(1) additional judges, Article 224(2) acting judges and Article 224A retired judges sitting in a High Court.
Additional judges may be appointed for a period not exceeding
two years
, generally to meet temporary increases in work or arrears.
The President appoints High Court Judges after consulting the CJI and the Governor; in the case of a puisne Judge, the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is also consulted.

secs.t: High Court judges — Articles → appointment, tenure, transfer and removal — Collegium → appointment process

x: Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC) resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha vote.

secs.t: High Court powers — Articles → writ, superintendence, appellate and contempt

x: Article 227
confers on High Courts the power of superintendence over courts and tribunals within their territory, excluding military tribunals.
Confirmation of Sessions Court death sentences by the High Court is now governed by the
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
, which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024.
Fair criticism and accurate reporting
are recognised exceptions or safeguards; wilful disobedience, obstruction and scandalising conduct may constitute contempt.

secs.t: Subordinate judiciary — Articles 233-237, district courts and AIJS

x: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court, and a direct recruit needs 7 years as an advocate or pleader.

Article 233 covers district judges appointed by the Governor in consultation with the HC (ii); Article 234 covers other judicial officers, with rules made after consulting the SPSC and the HC (iv); Article 235 vests control in the High Court (i); Article 237 lets the Governor extend the provisions to magistrates (iii).

secs.t: Acts → courts: Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts and FIRSTs

x: Lok Adalats are established under the
Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
A Gram Nyayalaya is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of Judicial Magistrate First Class rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level.
A Lok Adalat award is deemed a civil court decree, and the first camp was held in Gujarat in 1982.

secs.t: Data — pendency, vacancies and court reform tools

x: The
Department of Justice web portal
tracks vacancies in the district judiciary every month.
e-Courts Phase III covers 2023–2027 and, together with the National Judicial Data Grid, is intended to improve judicial administration and access to case information.
Fast-track courts may be used for paper-leak cases under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.

secs.t: Judicial review — meaning, origin, theory and basis

x: The term ‘judicial review’ is not used in the Constitution, but the power flows from several Articles and is part of the basic structure.
Judicial review
is the power of courts to test the constitutional validity of laws and executive actions and invalidate those that are ultra vires.
Judicial review is a symbol of
federal government
: courts act as umpire of the Centre-State division under a written, supreme Constitution.

secs.t: Articles → role in judicial review, grounds and reviewability — Articles → role

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2023 (PYQ match, APPSC-G2 2023) matched 137-review, 226-HC writs, 13-void laws, 32-SC writs.

Article 131 is the SC's original jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes (iv); Article 136 is Special Leave (iii); Article 143 is advisory jurisdiction on Presidential reference (ii); Article 227 is HC superintendence over subordinate courts (i).

Article 13 concerns laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights; Article 32 provides Supreme Court writs; Article 137 permits Supreme Court review; and Article 226 concerns High Court writs for Fundamental Rights and other purposes.

secs.t: Articles → role in judicial review, grounds and reviewability — Three grounds

x: The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure.

Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into ministerial advice to the President (iii); Article 163(3) is the same bar for advice to the Governor (ii); Article 361 makes the President and Governor not answerable to courts, so no mandamus lies against them (i).

secs.t: Limits, amendments and overcoming a judgment — Limits of judicial review

x: The 38th Amendment (1975) made the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352 non-justiciable; the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed that position.

Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations.
Indian review under ‘procedure established by law’ traditionally focuses on legal validity and procedure, while American due process includes procedural and substantive fairness.

secs.t: Limits, amendments and overcoming a judgment — Overcoming a judgment

x: The expression reflects the extensive policy impact of the United States Supreme Court’s constitutional review and interpretation.
An ordinary Act cannot replace the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution.
A constitutional amendment, a valid law removing the basis of the judgment, and a review petition under Article 137 are available remedies; a curative petition may be the last judicial resort.

secs.t: Judicial activism and PIL — terms → meaning and instruments — Terms → meaning

x: Under epistolary jurisdiction, courts treated letters and postcards as writ petitions and also acted on newspaper reports indicating violations of rights.
Although PIL democratised access to courts, its misuse has also contributed to the
overburdening of courts
PIL is also called
Social Action Litigation
(SAL); it is an outcome of judicial activism, not restraint.

secs.t: Judicial activism and PIL — terms → meaning and instruments — Judicial review / restraint vs judicial activism

x: Continuing mandamus keeps the case open to monitor compliance.
The Vishaka Guidelines of 1997 addressed workplace sexual harassment in the absence of legislation and operated until the POSH Act, 2013.
Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice, including interim remedies in situations involving legislative delay and institutional deadlock.

secs.t: Judicial activism and PIL — origin, FIRSTs, stages and doctrines

x: The sequence is: post-Emergency activism in the mid-1970s, expansion of Article 21 from 1979 to the 1980s, governance cases from the 1990s onward, and Puttaswamy in 2017.
Kapila Hingorani
filed Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, the first major PIL case, concerning the rights of undertrial prisoners.
Exemptions and restrictions relating to Fundamental Rights in Articles 31A–31C and 33 are constitutional provisions, not judicial evolutions created by the Supreme Court.
Removal of unnecessary handcuffing is associated with protection of prisoners’ dignity and the broader human-rights dimension of judicial activism.

secs.t: Persons → statements and contributions

x: Marbury v. Madison
(1803), decided under Chief Justice John Marshall, is regarded as the landmark case establishing judicial review in the United States.
Justices
O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai
are identified as having laid the base of judicial activism along with the better-known PIL pioneers.

secs.t: Cases → year → outcome (review, activism, PIL, restraint)

x: The basic-structure status of judicial review is associated with Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and was reaffirmed in the context of judicial review of tribunals in L. Chandra Kumar, 1997.
Olga Tellis (1985) recognised the right to livelihood of pavement dwellers as part of the protection afforded by Article 21.
The M. C. Mehta cases from the 1980s onward produced extensive environmental directions and also generated debate about judicial policy-making.

secs.t: Judicial overreach — concerns and debates

x: Judicial activism has been associated with concerns such as violation of separation of powers, courts doing executive work, weak enforcement of PIL orders, letter petitions and delays in other cases.
The broad and undefined expression ‘complete justice’ under Article 142 is viewed as capable of bypassing democratic scrutiny when used expansively.

secs.t: AP High Court — Guntur 1954 to Amaravati 2019, AP Reorganisation Act sections, Chief Justices — History and establishment

x: Section 30 provided the common High Court at Hyderabad (ii), Section 31 the separate High Court of AP with its seat notified by the President (iii), and Section 32 the judges of the AP High Court (i).
The Andhra State High Court was established at
Guntur
on 5 July 1954 with Koka Subba Rao as its first Chief Justice.

secs.t: AP High Court — Guntur 1954 to Amaravati 2019, AP Reorganisation Act sections, Chief Justices — AP Reorganisation Act sections (PYQ)

x: Exam angle: date of the separate High Court (1 Jan 2019), seat (Amaravati), first Chief Justice "in Vijayawada".
Section 31
provided for the separate High Court of Andhra Pradesh and stated that its principal seat would be notified by the President.
Justice C. Praveen Kumar took charge as the first acting Chief Justice on 1 January 2019, and Justice J.K. Maheshwari became the first regular Chief Justice in October 2019.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Judicial activism has democratised access to justice and promoted executive accountability, but it can also blur separation of powers and contribute to overburdened courts.
A criticism of fast-track courts is that they may increase the speed of disposal without increasing the number of judges, thereby not fully addressing structural capacity problems.
The First Amendment (assent 18 June 1951) created the Ninth Schedule, following early land-reform rulings.

rows.title: Tribunals - Articles 323A and 323B; administrative and specialised tribunals; tribunal reforms
sub: Group-II M1-B-41: Tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B; administrative adjudication

secs.t: Tribunals — definition, nature, merits and criticism

x: A tribunal is quasi-judicial: it is neither purely executive nor a regular court, but occupies an intermediate position between the two.
A major criticism is that parent ministries, which may be litigants before tribunals, also administer them, creating concerns about executive control and independence.
The criticism of executive control has been associated with the
Finance Act, 2017 and the Tribunals Reforms Ordinance, 2021

secs.t: Articles 323A and 323B — Amendments, subjects, who establishes

x: Article 323A deals with recruitment and service conditions of public servants.
Article 323A permits Parliament alone to establish tribunals for service matters.
Both Articles form Part XIV-A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

secs.t: Administrative tribunals — CAT and SATs: Act, composition, jurisdiction, AP tribunal — Central Administrative Tribunal - parent Act and setting up

x: CAT is empowered by Article 323A and was established under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985.
The CAT was set up in 1985 under Prime Minister
Rajiv Gandhi
Judicial Members must possess qualifications equivalent to those of High Court judges.
CAT has its main bench at New Delhi and 18 benches.

secs.t: Administrative tribunals — CAT and SATs: Act, composition, jurisdiction, AP tribunal — Jurisdiction and procedure

x: CAT is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure.
CAT has original jurisdiction over service disputes of Central civil servants, All-India Services officers and civilian defence employees.

secs.t: Administrative tribunals — CAT and SATs: Act, composition, jurisdiction, AP tribunal — State Administrative Tribunals

x: A State Administrative Tribunal is set up by the Central Government
at the request of the concerned State Government
Joint tribunals may be established for two or more States.
The 32nd Amendment inserted the constitutional basis under
Article 371D
for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh to deal with public-service grievances.

secs.t: Specialised tribunals → parent Acts and benches

x: NCLAT hears appeals from NCLT and also deals with appeals under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and appeals from the Competition Commission of India.
Appeals from Debt Recovery Tribunals lie to the
Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal
(DRAT).
ITAT deals with income-tax appeals, is cited as an example of a tribunal under Article 323B, and functions under the Law Ministry as stated.

secs.t: Cases → judicial review of tribunals: S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) to Madras Bar Association (2025) — L. Chandra Kumar (1997) - High Court review and the appeal route

x: Following L. Chandra Kumar (1997), CAT decisions are subject to review by the
High Court through a Division Bench
, with a further appeal to the Supreme Court where applicable.
Both statements are true, and the basic-structure status of judicial review explains why tribunals cannot replace the constitutional review jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court.

secs.t: Cases → judicial review of tribunals: S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) to Madras Bar Association (2025) — Case law timeline

x: The correct sequence is S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987), L. Chandra Kumar (1997), R. Gandhi (2010), and Rojer Mathew (2019).
The National Tribunals Commission was first recommended in the Rojer Mathew case of 2019.
R. Gandhi (2010) held that tribunal members performing judicial functions must remain independent of the executive.

secs.t: Cases → judicial review of tribunals: S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) to Madras Bar Association (2025) — Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025) → what was struck down

x: The 2025 Madras Bar Association case struck down provisions re-enacted by Parliament and restored the earlier framework.
The ruling struck down the minimum age of 50 and the 4-year tenure (made 5 years).

secs.t: Acts and Bills → provisions: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 and Bill 2026 (NTC)

x: The 2021 framework prescribed a four-year tenure, a minimum appointment age of 50 years, a maximum age of 70 years for the Chairperson and 67 years for members.
The Lok Sabha passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 by
voice vote
on 10 August 2026.
The Bill will repeal the 2021 Act once both Houses pass it, and it passed the Lok Sabha on 10 August and the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2026.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A national report on the tribunal system proposed universal filing on a Zero FIR-style model to improve access.
The Central Administrative Tribunal was established in 1985; the Godavari, Krishna-II and Vansadhara water tribunals are associated with 1969, 2004 and 2010 respectively.
The Election Commission set up 19 Appellate Tribunals under retired High Court judges for
West Bengal
roll disputes after the SIR.

rows.title: Federal structure of India - features of federalism and unitary bias; Seventh Schedule (three lists), residuary powers
sub: Group-II M1-B-1: Nature of the Indian Constitution - federal, quasi-federal and unitary characterisations
Group-II M1-B-69: Unitary features of the Indian Constitution
Group-II M1-B-70: Federal features of the Indian Constitution; the nature of Indian federalism

secs.t: Federalism — definitions, types and FIRSTs — Federalism - meaning

x: Federalism involves constitutionally divided powers between the Union and State governments, each supreme in its assigned sphere, with an independent umpire to settle disputes.
The absence of a right to secede and the strength of the Union produce a
centripetal bias
, drawing the constituent units towards the Union rather than away from it.
Switzerland
is a coming-together federation in which independent States or units pool sovereignty while retaining equal power.

secs.t: Federalism — definitions, types and FIRSTs — Genesis of the Indian federation

x: Sri Lanka is identified as a unitary country, not a federal country.
The United States federation was formed by an agreement and integration of States.
The Constitution was framed after Partition and during the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States.

secs.t: Federal vs unitary features — statement-based identification — Features table

x: Quasi-federal means federal in form but possessing a pronounced or strong unitary bias.
An emergency can substantially centralise the constitutional system and make it operate in a unitary manner without a formal constitutional amendment.
Article 3 enables Parliament to alter the boundaries or names of States, demonstrating the strength of the Union and the unitary bias in the federal structure.
Dual polity, a written and supreme Constitution, and an independent judiciary are federal features.

All four are unitary features: the Centre appoints Governors, controls the All India Services, has a single CAG auditing Union and State accounts, and can use emergency powers to make the system unitary.

secs.t: Federal vs unitary features — statement-based identification — Exam statements

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 - Governor, Central Services, CAG and Emergency powers all "violate federal principles" (answer: A, B, C and D).
Exam angle: assertion-reason - A: India is quasi-federal; R: residuary powers/emergency powers lie with the Centre.
Exam angle: "not a federal feature" answers are
Office of the Governor
and
CAG
. "Allocation of financial resources" is not a prominent federal feature.

secs.t: Scholars and leaders → statements on Indian federalism — Who said what

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 - "federation with a centralising tendency" =
Ivor Jennings
; APP MCQ - "quasi-federal" =
K.C. Wheare
Exam angle: one-line "Who described India as..." items, or scholar-quote matching.
H.V. Kamath
referred to the Indian Constitution as having an “Elephantine size.”.
Wheare described India as
a unitary state with subsidiary federal features
rather than a federal state with subsidiary unitary features.

Ivor Jennings described India as a federation with a strong centralising tendency; Granville Austin used the expression cooperative federalism; Morris Jones used bargaining federalism; and Paul Appleby called it extremely federal.
Ambedkar stated that the Constitution had not been set in a tight mould of federalism, making statement 4 incorrect.

secs.t: Scholars and leaders → statements on Indian federalism — Ambedkar's statements

x: Ambedkar gave two principal reasons: the Indian Union was not formed by an agreement among States, and no State has the right to secede from it.
Ambedkar emphasised that India was not formed by an agreement among States, that States had no right to secede, and that the system could be unitary or federal according to time and circumstances.

secs.t: Articles 1-4, 370 and 371 → Union of States and asymmetric federalism — Indestructible Union

x: The Territory of India is wider than the Union of India because it includes States, Union Territories and acquired territories, whereas the Union of India refers to the States.
Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States and alter the area, boundaries or names of existing States.
India is regarded as an integral whole, with division into States made for administrative convenience.

secs.t: Articles 1-4, 370 and 371 → Union of States and asymmetric federalism — Articles 1-4 - name of the Union, First Schedule, Territory vs Union of India

x: Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States into the Union, particularly territories not already part of India.
Article 370 provided the special arrangements, which were made inoperative in August 2019; the Supreme Court upheld the action in December 2023.
The special provisions referred to in the Article 371 series extend from Article 371 to Article 371J.

secs.t: Seventh Schedule and residuary powers — lists, entry counts, models

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 - "Art. 248 = residuary" and "Parliament has exclusive power over items in no list" →
both correct
Article 248
deals with residuary legislative powers and gives Parliament exclusive power over matters not included in the State or Concurrent Lists, including residuary taxes.
The
One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016
, inserted the GST-related constitutional provisions, including the qualification of Article 248 by Article 246A.
Union List
Entry 97
, read with Article 248, covers matters not enumerated in the State List or Concurrent List, including residuary taxation.

secs.t: Subjects → List and the 42nd Amendment transfers — Subject → List

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 / APPSC 2025 key matched High Courts (HC organisation) → Union, mineral-right taxes → State, education → Concurrent; social security → Concurrent; defence/atomic energy → Union.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on
1 July 2024
, replacing the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act respectively.
Concurrent List entries permit Union legislation, and examples cited include farm laws through Entry 33 and education-related measures such as the NEP and NMC Act.
The 42nd CAA moved 5 subjects (education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, administration of justice).

secs.t: Subjects → List and the 42nd Amendment transfers — Subjects transferred from State to Concurrent List → 42nd Amendment

x: moved
5 subjects
from State to Concurrent List.
Weights and measures.
Protection of wild animals and birds.
Administration of justice.
Farm Laws via
Entry 33.

secs.t: Emergency provisions → switching from federal to unitary mode — Mode switch

x: Article 249
empowers Parliament to legislate on a State List subject following a Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest.
Part XVIII, comprising Articles 352 to 360, enables the federal system to operate in a unitary manner during emergencies without a formal constitutional amendment.
Article 249 requires a resolution of the Rajya Sabha supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting.

secs.t: Emergency provisions → switching from federal to unitary mode — National Emergency - effects and safeguards (44th Amendment)

x: A law made by Parliament on a State List matter under Article 250 ceases to have effect six months after the National Emergency ends.
The 44th Amendment ensured that the protection against conviction for offences under Article 20 and the protection of life and personal liberty under Article 21 cannot be suspended.
The Lok Sabha's term can be extended one year at a time during a National Emergency, and judicial review barred by the 38th Amendment was reopened by Minerva Mills.

secs.t: Emergency provisions → switching from federal to unitary mode — Financial Emergency (Art. 360)

x: Exam angle: the President can
reduce or cancel
fund transfers, but "
increase
the transfer" is the wrong statement. Modifying the distribution of finances and giving directions to States are correct consequences.
The President may modify the distribution of revenues and may reduce or cancel transfers to States, subject to Parliament’s approval.
Article 360 can enable directions concerning State finances, salary reductions and reservation of State Money Bills.

secs.t: Emergency provisions → switching from federal to unitary mode — Emergency types compared - Arts 352, 356, 360

x: Exam angle: "Art. 311 - Financial Emergency" is the mismatch; Financial Emergency is
Art. 360
Continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year requires that a National Emergency is in operation and that the Election Commission certifies the difficulty of holding elections in the State.
Article 352 concerns war, external aggression or armed rebellion; Article 356 concerns failure of constitutional machinery; and Article 360 concerns financial stability or credit.

secs.t: Cases and amendments on federalism → year and holding

x: In
State of West Bengal v Union of India
(1962), the Supreme Court held that the Constitution was not truly federal and that States were not sovereign.
All three statements correctly describe the significance of S. R. Bommai v Union of India (1994).
The Constitution has been described as
fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements

secs.t: Borrowed features and India vs USA federal systems

x: The federal scheme and emergency provisions were borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935; the strong Centre reflects the Canadian model; and the Concurrent List was borrowed from Australia.
While the Government of India Act, 1935 provided the source of India’s federal scheme, the strong Centre was particularly modelled on
Canada
India has a single integrated judiciary, whereas the USA maintains
separate federal and State court systems

secs.t: Phases of federal practice → changes, 1952 to date

x: The Rajamannar Committee was set up in 1969 during the phase from 1967 to 1977, when non-Congress State governments led to greater Centre-State confrontation.
From 2014 onward, NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015 and GST was introduced in 2017, within the framework described as cooperative-competitive federalism.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The suggested measures included a narrower Concurrent List, a stronger Inter-State Council and reform of Governors;
complete abolition of the Concurrent List
was not stated as a proposed measure.
Fiscal transfer concerns, delays by Governors and ‘double engine’ politics were cited as weakening the federal spirit.
The resolution referred to
vertical fiscal imbalance, cesses and surcharges outside the divisible pool, and matching shares in Centrally Sponsored Schemes
The Committee was described as finding increasing centralisation, and the Chief Minister called for constitutional amendment to make the system more federal.
The debate connected possible election deferrals with prolonged President’s Rule and the limits associated with Article 356(5), while recalling earlier misuse addressed in the Bommai context.
Samvidhan Hatya Diwas is observed on
25 June
, recalling the Emergency proclaimed in 1975.

rows.title: Centre-State legislative relations - Articles 245-255, doctrine of repugnancy, parliamentary legislation on state list
sub: Group-II M1-B-42: Distribution of legislative powers - Seventh Schedule and Articles 245-255
Group-II M1-B-43: Parliament's power to legislate on State List subjects; residuary powers and repugnancy

secs.t: Articles 245-255 → number game and territorial extent — Part XI Chapter I at a glance

x: Article 248 is located in
Part XI
, which deals with relations between the Union and the States and extends from Articles 245 to 263.
Article 247 empowers Parliament to establish additional courts for the better administration of laws made by Parliament or existing laws relating to matters in the Union List.
Article 255 treats the requirement of recommendation or previous sanction as a matter of procedure.

secs.t: Articles 245-255 → number game and territorial extent — Article 245 - territorial extent of laws

x: Parliament may legislate for the whole or any part of India, and an extra-territorial operation does not by itself invalidate parliamentary legislation.
Regulations made by
the President
for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament.
The Governor may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament in Scheduled Areas.

secs.t: Seventh Schedule, Article 246 and residuary power — lists, entries, precedence

x: Article 246
gives the constitutional framework for the distribution of legislative subjects in the three lists of the Seventh Schedule.
Article 248
vests residuary legislative power in Parliament, including the power to legislate on residuary matters of taxation.
The idea of vesting residuary powers in the central legislature was borrowed from
Canada
, a federation with a strong Centre.
Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List
together confer residuary legislative power on Parliament.

secs.t: Parliament legislating on the State List — five special circumstances and limits — Special circumstances - overview

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2023 - during an Emergency, State List laws are made by
Parliament
; PYQ 2018 - international agreements =
Art. 253
Exam angle: statement sets asking which situations are valid ("request of two or more states" is valid; a request by one state is not).
A law made under Article 250 continues after the National Emergency but lapses six months after the Emergency ceases, unless otherwise continued under constitutional authority.
Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 and 356 are the stated constitutional routes permitting Parliament to legislate in fields otherwise within the State List.

secs.t: Parliament legislating on the State List — five special circumstances and limits — Limits on Parliament's legislative competence

x: Articles 301 to 303 restrict discriminatory or preferential treatment between States in laws relating to trade and commerce.

secs.t: Articles 249-253 → conditions, duration and effect — Article 249 - resolution and duration

x: Article 251 provides that a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 prevails over an inconsistent State law.
A law enacted under Article 249 continues for six months after the resolution authorising it lapses, after which it ceases to operate.
Article 249 needs a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by
two-thirds of the members present and voting
(APPSC-GS 2025).

secs.t: Articles 249-253 → conditions, duration and effect — Article 252 - consent of states

x: The Prize Competition Act, 1955, the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 were enacted under Article 252 on resolutions of two or more States.
Article 253
authorises Parliament to legislate for implementing treaties, agreements, conventions and decisions of international bodies, even on State List subjects.

secs.t: Doctrines → meaning and cases (repugnancy, pith and substance, colourable legislation)

x: The doctrine of repugnancy is contained in Article 254, which is located in
Part XI
dealing with Union-State relations.
In
State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
(1951), the prohibition law was upheld under the doctrine of pith and substance.
The doctrine of colourable legislation is expressed by the maxim that
what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly
Harmonious construction
requires apparently overlapping entries to be interpreted together so that both retain operative effect.

secs.t: Acts, cases and commissions on legislative relations → year

x: The Sarkaria Commission in 1988 recommended moving all residuary powers other than taxation to the Concurrent List.

secs.t: Subjects in the lists — odd one out and unusual central laws

x: Exam angle: a list of four subjects where one belongs to another list.
Prevention of cruelty to animals is placed in
Concurrent List Entry 17
, enabling Parliament to enact central legislation on the subject.
Parliament can legislate on the State subject through Articles 249, 250 or 252, among the specified routes.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Farm Laws were discussed as an example of Concurrent List Entry 33 being used in a field associated with agriculture, which is State List Entry 14.
The advisory opinion rejected deemed assent and fixed timelines concerning Governors and the President.
The Bill was reported as restricting State taxation power over
mineral rights and mineral-bearing land
Preventive detention-related powers are divided between Union List Entry 9 and Concurrent List Entry 3.

rows.title: Distribution of executive powers between the Union and the States
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-44

secs.t: Articles → vesting and extent of Union and State executive power

x: Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the
Governor
, who may exercise it directly or through subordinate officers.
The Governor of Nagaland has special responsibility under Article 371A, and the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh under Article 371H, in relation to law and order.
The exception to the State default arises where the Constitution or a Parliamentary law expressly gives the executive power to the Centre, through the provisos to Articles 73 and 162.

secs.t: Articles → entrustment of functions and compliance (258, 258A, 256, 257, 365)

x: Under Article 258(2), Parliament may confer powers or impose duties on State officers by law, and the State's consent is not required.
Articles 256 and 257 impose obligations on States, and non-compliance may attract Article 365, which can open the way to action under Article 356.
Article 258A lets a State entrust its functions to the Union (APPSC-GS 2023).

secs.t: Emergencies → effect on executive relations (Articles 353, 356, 360)

x: Under Article 353, the Union's power to issue directions expands during a National Emergency, but State governments continue to exist and are not suspended merely because of the Emergency.
During a Financial Emergency, the Centre may require Money Bills and other Financial Bills of States to be reserved for the President's consideration.

secs.t: Union Territories → executive heads (Art. 239, Art. 239AA)

x: The Lieutenant Governor or Administrator exercises executive power in a Union Territory as the representative of the President.
Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu are headed by Administrators.
The
69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991
inserted Article 239AA and provided Delhi with a Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The proposed sui generis elected body for Ladakh is intended to possess legislative, executive and financial powers.
The proposed model for Ladakh is based on safeguards similar to those under Article 371, rather than the Sixth Schedule.
The Governor's discretion is not unlimited and the Governor ordinarily acts on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers.

rows.title: Centre-State administrative relations - Articles 256-263, all-India services, directions to states
sub: Group-II M1-B-45: Administrative relations - Articles 256-263, all-India services, inter-state council and zonal councils

secs.t: Articles → Centre's directions to states (256, 257, 339, 350A, 365)

x: Article 256
requires State executive power to ensure compliance with laws made by Parliament and permits the Union to issue directions for that purpose.
Article 365
permits the President to hold that a State government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution when the State fails to comply with Union directions.

secs.t: Articles → delegation of functions (258, 258A)

x: Article 258A enables the Governor to entrust functions of the State to the Union or its officers with the consent of the Government of India.
Delegation under these Articles provides flexibility in administration and helps avoid rigidity and deadlock between the Union and the States.

Article 258(1) concerns Union-to-State entrustment by the President with State consent; Article 258(2) concerns Parliamentary entrustment by law without consent; Article 258A concerns State-to-Union entrustment with the Centre's consent.

secs.t: All India Services — Article 312, origin, removal, classification — Creation and existing services

x: Exam angle: "AIS officer can be removed only by the Union Government" is the correct statement.
Article 312 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by not less than
two-thirds of the members present and voting
before Parliament can create a new All India Service.
The correct sequence is IAS restructuring in 1947, UPSC replacing the Federal PSC in 1950, insertion of Article 258A in 1956, and creation of IFoS in 1966.

secs.t: All India Services — Article 312, origin, removal, classification — Federal critique and friction

x: The federal criticism is that Central rules govern the officers and States do not exercise full control over them, thereby restricting State autonomy.
The proposed amendments would enable the Centre to order central deputation without the consent of the State Government or the officer, with the Centre's order becoming final after a prescribed time.

secs.t: Armed and central forces in states — Art. 355, Entry 2A, CAPF dispute

x: States object because public order and police fall in Entries 1 and 2 of the State List, making deployment a sensitive issue concerning State authority.
The 1966 Administrative Reforms Commission supported deployment “on their request or otherwise,” meaning that a State request was not treated as indispensable.
The 2025 Supreme Court order referred to granting CAPF officers Organised Group A status and reducing IPS deputation.

secs.t: Commissions, PSCs and tribunals — JSPSC, CAT, ARC, Sarkaria

x: The ARC was established in 1966, initially chaired by Morarji Desai, later by K. Hanumanthaiya, and its study team was headed by M.C. Setalvad in 1969.
The Commission was set up in June 1983 under Justice R.S. Sarkaria (with B. Sivaraman and S.R. Sen), made 247 recommendations and urged sparing use of Article 356.

secs.t: Cooperation devices — constitutional vs extra-constitutional

x: Article 307 provides for an authority to carry out the purposes of the constitutional provisions relating to trade, commerce and intercourse within India.
Article 261 requires
full faith and credit throughout India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings
of the Union and every State.
Article 261(3)
provides that final judgments and orders of civil courts in any part of India may be executed anywhere within India according to law.

secs.t: Zonal Councils and North Eastern Council — Acts, chairman, AP's zone

x: The North-Eastern Council is a separate body established under the
North-Eastern Council Act, 1971
, unlike the five Zonal Councils created under the 1956 Act.
The 2002 amendment added Sikkim and gave the NEC the role of a regional planning body, while the Union Home Minister has served as its ex-officio Chairman since 2018.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The meeting was held near Mamallapuram on 20 August 2026, chaired by Home Minister Amit Shah, with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay as vice-chairman.
The Supreme Court-directed Supervisory Committee in the Mullaperiyar matter involves the
National Dam Safety Authority
under the Dam Safety Act, 2021.
The Inter-State Council has been criticised for meeting rarely; proposals seek to strengthen its role in Centre-State coordination.
