rows.title: Centre-State financial relations - Articles 264-293; taxes assigned, grants-in-aid, borrowing powers
sub: Group-II M1-B-46: Financial relations - tax distribution, divisible pool, grants-in-aid, borrowing powers

secs.t: Part XII Articles → content (264-293)

x: Articles 266 and 267
deal respectively with the Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts, and the Contingency Fund.
Part XII is titled Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits, and the financial-relations provisions stated here are Articles 268 to 293.
Article 354
lets the President modify the distribution of revenues during a National Emergency, until the end of the financial year in which the emergency ceases.

secs.t: Taxes → who levies, collects and keeps (Articles 268-272, divisible pool) — Articles 268-272

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2018 - taxes levied and collected by Centre but assigned to states =
Art. 269
Exam angle: statements that surcharges under Art. 271 are shared with states (false).
Article 269A provides for apportionment of IGST on inter-State supply between the Centre and the States on the advice of the
GST Council
Article 270 covers Union List taxes shared as recommended by the Finance Commission, but excludes Articles 268, 269 and 269A taxes, Article 271 surcharges and cesses.

secs.t: Taxes → who levies, collects and keeps (Articles 268-272, divisible pool) — Divisible pool - who levies which tax

x: Land revenue, agricultural income tax, State excise on alcohol and taxes on vehicles
are included among taxes associated with the State domain.
The
Comptroller and Auditor General of India
certifies the net proceeds used in determining the divisible pool.

secs.t: Amendments → changes to financial relations (60th, 80th, 88th, 101st) — 80th Amendment, 2000

x: The 80th Amendment enacted the 10th FC's Alternative Scheme of Devolution, under which states share gross proceeds of all Union taxes.
Pre-2000 taxes on stock-exchange transactions, estate duty, railway fares and newspapers were folded into the Article 270 pool.

secs.t: Amendments → changes to financial relations (60th, 80th, 88th, 101st) — 101st Amendment - GST

x: The 101st Amendment inserted
Articles 246A, 269A and 279A
for the GST framework and the GST Council.
Article 246A gives concurrent GST legislative power to Parliament and State Legislatures, while Parliament alone legislates on inter-State supplies.
Article 269A concerns IGST, with the revenue going to
the destination State
in accordance with the destination-based character of GST.

secs.t: GST Council — Article 279A, composition, voting, Mohit Minerals, compensation

x: Compensation Cess on
luxury and sin goods
was used to fund compensation to States for GST-related revenue loss.
The GST framework has been criticised because States surrendered independent indirect-tax powers and because of concerns regarding the weighted voting structure.
Both statements are true, and the Centre’s one-third vote share combined with the three-fourths threshold enables it to block a decision without support from other members.

secs.t: Grants-in-aid — statutory (Art. 275) vs discretionary (Art. 282)

x: Statutory grants under Article 275 are made on the recommendation of the Finance Commission, not NITI Aayog.
Article 282 permits discretionary grants for any public purpose.
The special grants in lieu of export duty on jute are associated with
Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha

secs.t: Finance Commissions and transfer formulas → shares, weights, special category — Finance Commissions → vertical share

x: The States’ share was fixed at
of the divisible pool for 2021–26 by the Fifteenth Finance Commission and retained by the Sixteenth Finance Commission for 2026–31.
Tax devolution is formula-based and generally untied.
An increase in tax devolution does not eliminate all forms of grants to States.

secs.t: Finance Commissions and transfer formulas → shares, weights, special category — Plan formulas → year → weights

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2017 - Gadgil formula =
devolution of funds

Special category parameters included difficult terrain, low population density or sizeable tribal population, strategic border location, economic and infrastructural backwardness, and non-viable State finances.
Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the abolition of the Planning Commission together with the ending of Plan grants explains why the formulas lost their earlier role.

secs.t: Borrowing — Articles 292 and 293, Net Borrowing Ceiling, AP data — Articles 292 and 293

x: Article 292 authorises Union borrowing on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, subject to limits fixed by Parliament by law.
Article 293(2) empowers the Union to make loans to States and to give guarantees in respect of loans raised by States.
When a Union loan or guarantee remains outstanding, the State requires the consent of the Union to raise a further loan; the consent may be subject to conditions.

secs.t: Borrowing — Articles 292 and 293, Net Borrowing Ceiling, AP data — Borrowing limits - Net Borrowing Ceiling

x: An additional borrowing allowance of
0.5 per cent of GSDP
was permitted above the normal ceiling for power-sector reforms, including again in 2025–26.
The Sixteenth Finance Commission caps the State fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP and calls for ending off-budget borrowing.
Kerala's 2024 suit under Article 131 challenged
the Net Borrowing Ceiling imposed under Article 293(3)

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The protest concerned the perceived adverse effect of population-heavy or population-based criteria on the devolution share of southern States.
Vertical fiscal imbalance, non-shareable cesses and CSS conditionality are identified criticisms.
Non-shareable cesses, estimated at about 18% of gross tax revenue, reduce the effective devolution to around 31–32%, below the 41% award share.

rows.title: Centre-State relations - the constitutional scheme and areas of friction
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-46

secs.t: Parts and Articles → constitutional scheme of Centre-State relations

x: Part XI contains legislative relations in Articles 245–255 and administrative relations in Articles 256–263 between the Union and the States.
Part XII deals with financial relations, including Articles 268 to 293.
All India Services are a unitary feature because they provide a common administrative structure serving both the Union and the States.

secs.t: Articles → Union's protective and emergency powers (355, 356, 365, 250, 353, 354)

x: A National Emergency strengthens the Union and makes the constitutional system operate in a unitary or quasi-unitary manner.
The term of the Lok Sabha may be extended by Parliament for one year at a time during a National Emergency, subject to the constitutional limitation concerning the period after the Emergency ends.

secs.t: Areas of friction → issue (Governor, 356, fiscal, AIS, waters, CBI)

x: Cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool, leaving the pool at approximately 81% of gross tax revenue and reducing the shareable base for States.
Article 262 concerns inter-State river-water disputes, Section 6 of the DSPE Act concerns State consent for CBI investigation, and Article 156 concerns the Governor's office.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh issues — SCS, APRA 2014 assurances, Polavaram

x: The cited unmet assurances include the
Kadapa steel plant, Dugarajapatnam port and metro rail
, and were valued at about ₹5 lakh crore by the opposition.
The stated figures are total sanctions of ₹12,157 crore, 89% completion and a target for dedication by March 2027.
Prime Minister Manmohan Singh promised SCS in Parliament, but the promise was not written into APRA 2014, and AP got special packages instead.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Tamil Nadu Kurian Joseph Committee was associated with the call for a structural reset of federalism.
For Andhra Pradesh, the principal federal grievances are the demand for Special Category Status and implementation of assurances under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act.

rows.title: Emergency provisions - National Emergency (352), President's Rule (356), Financial Emergency (360); S.R. Bommai case

secs.t: Emergency types → source, grounds, approval, duration

x: The 38th Amendment attempted to make the satisfaction non-justiciable; this position was later reversed, and Minerva Mills affirmed that the proclamation is reviewable.
Article 365
provides that failure to comply with, or give effect to, Union directions can justify the conclusion that the State government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
Ambedkar hoped that the emergency provision under Article 356 would remain a “
dead letter
” and be used only in exceptional circumstances.

secs.t: Amendments → changes to emergency provisions (38th, 39th, 42nd, 44th)

x: 44th Amendment 1978 on Art. 358:.

secs.t: Effects of National Emergency — Centre-state relations, terms, Articles 358 and 359

x: Exam angle: LENS Jul 2026 MCQ - the statement "Arts 20 and 21 can be suspended under Art. 359" is
wrong

Parliament may extend the term of the Lok Sabha (and of State Assemblies) by law for one year at a time during a National Emergency, but the extension cannot continue beyond six months after the Emergency ceases.

secs.t: President's Rule (Art. 356) — effects on organs and misuse

x: The Governor administers the State on behalf of the President, Parliament legislates for the State, and the High Court remains unaffected.
The second extension of President’s Rule in Manipur was approved up to
February 2026

secs.t: Cases → ruling on emergencies (Bommai, Minerva Mills, ADM Jabalpur, Rameshwar Prasad)

x: The Allahabad High Court judgment voiding Indira Gandhi’s 1971 election formed the immediate political background to the 1975 Emergency.
The K.S. Puttaswamy judgment of 2017 overruled the approach taken in ADM Jabalpur concerning the suspension of Article 21 protections.
The proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, particularly where it is mala fide or founded on irrelevant grounds.

secs.t: Instances and FIRSTs — National Emergencies, PR in AP, Financial Emergency

x: 25 June is observed as “
Samvidhan Hatya Diwas
” in remembrance of the proclamation of the 1975 Emergency.
President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency on 25 June 1975 on the ground of internal disturbance.
A breakdown of constitutional machinery in a State is the ground for President's Rule under
Article 356
, which the AP High Court referred to in December 2020 (PYQ 2021).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Article 356(5)
allows President's Rule to continue beyond one year only if a National Emergency is in operation and the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held.
The 1973 spell of President's Rule in Andhra Pradesh (following the Jai Andhra agitation) ended after the
Six-Point Formula
, which was validated by the 32nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1973 inserting Article 371D.

rows.title: Inter-state relations - inter-state council, zonal councils, river-water disputes (Article 262), full faith and credit

secs.t: Articles → provisions on inter-state relations

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2018 - a bill restricting goods from other states needs the
President's
previous sanction.
A bill imposing reasonable restrictions in the public interest under Article 304(b) requires the
previous sanction of the President
before its introduction in the State Legislature.
An
Inter-State Commerce Commission
is an example of the authority contemplated under Article 307 for carrying out the purposes of Articles 301 to 304.

secs.t: Councils → chairman, members, nature — Inter-State Council

x: The Central Council of Health, Central Council of Local Self-Government and Transport Development Council are all stated to have been set up under Article 263.

The Administrative Reforms Commission during 1966–69 and the Rajamannar Committee in 1969 were earlier advocates, while the Sarkaria Commission later recommended the Inter-State Council that was set up in 1990.
Chief Ministers, Administrators of UTs without legislatures and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister are included.

secs.t: Councils → chairman, members, nature — Zonal Councils

x: Exam angle: Assertion-Reason pairs on Art. 263 and the commission that recommended the Council.
Chief Ministers serve as Vice-Chairmen by annual rotation, and the Councils are deliberative and advisory.
The Southern Zonal Council includes Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala,
Telangana
and Puducherry.

secs.t: Acts and tribunals → year, states

x: Godavari Tribunal 1969 (a-ii), First Krishna Tribunal 1969 (b-iv), Second Krishna Tribunal 2004 (c-i) and Vansadhara Tribunal 2010 (d-iii), so the code is A. B wrongly gives the Second Krishna Tribunal 2010 and Vansadhara 2004.
The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal was constituted in 1990.
The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 provides for tribunals.

secs.t: Disputes and meetings → Mullaperiyar, Krishna-Godavari, Southern Zonal Council

x: Andhra Pradesh rejected Telangana’s 50:50 Krishna demand, stating that it was contrary to the KWDT awards and the decisions of the Apex Council.
Telangana proposed to raise Karnataka’s unauthorised Krishna projects under
Section 3 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act
Telangana sought national status for the
Kaleshwaram and Palamuru-Rangareddy
projects at the Southern Zonal Council.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Zonal Councils are generally regarded as recommendatory bodies, and their effectiveness is criticised as being constrained by inadequate resources.

rows.title: Issues and challenges in Indian federalism - governor's role, GST Council, central agencies, All India Services
sub: Group-II M1-B-64: Need for reforms in Centre-State relations - the case for greater state autonomy

secs.t: Centre-State relations → phases and drivers of centralisation

x: Congress dominance characterised the 1950s and early 1960s, opposition State governments became prominent from the mid-1960s, and the coalition era began in the 1990s.
The constitutional design, party politics, planning and judicial decisions are identified factors; exclusive control of local bodies over inter-State trade is not.
Autonomy demands grew once the Congress lost many States in the mid-1960s.

secs.t: States → autonomy demands, documents and parties

x: The Rajamannar Committee, Anandpur Sahib Resolution and West Bengal memorandum are correctly associated with Tamil Nadu, Punjab and West Bengal respectively.
Punjab and West Bengal wanted the Centre to be confined to
defence, foreign affairs, communications and currency
State autonomy demands generally sought more powers, greater control over own revenue, less central administrative control and protection of linguistic interests.

secs.t: Commissions on Centre-State relations → year, chairman, appointing government

x: Exam angle: "constituted in 1983 under a retired SC judge" = Sarkaria; order is State first (1969), then Centre (1983, 2007).
The
Indrajit Gupta Committee
(1998) dealt with State funding of elections (partial funding in kind to recognised parties), not Centre-State relations.
The Sarkaria Commission
was set up by the Centre in June 1983 under Justice R.S. Sarkaria, a retired Supreme Court judge, and reported in 1988 with 247 recommendations.

secs.t: Commissions → key recommendations

x: Rajamannar recommended deleting Article 356, Sarkaria treated its use as a last resort, and Punchhi proposed the concept of a localised emergency.
The
Punchhi Commission
recommended a fixed tenure for Governors and a President-like (impeachment) removal procedure (APPSC-G1 2024 key), along with time-bound disposal of Bills and the localised emergency idea.

secs.t: Articles → Inter-State Council, All India Services, Article 371

x: All India Service officers serve the States under immediate State control, while ultimate control rests with the Centre.
Article 371A relates to Nagaland, Article 371D to local cadres, education and jobs in Andhra Pradesh, Article 371E to a Central University in Andhra Pradesh, and Article 371F to Sikkim.
The Centre offered Article 371 safeguards to Ladakh instead of safeguards under
the Sixth Schedule

secs.t: Acts → central agencies and state consent

x: Section 6 of the DSPE Act requires State consent for the CBI.
Withdrawal of general consent means that the CBI must obtain consent separately for each case.
All three pairs are correctly matched.

secs.t: Issues and debates → state autonomy, All India Services, fiscal centralisation

x: The resistance to Hindi in Tamil Nadu illustrates the
linguistic and cultural identity
argument for greater State autonomy.
GST subsumed several State taxes, whereas cesses and surcharges continue to remain outside the divisible pool.
Articles 356, 256, 257 and 365 are all identified in federalism debates as provisions that may enable excessive Union intervention.

secs.t: Special Category Status → criteria, Finance Commission and AP's demand

x: The Centre subsequently provided
a special assistance package in 2016
instead of granting SCS.
Special Category Status involved 90 per cent Central funding of plan spending.
On 20 February 2014 the Prime Minister assured the Rajya Sabha that AP would get SCS for
five years

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Tamil Nadu Assembly unanimously resolved in favour of
a fair share of tax devolution
for the States.
Cesses, Centrally Sponsored Schemes and GST are cited in debates on centralisation.
The Andhra Pradesh-specific concerns highlighted are the demand for
Special Category Status and Article 371D
The defeat of the 131st Amendment Bill relating to Lok Sabha expansion sharpened
the North–South debate

rows.title: Rajamannar Committee (1969) - appointment and recommendations
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-49

secs.t: Rajamannar Committee → appointing state, members and FIRSTs

x: Its principal task was to study
Centre-State relations
and recommend measures for greater State autonomy.
A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar and P. Chandra Reddy were the other two members.
The committee was set up by the DMK government under
M. Karunanidhi
, who carried forward C.N. Annadurai’s earlier autonomy position.
P.V. Rajamannar chaired the Rajamannar Committee and also chaired the Fourth Finance Commission.

secs.t: Terms of reference and findings → why Tamil Nadu set it up

x: The committee sought to reduce central control, including over subjects such as education and health.
The committee found the States reduced to administrative units of the Centre.

secs.t: Rajamannar recommendations → institutions and Articles

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT a Rajamannar recommendation" - look for any option that strengthens the Centre or the Governor.
The committee criticised the Planning Commission as an extra-constitutional body that
alone decided grants to the States
and recommended its abolition.
Abolition of the All-India Services was recommended to
reduce central administrative control over State governments

secs.t: Seventh Schedule → transfers to State List and residuary powers

x: It recommended moving subjects from the Union and Concurrent Lists to the
State List
to enlarge State autonomy.
Inland waterway navigation, industrial disputes, and oil fields regulation and development were cited examples.
Rajamannar recommended that residuary powers go to the States, while the Sarkaria position concerned the Concurrent List for residuary powers other than taxation.

secs.t: Aftermath and commissions compared → year, appointing body

x: The Inter-State Council was established in 1990 through the influence of the
Sarkaria Commission
, not directly through the Rajamannar Committee.
The correct sequence is Rajamannar (1969), Sarkaria (1983), Punchhi (2007), and Kurian Joseph (April 2025).
The respective report details are 1971, 1988, 2010, and Part I on 16 February 2026, with the chairmen named in each pair.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Its autonomy-oriented ideas influenced later demands such as the Anandpur Sahib Resolution and the West Bengal memorandum.
The Kurian Joseph Committee was appointed by Tamil Nadu in April 2025 and consciously followed the Rajamannar Committee’s approach to Centre-State relations.

rows.title: Sarkaria Commission (1983) - recommendations on legislative, administrative and financial relations
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-49

secs.t: Sarkaria Commission → set up, chairman, members, report and implementation

x: The Central Government set up the Sarkaria Commission in June 1983.
Justice Rajinder Singh Sarkaria, a retired SC judge, chaired it.
It was to examine the Centre-State balance of power and suggest changes within the constitutional framework.
The Inter-State Council, established in 1990 under Article 263, is regarded as the main implemented recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission.

secs.t: Governor → Sarkaria's recommendations

x: The Governor should not be closely involved in the local politics of the State.
The
Chief Minister of the State concerned
should be effectively consulted before the Governor is chosen.
The Commission recommended a secure five-year tenure, which should not be cut short except for extremely compelling reasons.
Strictly non-partisan appointments and decision on Bills within a specified period were recommended.

secs.t: Articles and Lists → Art 356, floor test, Concurrent List, residuary powers

x: The
Punchhi Commission
, constituted in 2007 (report 2010), later endorsed the approach concerning the order of preference in a hung Assembly.
The Centre should consult the States before legislating on a Concurrent List subject, preferably through an institutionalised process of prior consultation.
Sarkaria wanted the residuary power of taxation to
remain with Parliament
; only residuary powers other than taxation were to go to the Concurrent List.

secs.t: Administrative and financial relations → AIS, central forces, cesses

x: Sarkaria recommended strengthening All-India Services and creating more such services, whereas Rajamannar wanted them abolished.
The Centre may deploy Central armed forces in a State even without its request, though consulting the State beforehand is desirable.
The Commission recommended that cesses and surcharges be kept to a minimum and made time-bound, with their subsequent merger into the shareable tax pool.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Commission established a standard framework for considering the Governor’s role, Article 356 and cooperative federalism.
Bommai (1994) and Rameshwar Prasad (2006) relied on Sarkaria.
The Sarkaria Commission was constituted at the Centre in 1983, while the Rajamannar Committee was associated with Tamil Nadu in 1969.
Sarkaria worked within the Constitution to strengthen All-India Services and retain a strong Centre.

rows.title: M.M. Punchhi Commission (2007) - recommendations and their status
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-49

secs.t: Punchhi Commission → appointing government, chairman, members, report

x: Exam angle: "When was it appointed?" Answer 2007, not 2010. Remember the order 1969, 1983, 2007.
Justice Madan Mohan Punchhi
, a former Chief Justice of India, chaired the Commission on Centre-State Relations appointed in 2007.
It reviewed arrangements in light of changes since Sarkaria (1983-88).
Dhirendra Singh, V.K. Duggal and N.R. Madhava Menon were among the members mentioned.

secs.t: Governor → Punchhi's recommendations

x: Exam angle: impeachment of the Governor, the 5-year tenure and the chancellor role are Punchhi's. Periodic "rotation of Governors" and "abolish the office" are distractors.
The Punchhi Commission recommended that Governors should not be made Chancellors of universities or given other statutory roles, to avoid day-to-day clashes with State Governments.

secs.t: Articles → proposed amendments (156, 243G, 243W, 355, 356)

x: Exam angle: "The Commission said there is no need to amend Articles 355 and 356" is the
wrong
statement.
The proposed localised emergency would permit the Centre to
take over a specific troubled area, such as a district or part of a district, for a limited period
instead of the whole State.
The idea goes back to
the First Administrative Reforms Commission
, which recommended deployment of central armed forces either on the State's request or otherwise.

secs.t: Councils and Lists → meeting frequency, Concurrent List, Union List

x: The Punchhi Commission recommended that the Inter-State Council should meet at least three times a year and function as a working forum for Centre-State and inter-State issues.
The Commission recommended that the Centre should
reach broad agreement with the States through the Inter-State Council
before legislating on Concurrent List subjects.
The Commission recommended adding a specific Union List entry on
environment, ecology and climate change

secs.t: Financial recommendations → Finance Commission, backward States, cesses

x: Punchhi wanted the Finance and Planning Commissions coordinated, with time periods synchronised with the Plans.
The recommendation was to limit cesses and surcharges; the cited model answer expresses this as capping cesses at 5%.
The Punchhi Commission recommended that the
National Water Resources Council
should play a bigger role in water policy.

secs.t: Status and cases → implementation, time limits for bills

x: Since Article 156 remains unchanged, Governors continue to hold office during the pleasure of the President.
The Tamil Nadu case of 8 April 2025 fixed timelines, but the Presidential Reference opinion of 20 November 2025 held that courts cannot impose fixed timelines or deemed assent.
The 11th ISC meeting (16 July 2016), the first in about a decade, took up the Punchhi recommendations.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The treatment of cesses and surcharges affects the distribution of fiscal resources between the Union and the States, which is the same federal-finance issue raised by the Punchhi Commission.
The CDI identifies
bill deadlines, a mandatory Inter-State Council and a cap on cesses
as the Punchhi agenda capable of contributing to cooperative federalism.

sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-49

secs.t: Commissions and committees → chairman, year

x: Exam angle: "Commission chaired by Veerappa Moily" means
Administrative Reforms
Bhagwan Sahay
headed the Committee of Governors (set up 1970, reported 1971).
The NCRWC, chaired by M.N. Venkatachaliah, was set up in 2000 and submitted its report in 2002 after reviewing the first 50 years of the Constitution, so it functioned during 2000-02.

secs.t: Recommendations → Governors, Art. 356, fiscal autonomy, judiciary

x: The NCRWC recommended greater fiscal autonomy, safeguards against misuse of Article 356 and a stronger third tier.

The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended a Code of Ethics, Right to Public Services laws, a Department of E-Governance and financial autonomy for Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies.
The Commission advocated cooperative federalism, restraint in the use of emergency powers and better Centre-State coordination.

secs.t: Reports → relevance to federal governance

x: The Fifth Report dealt with Public Order, the Sixth with Local Governance, the Seventh with Capacity Building for Conflict Resolution and the Fifteenth with State and District Administration.
Department-related Standing Committees examine the Demands for Grants and Bills of the concerned Ministries.
Centre-State questions involving police, education and the Inter-State Council usually come before the Department-related Standing
Committee on Home Affairs

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The First ARC study team reported in 1969, the Sarkaria Commission functioned during 1983–88, the Inter-State Council was set up in 1990 on Sarkaria’s advice, and the Punchhi Commission functioned during 2007–10.
The committee stated that Indian federalism needs a structural reset comparable in ambition to the economic reforms of 1991.

rows.title: Cooperative and competitive federalism - NITI Aayog, GST Council, state rankings
sub: Group-II M1-B-71: Cooperative and competitive federalism - NITI Aayog, GST Council and inter-state institutions

secs.t: Federalism — definitions, types and FIRSTs

x: NITI Aayog uses the expression “marble-cake federalism” for cooperative federalism, in which the Centre and States work together through a bottom-up approach.
The
SDG India Index
, released by NITI Aayog, tracks States and Union Territories on the Sustainable Development Goals and encourages competitive federalism.
NITI Aayog follows a bottom-up approach in which credible village-level plans are formulated and aggregated at higher levels of government, unlike the top-down Planning Commission model.

secs.t: NITI Aayog and its predecessors — how established, status and composition

x: NITI Aayog is a non-constitutional and non-statutory advisory think tank established through a Union Cabinet resolution.

The Planning Commission was created by a Cabinet resolution in 1950; the National Development Council by an executive resolution in 1952; and NITI Aayog by a Union Cabinet resolution on 1 January 2015 with advisory status.

secs.t: NITI Aayog and its predecessors — how established, status and composition — NITI Aayog composition

x: Ashok Kumar Lahiri
became Vice-Chairperson of NITI Aayog in April 2026, replacing Suman K. Bery.
At the eleventh meeting, the Prime Minister spoke on AI safeguards, El Nino and cooperative federalism, while N. Chandrababu Naidu presented Swarna Andhra @2047.
The Governing Council includes the Chief Ministers of Union Territories having legislatures:
Delhi, Jammu and Kashmir, and Puducherry

secs.t: NITI Aayog — functions, hubs and mandate

x: Exam angle: "Team India Hub" is the hub that leads State engagement.

Knowledge and innovation corresponds to innovation-related work; NITI for States covers cooperative and competitive federalism; transformational change concerns transformative policy action; and monitoring and evaluation is associated with DMEO.
NITI Aayog has two hubs: the
Team India Hub
, which leads State engagement with the Centre (APPSC-GS 2018), and the Knowledge and Innovation Hub, its think-tank arm.

secs.t: Chief Ministers → sub-groups and roles (2015)

x: Exam angle:
Digital payments
is the odd one out among the CM sub-groups.
Rationalisation of Centrally Sponsored Schemes
was one of the three 2015 sub-groups of Chief Ministers constituted by NITI Aayog.
The digital-payments committee was set up in 2016 and was convened by N. Chandrababu Naidu.
The 2015 sub-group divided CSS into
core of the core, core and optional
schemes.

secs.t: Articles, Acts and institutions of Centre-State cooperation

x: The suggested measures include revisiting CSS, increasing the role of States in GST design and holding regular Inter-State Council meetings.
The GST Council is generally cited as a model of cooperative federalism, whereas NITI Aayog rankings encourage competitive federalism.
The GST subsumed many local taxes, thereby curtailing several State taxation powers, and compensation disputes emerged between the Centre and States.

secs.t: State rankings — index → publisher and AP's position

x: State rankings in areas such as SDG, health and fiscal health foster competitive federalism while also encouraging intergovernmental cooperation.
Performance competition and rankings encourage States to improve social and developmental indicators, thereby supporting sustainable development.
The State Business Reform Action Plan rankings are associated with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (
DPIIT
The School Education Quality Index is associated with NITI Aayog with MHRD, not with the Institute for Competitiveness alone.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A criticism is that
some States skip Centre-State meetings
, weakening regular intergovernmental coordination.
Andhra Pradesh was showcased for
Real Time Governance and AI-enabled tools such as AWARE
Andhra Pradesh contributes approximately 70 percent of India’s shrimp exports, a factor associated with its EPI ranking.

rows.title: Devolution of powers and finances to local levels - Finance Commission and State Finance Commission transfers
sub: Group-II M1-B-99: Finances of local bodies - own revenue, devolution and the State Finance Commission of AP

secs.t: Decentralisation and devolution — terms → meaning

x: Democratic decentralisation involves elected local bodies, whereas delegation or deconcentration keeps functions within the administrative bureaucracy; therefore; .
Vertical devolution divides the divisible pool between the Union and States, while horizontal devolution distributes the States' share among the States.
Vertical fiscal imbalance arises because the Centre controls more buoyant taxes, while States bear major expenditure responsibilities such as health, education, agriculture and police.

secs.t: Articles → local body powers and finances

x: The 73rd Amendment provided constitutional status, a three-tier structure, direct elections, a five-year term and reservation for Panchayati Raj institutions.
Property tax is a major own-source revenue of Panchayats, and their power to levy taxes, duties, tolls and fees depends on authorisation by the State Legislature under Article 243H.
Article 243X is the municipal equivalent of Article 243H and concerns the power of Municipalities to levy taxes and the constitutionally related financial provisions.

secs.t: Sources of Panchayat revenue

x: Assigned taxes are State-levied taxes handed over to Panchayats; shared taxes are shared according to the State Finance Commission; State Consolidated Fund grants relate to Article 243H and SFC recommendations; Union Finance Commission grants arise under Article 280.
Property tax, also called house tax, is the principal own-source revenue of Gram Panchayats.

secs.t: Finance Commissions → chairs and vertical shares

x: 13th – 14th – 15th FC.

secs.t: Horizontal devolution — criteria weights, 13th to 16th FC, and AP

x: The Thirteenth Finance Commission assigned 47.5 per cent to income distance, termed fiscal capacity distance by that Commission.
Income distance
received the highest weight under the Fifteenth Finance Commission, at 45 per cent.

secs.t: Horizontal devolution — criteria weights, 13th to 16th FC, and AP — 16th FC changes

x: Exam angle: "highest weight" and "new criterion" questions for each FC.
The contribution to GDP criterion uses the square root of a State's GSDP divided by the sum of the square roots of the GSDPs of the States.
Andhra Pradesh's above-average per capita income works against it because the income-distance criterion gives greater weight to States with lower per capita GSDP.

secs.t: Horizontal devolution — criteria weights, 13th to 16th FC, and AP — Effect on AP

x: Uttar Pradesh had 17.619 per cent, while Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu had 4.217, 4.131 and 4.097 per cent respectively.

secs.t: Finance Commission grants to local bodies — data

x: Exam angle: the 14th FC split is 90:10 for GPs and 80:20 for municipalities (the 2019 question's key); panchayat total
Rs 2,00,292 crore
The Fourteenth Finance Commission used a 90:10 basic-performance ratio for Gram Panchayats, 80:20 for Municipalities, and distributed grants using 2011 population and area in a 90:10 ratio.
The Fifteenth Finance Commission attached performance-linked conditions such as
audited accounts and property-tax floor rates

secs.t: Schemes, reforms and audit bodies → features

x: AMRUT 2.0 rewards progress in property-tax reform and the mobilisation of resources through municipal bonds.
SVAMITVA drone mapping helps create a baseline for rural properties, which can support the development of rural property-tax systems.
Weak accrual accounting and the absence of credit ratings keep most local bodies outside the municipal bond market.
CAG Technical Guidance and Support over local-body audits was recommended by the
Eleventh Finance Commission

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The end of revenue-deficit grants has prompted criticism described as the “
tyranny of the base year
Only duly constituted local bodies qualify for the relevant Sixteenth Finance Commission grants, making local elections important; approximately ₹12,150 crore is at stake.
Tied grants may restrict local priority-setting, and the annual urban local-body transfer of about ₹75,000 crore has been viewed as small compared with urban GDP.

rows.title: Challenges in local devolution - funds, functions, functionaries; parallel bodies and capacity gaps
sub: Group-II M1-B-96: Implementation gaps - funds, functions, functionaries, parallel bodies and capacity

secs.t: 3Fs and key terms → meaning

x: Functions are subjects transferred to local bodies, funds are untied money matching those functions, functionaries are staff answerable to the local body, and the Eleventh Schedule contains 29 Panchayat subjects.
The standard finding is that functions exist on paper, funds are commonly tied to schemes, and functionaries continue to report to State line departments.
When local bodies lack adequate untied funds and control over personnel, PRIs are reduced largely to
implementing agencies

secs.t: Articles → devolution provisions

x: The Schedules do not themselves transfer subjects automatically; Articles 243G and 243W use the discretionary expression 'may' for devolution.
The State Election Commission and the constitutional five-year term, with elections before expiry or within six months of dissolution, made local government a permanent institution after 1993.
Article 243D
provides the constitutional floor of one-third reservation for women in Panchayats.

secs.t: Funds — own-source revenue and FC transfers (data)

x: Property tax
is the main own-source revenue of ULBs, although it remains under-assessed and under-collected.
Weak own-source revenue and outdated property registers make local bodies dependent on tied grants.
Weak balance sheets prevent most ULBs from accessing the municipal bond market effectively.
The urban share rises to 45%, the division is 80% basic and 20% performance, and 50% of basic grants are tied to sanitation and water.

secs.t: Parallel bodies and bureaucratic control → effect

x: DRDAs, user groups, SHGs and MPLADS/MLA LADS
were identified as arrangements that bypass elected local bodies.
State-appointed parastatals and SPVs may
bypass citizen participation and elected local bodies
by operating outside the regular local-government framework.
Janmabhoomi committees operated during 2014-19, while village and ward secretariats and volunteers were introduced in 2019; both were criticised as parallel to gram panchayats and wards.

secs.t: Local body elections and SFCs — conditions and AP status

x: The Cabinet decision included 34% BC reservation in rural local bodies, 33⅓% in urban local bodies, and direct elections for Mayors and municipal chairpersons.
The conditions include properly constituted local bodies, published audited accounts and timely State Finance Commissions.

secs.t: Elected women representatives — issues and responses

x: A male relative exercises power in the elected woman's name.
Sashakt Panchayat Netri Abhiyan and Model Women-Friendly Gram Panchayats are stated responses.

secs.t: Capacity-building schemes and institutions → features

x: RGSA was introduced to strengthen Panchayati Raj Institutions and enable them to contribute to the achievement of
Sustainable Development Goals
RGSA promotes convergence with Mission Antyodaya, focuses on 117 aspirational districts and also covers areas outside Part IX.
EGramSwaraj was launched along with SVAMITVA on 24 April 2020; SVAMITVA is implemented by the Survey of India; and it gives a 'Record of Rights' for rural homes plus a property-tax baseline.

secs.t: Committees, reports and the Devolution Index

x: The Ministry of Panchayati Raj advisory committee, whose report was issued in 2025, was chaired by former secretary
Sushil Kumar
The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended a Local Body Ombudsman in its Sixth Report, titled Local Governance, published in 2007.
The Roadmap identifies weak 3F devolution, bureaucratic control, tied funds, dependence on grants and reluctance to tax.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The criticism is that PRIs function mainly as implementing agencies rather than planning units, while parallel bodies such as Janmabhoomi committees and secretariats may further reduce their institutional centrality.
The 16th Finance Commission (2026-31) raised the urban share of local-body grants from 36% to
(about ₹3.6 lakh crore for ULBs against ₹4.4 lakh crore for rural local bodies).

rows.title: Election Commission of India - composition, appointment (2023 Act), powers and functions
sub: Group-II M1-B-48: Election Commission of India - composition, powers and functions

secs.t: ECI — status, composition, FIRSTs and landmark dates — Status

x: The CEC and the other Election Commissioners have equal powers, and differences are resolved by majority decision.
The President may appoint Regional
Election Commission
ers after consulting the Election Commission.
The India International Institute of Democracy and Election Management (IIIDEM), New Delhi, is the training arm of the Election Commission of India.

secs.t: ECI — status, composition, FIRSTs and landmark dates — From single-member to multi-member body

x: Two Election Commissioners were added in 1989 after the 61st Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years.
Decisions are governed by the majority rule and the CEC does not possess an absolute veto over every decision.
The Election Commission of India was set up on
25 January 1950
, a day before the Constitution came into force; this date is observed as National Voters' Day since 2011.

secs.t: Persons → roles and contributions

x: T.N. Seshan
, the tenth CEC, is associated with major election reforms, enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct and Elector Photo Identity Cards.

secs.t: Articles → provisions on elections

x: Article 324(1) covers elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President.
Election petitions concerning Parliament or State Legislatures are tried by the High Court, and an appeal lies to the Supreme Court.

Article 329(a) concerns the bar on challenges to delimitation and seat allotment, Article 329(b) requires an election petition, and Article 71 covers disputes regarding Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections.

secs.t: Acts, cases and committees on the ECI

x: Article 324 operates as a reservoir where no law holds the field; it cannot ordinarily override an existing law governing the matter.
The Supreme Court upheld the multi-member structure and majority rule in
T.N. Seshan v. Union of India

Until Parliament enacted a law, the Constitution Bench directed selection by a panel comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition or leader of the largest opposition party in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India.
Before the interim mechanism laid down in Anoop Baranwal, the President appointed the CEC and ECs on the advice of
the Prime Minister alone

secs.t: Appointment, tenure, salary and removal

x: The Search Committee is headed by the Law Minister, has two Secretary-rank or above members, and shortlists five names.
The Selection Committee may choose names outside the shortlist prepared by the Search Committee.
An eligible person must hold or have held a post equivalent to Secretary to the Government of India and possess election-management experience.

secs.t: Appointment, tenure, salary and removal — Tenure, salary, removal

x: The CEC is removable like a Supreme Court judge for proven misbehaviour or incapacity.
The motion requires the signatures of at least 100 members in the Lok Sabha or 50 members in the Rajya Sabha.
The CEC and ECs receive equal salaries on a par with a Supreme Court judge.

secs.t: Appointment, tenure, salary and removal — Constitutional gaps (listed flaws)

x: The Constitution does not prescribe qualifications or a fixed term for members of the Election Commission.
The Constitution does not expressly bar retiring Election Commissioners from further government appointment.

secs.t: Powers and functions — administrative, quasi-judicial, advisory — Administrative

x: The Commission can cancel polls in cases such as
rigging or booth capturing
to protect the integrity of the electoral process.
The Model Code of Conduct is not a statute; it rests on Article 324 and applies from the announcement of the election schedule, as recognised in Harbans Singh Jalal (1997).

secs.t: Powers and functions — administrative, quasi-judicial, advisory — Quasi-judicial and advisory

x: Party recognition and symbol allotment are governed by the
Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968
, issued under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and Article 324.
The Election Commission decides disputes concerning political parties and election symbols and advises on disqualification.
The Election Commission cannot review an election result; challenges must follow the election-petition route.

secs.t: State machinery — Chief Electoral Officer vs State Election Commission

x: The Chief Electoral Officer is the state-level officer under the ECI; the SEC conducts local-body elections; the Collector serves as District Election Officer/District Returning Officer; and the ECI conducts Parliamentary and State Legislative elections.
The Chief Electoral Officer is removed by the Election Commission, whereas the State Election Commissioner enjoys protection comparable to that of a High Court judge.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court described the CJI's place as temporary pending legislation, while the petitions challenge the 2:1 government majority in the Selection Committee.

The Commission's dependence on these ministries and its limited authority over internal party democracy and party finances have generated criticism, including the demand for charging its expenses on the Consolidated Fund.

rows.title: Elections - delimitation, model code of conduct, EVM-VVPAT, NOTA, election petitions
sub: Group-II M1-B-76: Elections in India - the electoral system, first-past-the-post, delimitation and reservation of seats
Group-II M1-B-77: Election Commission's powers; the Model Code of Conduct and election machinery

secs.t: Elections — definitions, types and FIRSTs — Electoral systems

x: A general election is held at the normal end of a legislature’s term, a mid-term election follows premature dissolution, and a by-election fills a single vacancy, ordinarily within six months.
Difficulty for voters, fragmentation, unstable governments, expense, absence of by-elections and a weaker voter–MP link are cited concerns.
The security deposit is forfeited if the candidate obtains less than
one-sixth of the valid votes

secs.t: Elections — definitions, types and FIRSTs — Key terms

x: Article 81(2) embodies uniformity of representation, while Articles 82 and 170 provide the constitutional basis for readjustment of Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies.
India's first general election was held in 1951-52 (the 1st Lok Sabha is dated 1952); it and the next three (1957, 1962, 1967) were held simultaneously with Assembly polls.

secs.t: Constitutional Articles on elections → provisions

x: Article 325 provides for one general electoral roll and prohibits exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
Panchayat and municipal polls are run by the State Election Commissions under Articles 243K (panchayats) and 243ZA (municipalities), not by the ECI.
Article 326 permits voting by citizens aged 18 or above subject to disqualifications such as non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime and corrupt or illegal practice.
The
61st Amendment Act, 1988
amended Article 326 to lower the voting age from 21 to 18 (in force 1989).

secs.t: Delimitation — Articles, Commissions and Amendments — Basis

x: The Delimitation Acts were enacted in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002, while the Commissions were constituted in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002.
The Commission is constituted under parliamentary legislation and works with the ECI.
Delimitation Commission orders enjoy finality: they cannot be challenged in court or modified by the Lok Sabha or State Legislative Assemblies.

secs.t: Delimitation — Articles, Commissions and Amendments — Amendments → effect on seats

x: ST seats are concentrated in areas with the highest ST population share, SC seats are spread and rotated at delimitation, and reserved constituencies have a common electorate of all voters.
The
104th Amendment
(Act of 2019, in force January 2020) extended SC/ST seat reservation under Article 334 to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination.

secs.t: Delimitation — Articles, Commissions and Amendments — Lok Sabha seat numbers

x: The resolution proposed women’s reservation from 2029 without linking it to delimitation.
The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats against a ceiling of 550, comprising 530 seats for States and 20 for Union Territories in the stated allocation framework.
The per-State Lok Sabha seat numbers have remained unchanged since 1976.

secs.t: Reserved constituencies → States and seats

x: Andhra Pradesh has 4 SC and 1 ST Lok Sabha seats and 29 SC and 7 ST Assembly seats.

secs.t: RPA sections → content — RPA 1950 vs RPA 1951

x: The Representation of the People Act, 1950 deals with allocation of seats, delimitation and electoral rolls.
Sections 19 and 21 belong to the 1950 Act, while Sections 8 and 77–78 belong to the 1951 Act.

secs.t: RPA sections → content — Sections → content

x: Section 126A prohibits conducting or publishing exit polls from the commencement of polling in the first phase until half an hour after polling closes in the last phase.
Opinion polls are barred during the 48 hours before the close of poll under Section 126, while Section 126A governs the longer phase-to-phase restriction on exit polls.

secs.t: RPA sections → content — Electoral rolls

x: The Bihar Special Intensive Revision removed about 70 lakh names, and the turnout that followed was reported as the highest since Independence.
The four qualifying dates are 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October.
A Special Intensive Revision rebuilds the electoral roll, whereas summary revision is conducted annually.

secs.t: Cases → holdings on elections

x: In PUCL v Union of India on 27 September 2013, the Supreme Court directed that a NOTA button be provided on all EVMs.
NOTA has no electoral effect on the result.

secs.t: Election machinery — officers → role

x: The DEO at district level is usually the Collector.
Judicial observer
is not among them.
The Election Commission controls officers on poll duty and may transfer them or act against partisan conduct.

secs.t: Party recognition — criteria and delisting

x: Recognition is governed by the Election Symbols Order, 1968, whereas registration of political parties is under
Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951

All three are alternative criteria (any one suffices) under the Election Symbols Order, 1968: State-party recognition in 4 or more States; 6% of valid votes in 4 States plus 4 Lok Sabha seats; or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least 3 States.

secs.t: Model Code of Conduct — status, timeline and Part VII

x: The sequence is 1960 drafting by Kerala, 1968 formalisation by the ECI, 1974 revision, and 1979 addition of Part VII.
Part VII (party in power) bars combining official visits with electioneering, using official machinery or transport, and announcing new schemes or grants once polls are announced (options A, B, C).
Sanctions for MCC violations range from censure up to suspension or withdrawal of recognition under Paragraph 16A of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.

secs.t: Voter facilitation — apps, campaigns, polling measures

x: SVEEP promotes voter education and turnout; cVIGIL reports Model Code violations; Saksham assists voters with disabilities; and Voter Helpline provides registration, correction, search and complaint services.
The NETA app allows voters to rate their representatives and was built by a private start-up, not conceptualised by the Election Commission of India.
cVIGIL enables citizens to report Model Code violations using geo-tagged photographs or videos, with action envisaged within 100 minutes.
The measures include a 1,200-elector cap, mobile-deposit facilities, colour candidate photographs on EVMs and candidate booths just beyond 100 metres from polling stations.

secs.t: Postal ballot and indelible ink

x: The senior-citizen threshold for the absentee-voter postal ballot category is 85 years or above, raised from 80 years.

Postal ballot covers service voters, special voters, electors on election duty and those in preventive detention; absentee voters include seniors aged 85+, persons with 40%+ benchmark disability and essential-service staff on duty.
Indelible election ink is manufactured by Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd and is based on silver nitrate.

secs.t: Election petitions — sections, court, grounds, offences

x: All four circumstances are recognised grounds under Section 100 for declaring an election void, subject to the statutory requirements concerning their effect on the election result where applicable.
From 1 July 2024, electoral offences such as bribery, undue influence and personation are placed in Chapter IX of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Sections 169–177.
Section 80 contains the election-petition bar, Section 80A specifies the High Court, Section 81 prescribes 45 days, and Section 100 lists grounds for declaring an election void.

secs.t: Lok Sabha general elections → year

x: Count:
general elections so far;
18th Lok Sabha
elected in
Key:
APPSC 2019 answer was 17 (correct then)

secs.t: Universal angles

x: EVM was first used at Parur in 1982, while VVPAT was first used at Noksen in 2013 and NOTA was first used in a Lok Sabha general election in 2014.
The Bill proposed increasing the Lok Sabha ceiling from 550 to 850 and conducting delimitation on the 2011 Census.
Southern States fear that population-based delimitation would transfer political representation towards more populous States such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan.
The Election Commission was constituted in 1950, is a permanent independent constitutional body, and its IIIDEM provides training to election managers.

rows.title: Electoral reforms - state funding, electoral bonds, criminalisation of politics, RPA 1951 provisions
sub: Group-II M1-B-78: Electoral reforms - committee recommendations, criminalisation of politics, money power
Group-II M1-B-79: Electoral reforms - state funding, electoral bonds, EVM-VVPAT and proposals such as simultaneous elections

secs.t: Committees and reports → recommendations — Electoral-reform committees → subject

x: Exam angle: match committee → subject (APPSC 2025: Indrajit Gupta = electoral reforms; APPSC-G2 2023 matching Vohra/Gupta/Goswami/Verma); Vohra = crime-politics nexus is the most repeated pair.
The J.S. Verma Committee dealt with
criminal-law reform concerning sexual offences
and also urged restrictions on candidates charged with such offences.
The Law Commission's 255th Report (2015) recommended totalisers, which pool the count of several control units so booth-wise voting patterns stay hidden.

secs.t: Committees and reports → recommendations — State funding recommendations

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT on Centre-State relations?" The answer is the
Indrajit Gupta Committee
The
Indrajit Gupta Committee
(1998) dealt with state funding of elections (an electoral reform), so it is the odd one out (APPSC-G2 2025, UPPSC 2015).
The Law Commission considered full state funding desirable only if political parties were barred from receiving funds from other sources.

secs.t: RPA 1951 sections → content — Key sections

x: Section 8 concerns disqualification on conviction, Section 29A registration of political parties, Section 33A criminal-antecedent disclosure, and Section 123 corrupt practices.
Section 123 covers corrupt practices such as bribery, undue influence and appeals based on religion or caste.
Section 126A
of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 concerns the ban on exit polls.

secs.t: RPA 1951 sections → content — Contesting from more than one constituency - Section 33(7)

x: Under Section 70 of the Representation of the People Act, the candidate must vacate one seat within
14 days
after being elected from both constituencies.
The Law Commission proposed the principle of one candidate, one seat, while the Election Commission proposed that a candidate vacating a seat should bear the cost of the by-election.
The 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies, increased security deposits, and required more proposers for independents and unrecognised parties.

secs.t: Cases → holdings on electoral reform

x: Ramesh Dalal v. Union of India held that a sitting MP or MLA convicted and sentenced to imprisonment of two years or more is barred from contesting elections.
In
Subramanian Swamy v ECI
(2013), the Supreme Court held that VVPAT was needed for free and fair polls and required phased introduction.
The 2019 decision raised the random VVPAT-EVM tally from
one to five polling stations per Assembly segment

secs.t: Criminalisation of politics — disclosure, data, reforms

x: A PIL seeking a lifetime ban on convicted legislators is pending, while 12 special courts have been established for cases involving MPs and MLAs.

secs.t: Money power — expenditure limits, donations, electoral bonds — Candidate expenditure limits

x: The limits concern candidates, exclude the travel expenses of 20 star campaigners, and are fixed under Rule 90.
Failure to comply with the expenditure-account requirements can lead to disqualification by the
Election Commission of India
The perceived loophole is that Section 77 caps candidate expenditure while not imposing a comparable ceiling on the parties’ own election spending.

secs.t: Money power — expenditure limits, donations, electoral bonds — Party donations - cash limits and evasion

x: The stated conditions include no cash donation above ₹2,000 and maintenance of records for donations above ₹20,000.
Evasion may occur by splitting large gifts into amounts below ₹20,000 and by diverting money through surrogate digital advertisements and paid news.
Only a registered political party that had secured at least 1% of the votes in the last election could encash electoral bonds.

secs.t: Money power — expenditure limits, donations, electoral bonds — ADR v Union of India, 15 Feb 2024 (Association for Democratic Reforms v Union of India)

x: A five-judge Constitution Bench unanimously struck down the scheme and directed SBI to provide donor data to the ECI.
The cited assessment stated that 60% of party funds during 2004–2023 came from undisclosed sources, amounting to ₹19,083 crore.
The five-judge bench unanimously held that donor anonymity violated voters' right to information, part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

secs.t: State funding of elections — types, models, debate

x: State funding may be full or partial and may be in cash or in kind.
Curbing black money and quid-pro-quo funding is an argument for.
The Supreme Court described elimination of black money from elections as a core responsibility of
the Election Commission of India
The National Election Fund is envisaged as an IPL-style pooling mechanism linked to vote share.

secs.t: EVM, VVPAT, NOTA and RVM — FIRSTs and features — FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: "first" statements. Parur 1982 = first use; Goa 1999 = first whole State; 2004 = all-India.
EVMs were first piloted at 70-Parur in Kerala in 1982 and were used universally in the 2004 Lok Sabha election.
VVPAT was first used in the 2013 by-election to the 51-Noksen Assembly constituency in Nagaland, after the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961 were amended.

secs.t: EVM, VVPAT, NOTA and RVM — FIRSTs and features — EVM - manufacturers and capacity

x: BEL, Bengaluru, and ECIL, Hyderabad, are the two public sector undertakings that manufacture EVMs.
M2 EVMs support four ballot units and 64 candidates; an M3 control unit can take up to 24 ballot units and accommodate 384 candidates including NOTA.
The Supreme Court refused to order a return to paper ballots in ADR v ECI (2024).

secs.t: EVM, VVPAT, NOTA and RVM — FIRSTs and features — VVPAT - working and verification

x: The voter views the slip through the VVPAT window; it is not handed over to the voter.
VVPAT slips are required to be counted wherever the EVM data and Form 17C do not match.
Postal ballots are counted before the penultimate EVM/VVPAT round; the final EVM/VVPAT round follows subsequently.
The VVPAT generations are M1, M2 and M3; M3 is the current generation.

secs.t: EVM, VVPAT, NOTA and RVM — FIRSTs and features — Remote voting machine and totalisers

x: The ECI's RVM prototype is intended to enable domestic migrants to vote for up to 72 constituencies from one remote polling station.

The ECI objected that neither the RPA nor the Conduct of Election Rules provides a legal framework, and that pooling would make booth- and machine-wise checks involving EVMs, VVPATs and Form 17C harder.

secs.t: One Nation One Election — Kovind Committee, 129th Amendment Bill — Background and debate

x: Both the 170th Report and the 2018 draft report supported simultaneous elections, and simultaneous Lok Sabha–Assembly polls were held from 1951-52 to 1967.
Ex-President Kovind chaired it, and its members included Amit Shah, Ghulam Nabi Azad, N.K. Singh, Subhash C. Kashyap, Harish Salve and Sanjay Kothari.
The criticisms identified are that simultaneous elections may weaken federalism and require huge numbers of EVMs and forces.

secs.t: One Nation One Election — Kovind Committee, 129th Amendment Bill — Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024

x: The Bill proposes amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327.
Article 356 concerns President's Rule, not appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner.
The 129th Amendment Bill (introduced December 2024, referred to a JPC) aims at simultaneous Lok Sabha and Assembly elections (APPSC 2024 key); it inserts Art 82A and amends Arts 83, 172 and 327.

secs.t: Acts and reforms chronology — 1982 to 2025

x: EPIC was introduced in 1993, and its number remains valid for life despite a change of address.
The correct sequence is 61st Amendment and voting-age reduction in 1988, EPIC in 1993, nationwide EVM use in 2004, and VVPAT/NOTA in 2013.
The 2023 Act provides for a panel comprising the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Election Commission delisted 808 RUPPs and capped the number of electors per polling station at 1,200.
State funding, disqualification on framing of charges and a party spending cap are identified as unfinished agendas.
The expression refers to the use of
muscle power
and its adverse effect on trust in legislatures.

x: Exam angle: the party founded by Ambedkar is the
Republican Party of India
. BSP was founded in
by
Kanshi Ram
, and AAP in
BSP was founded by Kanshi Ram (1984); A.B. Vajpayee was the first president of the BJP (1980); Mulayam Singh Yadav founded the Samajwadi Party (1992); Sharad Pawar founded the NCP (1999).

x: FIRST presidents:
INC
W.C. Bonnerjee;

Sequence:

→ Forward Bloc (1939) →

secs.t: Splits and mergers → parent and year

x: The Janata Party was formed in 1977 through the merger of Congress (O), Jana Sangh, the Bharatiya Lok Dal and the Socialists.
The Janata Dal was formed on 11 October 1988 through the merger of
Jan Morcha, Congress(S), Janata and Lok Dal
In the 2023 split the Ajit Pawar faction kept the NCP name, which the top court upheld, while Sharad Pawar's group became the NCP-SP (Sharadchandra Pawar).

secs.t: Leaders → party

x: N. Chandrababu Naidu is associated with the Telugu Desam Party, not the Samajwadi Party.

Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao and others were associated with the Andhra Swaraj Party (1934); Puchalapalli Sundarayya was secretary of the Andhra Communist Party at Kakinada (1936); Madduri Annapurnayya was the first Andhra leader in the Forward Bloc (1939).
M.N. Roy was associated with the
Radical Democratic Party

secs.t: Party system — phases, social bases and terms

x: The TDP rapidly gained power by mobilising the sentiment of “
Telugu atma gauravam
”, or Telugu self-respect.
The Congress system covered 1952–77, the transition and first alternation 1977–89, the coalition era 1989–2014 and the BJP majority phase began in 2014.
The Kamaraj Plan of 1963 had senior Congress ministers resign to strengthen the party organisation.

secs.t: Acts, sections, cases and committees on parties

x: The party constitution must pledge allegiance to the Constitution and to socialism, secularism, democracy and national integrity.
Political parties entered the constitutional framework through the Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment in 1985.
The decision restricted the Election Commission's deregistration power, while recognising exceptions involving fraud, loss of allegiance and a party being declared unlawful.

secs.t: Recognition and classification — symbols, State party criteria, RUPPs

x: Recognised parties receive reserved symbols.
The list may change after successive Election Commission reviews.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Telugu Desam Party was founded by NTR in 1982 and represents a textbook regional party, while the YSRCP emerged from a Congress split in 2011.

The Janata Party formed the first non-Congress (and first coalition) government under Morarji Desai in 1977; NTR founded the TDP in 1982; the 1989 election began the coalition era that lasted until 2014; the YSRCP came from a Congress split in 2011.

rows.title: Party system in India - one-party dominance, multi-party and coalition eras
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-55

secs.t: Party system — definitions, types and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: "first non-Congress government" = 1977 (not 1989, which was the first non-Congress coalition of the multi-party era).
A two-party system generally presumes one dominant axis of political or social division, unlike India’s multiple cleavages.
The Janata Party government of 1977 was the first non-Congress government at the Centre and was stable initially because it possessed a Lok Sabha majority.

secs.t: Scholars → terms on one-party dominance

x: From 1952 to 1977, Congress governed at the Centre and in most States as an umbrella accommodating diverse interests within itself.

Rajni Kothari coined 'Congress system' (1964); W.H. Morris-Jones described 'one-party dominance' (dominance co-existing with competition); Myron Weiner wrote Party Building in a New Nation on Congress as a party-building organisation.

secs.t: Elections → claims (1967, 1971, 1977, 1989)

x: Exam angle: match the election to the claim - 1967 (States), 1971, 1977 (Centre), 1989 (end of Congress system, multi-party era).
The
1989 Lok Sabha election
marked the end of the Congress system; Congress lost power, remained the single largest party, and chose to sit in opposition.
The APPSC 2007 key gives the fifth general election (1971): after the 1969 split, the umbrella Congress system gave way to Indira Gandhi's personalised politics.

secs.t: Coalition and minority governments → PMs and support

x: Chandra Shekhar
headed the Samajwadi Janata Party minority government from 1990 to 1991, with outside support from Congress.
The United Front governments during 1996–98 were headed successively by Deve Gowda and Gujral and received outside support from Congress.
The NDA government led by A.B. Vajpayee governed from 1998 to 2004 and involved parties that had no prior experience of working together; it governed for about six years.

secs.t: Data — Lok Sabha seats of major parties

x: 1989: INC 197 (largest), Janata Dal 143, BJP 85; 1996: BJP 161 (largest), INC 140; 1999: BJP 182, INC 114.
All three figures are correct for the Fourteenth Lok Sabha: Congress 145, BJP 138 and CPI(M) 43.
In 2014, BJP won 282 of the 543 Lok Sabha seats, marking the first single-party majority since 1984.

secs.t: States → party system pattern

x: The coalition governments formed in several States after the fourth general election were commonly known as
Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments
After 1967, rich and middle peasants defected from Congress, while Jana Sangh and Swatantra were among the parties that formed political fronts.
Except
Tamil Nadu
, where the DMK governed alone, almost every opposition-ruled State had a coalition after the 1967 elections.

secs.t: Consequences of coalition politics — effects

x: Coalition politics may promote consensus, but the need for compromise can slow decisions, cause policy reversals or delays, and dilute strong measures.
Coalition politics creates checks and balances because no single party ordinarily holds absolute power, while regional parties gain representation in national policy.
Defections and horse-trading led to the anti-defection law, introduced through the Tenth Schedule by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The multi-party era of 1989–2014 ended when the BJP won a majority on its own in the 2014 general election.
The Justice Party-era awakening of
non-Brahmin agrarian castes
laid the social base for regional parties in Andhra.
The stated distribution records the Bharatiya Janata Party as ruling alone in 11 States.

src: Sources: APP (Polity > Unit 9 The Party System; Recognition of National and State Parties); UPSC (Post Independence History pp.42, 66, 71; Indian Polity p.190); CDI (Block06 Impact of Coalition Governments; Block12 Justice Party); LENSD 11 Sep 2026; TH 12 Aug 2026, 11 Jun 2026, 2 May 2026

rows.title: Regional parties in India and in Andhra Pradesh - rise, role and impact
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-55

secs.t: Rise of regional parties — causes and roots

x: Identity, regional neglect and the failure of national parties to accommodate State leaders, plus post-1989 coalition arithmetic, explain their rise.
The identified roots of regionalism are historical, geographical, linguistic, religious and ethnic.
The Andhra non-Brahmin agrarian castes identified as becoming politically awakened during the Justice Party era were
Reddys, Kammas, Kapus and Velamas

secs.t: Regional parties → state, founder and year — Across India

x: The Shiromani Akali Dal was founded in Punjab in 1920, not 1985.
The DMK began with anti-Brahmin, anti-North and anti-Hindi positions and demanded
Dravidanadu
; it later scaled back these demands and formed the Tamil Nadu government in 1967 under Annadurai.
Shiv Sena mobilised around the idea of “Bombay for Maharashtrians” and the demand for jobs for the sons of the soil.

secs.t: Regional parties → state, founder and year — Other AP regional parties

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 keyed order
DMK, TDP, BSP, SP
The correct order is DMK (1949), Shiv Sena (1966), TDP (1982) and BSP (1984).
The sequence is AGP (1985), Samajwadi Party (1992), BJD and RJD (1997), TRS (2001), and YSRCP (2011).
The Lok Satta Party was founded by Jayaprakash Narayan in 2006, not Pawan Kalyan, so D is wrongly matched.

secs.t: Regional vs national parties — identify, states ruled

x: The cited sequence states that the BJP defeated BJD in Odisha in 2024, AAP in Delhi in 2025 and Trinamool Congress in West Bengal in 2026.

secs.t: Telugu Desam Party — founding and FIRSTs

x: NTR founded the TDP in 1982 on Telugu self-respect and it won power within nine months (January 1983).
N. T. Rama Rao served as Chief Minister during all three periods: 1983–84, 1984–89 and 1994–95.
With 30 seats in 1984, the TDP became the main opposition party in the Eighth Lok Sabha and was the first regional party to attain that position.

secs.t: Impact of regional parties — effects

x: Regional parties have acted as coalition kingmakers, supplied Speakers and Union Ministers, and provided votes necessary for government survival.
More genuine federal bargaining is linked to the period after 1989, when coalition politics increased the negotiating power of regional parties.
Regional parties can improve representation of backward regions and promote balanced development, but may also encourage parochialism and instability.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Vote share
is considered an important indicator of the extent of regional support, whereas seats alone may not fully reflect that support.
In Andhra Pradesh, the Telugu Desam Party leads the ruling coalition with support from the Bharatiya Janata Party.
Critics fear it would weaken regional parties.

rows.title: Recognition of national and state parties - criteria and the Symbols Order
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-55

secs.t: Laws, paragraphs and cases on registration and recognition

x: The Election Commission handles both processes: registration under Section 29A of the RPA, 1951, and recognition under the Election Symbols Order, 1968.
The ECI's deregistration power is limited and may arise in cases such as fraud, ceasing allegiance or an unlawful declaration.
Paragraph 16A empowers the ECI to suspend or withdraw recognition for defiance of the Model Code of Conduct.

secs.t: Registration — stages and conditions

x: The three relevant states are unregistered, registered but unrecognised—commonly referred to as an RUPP—and recognised.

secs.t: National party criteria — paragraph 6B of the Symbols Order

x: Exam angle: distractors use "2 or more States", "4% / 10% / 15% of votes" - all wrong; APPSC-G2 2025: every listed condition was valid, so the key was "None of the above".
The second route requires at least 6% of valid votes in four or more States at the last Lok Sabha or Assembly elections and at least four Lok Sabha seats.

secs.t: National parties — number, list and FIRSTs

x: The April 2023 review derecognised CPI, NCP and AITC and recognised AAP as a National Party.
The National People's Party (
NPP
), based in Meghalaya, was the first North-Eastern party to obtain National Party status.
DMK, Revolutionary Socialist Party, All India Forward Bloc and Peasants and Workers Party
are not National Parties in the classification referred to here.

secs.t: State party criteria — vote share and seat combinations

x: Routes 1 (6% + 2 Assembly seats) and 2 (6% in the Lok Sabha poll + 1 Lok Sabha seat) are valid.
The requirement is 3% of the Assembly seats or three seats, whichever is more.
A party may qualify by winning one Lok Sabha seat for every 25 Lok Sabha seats allotted to the State.

secs.t: Symbols — terms and recognition benefits

x: An RUPP can obtain a common symbol when it contests two Lok Sabha seats or 5% of the Assembly seats, subject to the applicable rules.
Recognised parties receive two free sets of electoral rolls, broadcast or telecast time on Akashvani and Doordarshan, and consultation by the ECI.
RUPPs must disclose donors giving above Rs 20,000, and any donation above Rs 2,000 must come by cheque or bank transfer.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: TDP and YSRCP are recognised State Parties in Andhra Pradesh; neither has National Party status.
The Trinamool rebel MPs chose a merger rather than pursuing a paragraph 15 symbol claim before the Election Commission.
Criticisms include prolonged factional litigation, allegations of bias, rising RUPP numbers and voter confusion arising from similar symbols.
